# The Mirror of Divine Wisdom

## Concerning the First Principles of the Soul

->**Introduction**<-

In the beginning of this inquiry, we must consider the nature of the human spirit as it relates to its Creator. As the <term>Philosopher<note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and early modern texts.</note></term> says, all men by nature desire to know. This desire is not a mere accident of our biology, but a <insert>divine</insert> spark placed within the vessel of the heart.

<margin>The soul is the image of the Eternal.</margin>

We must therefore distinguish between the three types of knowledge:
1. **Natural Knowledge**, which we gain through the senses.
2. **Rational Knowledge**, which we gain through the intellect.
3. **Revealed Knowledge**, which is granted by Grace alone. <gloss>This is the highest form.</gloss>

| Level of Soul | Faculty | Object of Study |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vegetative | Growth | The Body |
| Sensitive | Perception | The World |
| Rational | Reason | The Truth |

It is written in the sacred tongue, <note>original: "Berit Olam"</note> **An Everlasting Covenant**, that the truth shall remain even when the heavens grow old like a garment. We see this reflected in the <unclear>harmony</unclear> of the spheres, where each celestial body moves according to a law it did not write for itself. 

<column-break/>

As we transition from the general to the specific, let us look at the <term>Microcosm<note>The concept that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the structure of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note></term>. If the universe is a great book, then man is the summary of its chapters. 

<margin>See the works of the Great Master on this point.</margin>

We find in the Latin tradition the phrase <note>original: "Nosce te ipsum"</note> **Know thyself**, which serves as the gateway to all higher mysteries. Without this self-reflection, the student is like a traveler who seeks a distant city but has forgotten how to walk. 

*Note well:* The path is narrow, and many are the distractions of the flesh. <insert>But the reward is certain.</insert>

<summary>This page introduces the philosophical and theological framework of the manuscript, defining the levels of knowledge and the relationship between the human soul and the divine order. It establishes the "Microcosm" theory as a central theme for the upcoming chapters.</summary>
<keywords>soul, divine wisdom, Aristotle, microcosm, types of knowledge, self-knowledge, theology</keywords>

# Sire.

**W**hen *Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: "Lionardo da Vinci"</note> breathed his last breath in the arms of that great King *Francis* <note>Francis I of France (r. 1515–1547), who was Leonardo’s final patron.</note>, **Your** magnanimous *Predecessor*, I believe there was nothing for which he was so sorrowful as not having been able, due to the infirmity of old age, to offer him a testimony of his grateful soul for the kind benefits he had received from him. Therefore, by entitling this *Treatise* of his to **Your** Majesty, I am certain that I am fulfilling the will of this great man, whose spirit <note>original: "l'ombra," literally "the shadow" or "the shade."</note> seems to me to rejoice and applaud this thought of mine. *France*, by some unknown destiny, was the first to appreciate his writings, and as he

<summary>This page contains the opening of a formal dedication to the King of France, invoking the famous historical account of Leonardo da Vinci dying in the arms of King Francis I. The editor, Guglielmo Manzi, frames the publication of this treatise as the fulfillment of Leonardo's own unexpressed gratitude toward the French Crown.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Francis I, Louis XVIII, dedication, Treatise on Painting, France, royal patronage</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to King Louis XVIII by Guglielmo Manzi, following the narrative of Leonardo da Vinci's legacy moving from Italy to France.</meta>

poor and neglected in his own homeland, had taken refuge with **Your** August Ancestor, so too a portion of the present *Treatise*, neglected and ignored in Italy, was honorably brought to light there <note>Referring to the first printed edition of the Treatise on Painting, published in Paris in 1651.</note>. Now this Work, reordered and made whole through my care, comes into France and presents itself to **Your** Majesty; it can be said that in this alone, after such a long period of oblivion, has it experienced favorable fortune: that it is given to come to light under the powerful name of a philosopher King, a lover of pleasant studies, and a protector of every science and every art. Receive it, O Sire, with a benign disposition of soul, and grant also to me the supreme honor of giving you this public testimony of my true and profound veneration for **Your** Sacred Person, excited in me by nothing other than the fame of **Your** merits and **Your** virtues. And here I make an end, wishing to **Your** Majesty perpetual glory and happiness.

->Of Your Majesty<-

The Most Humble, Most Devoted, and Most Obedient Servant
GUGLIELMO MANZI. <note>Guglielmo Manzi (1784–1821) was an Italian scholar and librarian who discovered the "Codex Urbinas," the most complete manuscript of Leonardo's Treatise, in the Vatican Library.</note>

<meta>This page begins the formal preface "To the Readers" by Guglielmo Manzi, following his dedication to King Louis XVIII. It transitions from the political and royal context to the philosophical foundations of Leonardo da Vinci's work.</meta>

# GUGLIELMO MANZI

## LIBRARIAN OF THE BARBERINI LIBRARY <note>The Barberini Library was one of the most significant private collections in Rome, eventually incorporated into the Vatican Library.</note>

### TO THE READERS.

---

**The** discourse of reason was granted by God to men so that they alone might understand the secrets of nature, and according to its causes, might then philosophize; so that Aristotle does not wrongly instruct us at the beginning of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "metafisica"</note> that by natural instinct we desire wisdom. From this, therefore, it follows that our souls, being drawn to the admiration of the marvelous works of nature and art, give ourselves over to seeking their various causes. This research then leads us to possess wisdom, which according to Plato—a philosopher who raised his concepts higher than any other—is nothing other than the knowledge of things divine and human. This was divided by the ancient philosophers into two parts: namely, into speculation and operation, or rather into theory and practice. The goal of the first is the knowledge of truth, and of the second, the completion of the work. For this reason, we must consider as arrogant those who, paying no regard to these philosophical principles, attribute everything to their own judgment—not only in matters pertaining to civil life, but even in the contemplative considerations of the sciences. They oppose the most approved and wisest opinions, and lead themselves to believe that in the fine arts, and especially in painting, practice alone is sufficient to reach excellence. For besides this being manifestly contrary to the aforementioned principles, which are the primary foundations of every science and every art, it is also denied for other specific reasons by the wisest men; it appears, according to them, that the nobility of every science arises above all from two things: first from the subject, and then from the certainty of the demonstrations; meanwhile...

<summary>Guglielmo Manzi opens his preface by grounding the study of painting in classical philosophy, citing Aristotle and Plato to argue that art requires both theoretical wisdom and practical application. He critiques those who believe painting is merely a manual craft rather than a noble science based on rational principles.</summary>
<keywords>Guglielmo Manzi, Barberini Library, Aristotle, Plato, Metaphysics, theory and practice, philosophy of art, nobility of painting, scientific demonstration</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Readers" by Guglielmo Manzi. It transitions from the general philosophical definition of wisdom (theory vs. practice) to the specific application of these principles to the art of painting, emphasizing the necessity of mathematics and the historical progression from the Middle Ages to the early Renaissance.</meta>

...touching upon the fact that since the goal of painting is an ingenious imitation of nature, and since it contains within itself—just like all other sciences—various parts that are disjointed and uncomposed, this art can never be perfectly mastered if all these parts are not first demonstrated together. In doing this, great help is offered to us by mathematics, which the ancient Greeks and Latins, not without great and true reason, considered most excellent; by adapting these mathematical principles to the sciences and arts, they acquired through them the highest merit and honor. Nor is there any doubt that those great painters of Greece, whose fame and names alone have reached us, were quite expert in such disciplines. For although the course of the centuries has deprived us of their marvelous works, it nevertheless appears sufficiently clear—both through the records of writers and because we know for certain—that this art was noble, divine, and practiced by men of no common sort among those people. So it was also among our Latins <note>The author uses "Latins" to refer to the ancient Romans.</note>, until, through the unhappy turns of time and the extinction of the Roman Empire, it remained in Italy—along with every other noble discipline—forgotten and buried.

Through the genius and virtue of our Italians, it then began to revive in the **14th Century** <note>original: "Secolo XIV"</note>. And although those first good masters did not have the ancient Greek and Roman sculptures before their eyes, they nonetheless devoted themselves to a perfect imitation of nature and truth. One discerns in their figures such vitality and beauty that they are admired even among the most beautiful modern works. And if they erred somewhat in foreshortenings <term>scorci: the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth</term> and in the natural attitudes of the body, and even more so in perspective, those paintings conversely improve so much in their coloring and the expressions of the faces—in which the movements of the soul are seen expressed with admirable skill—that we could not, without the stain of ingratitude, deny to Giotto, Simone of Siena <note>Simone Martini (c. 1284–1344), a major figure in Sienese painting.</note>, Masaccio, Blessed Angelico <note>Fra Angelico (c. 1395–1455).</note>, and the remaining host of those first superior craftsmen the boast of having, as much as was then possible, well considered and better understood the disciplines of art. Once that disproportion and clumsiness, which the barbarism of the times had imposed upon them, was stripped away by these men, there still remained a void in this art: and this was precisely Philosophy, which, just as had happened among the Latins and Greeks, was destined to...

we come to its rescue, to elevate and direct imitation, and to discover and correct those defects that are sometimes encountered even in nature itself. This Philosophy has, however, been granted to very few craftsmen, and those who possess it can be called truly perfect, because art becomes richer in their hands; furthermore, learned craftsmen deserve greater praise and far more credit through their advice and writings than the simple words of those who—whether they practice the art well or poorly—know nothing of it other than the exercise of it. This truth was seen in **Leon Battista Alberti**, the Florentine; who, having applied himself to literature and perfectly understanding architecture, dictated the wisest instructions on the fine arts above any other of his century. Through these, it was recognized by craftsmen that mere practice in the arts was not enough, and that it was necessary to join to it the study of philosophy. Moved by this principle, the most intelligent men gave themselves over to investigating nature by means of philosophy, and by the completion of the **15th Century** <note>original: "Secolo XV"</note>, to the eternal glory of modern Italy, those men were already born and working who, in the fine arts, were destined to equal the fame of the most celebrated ancients. 

However, the one among these great men who was the most philosophical craftsman, and who, being versed in every study, proved excellent in all—making the most difficult secrets of every science and every art his own—was, without anyone disputing it, **Leonardo da Vinci**, the Florentine Painter and Sculptor. Not content that his discoveries in the art of painting should be useful to himself alone, he wrote for the common benefit an extensive <term>Treatise</term> <note>Referring to the *Trattato della pittura*, a collection of Leonardo's notes on art and science.</note>, which can be called the foundation and the principle of the art. The wandering life of the author in his final years, or perhaps his own nature—never satisfied with any work—were likely the reasons that, as it was never published while he lived, it remained thereafter unknown and buried until the year 1651. In that year, a part of it was drawn from the darkness and published in Paris by **Raffaele Du Fresne**. This edition proved most welcome to lovers of Painting, and because the edition was sold out due to the many requests that came from every place, another very similar edition was made in Naples in the year 1733, in which, except for the beauty of the printing, the paper, and the copperplate engravings, which are far su—

<meta>This page continues the bibliographic history of Leonardo da Vinci's "Treatise on Painting," detailing the various flawed editions published across Italy and the discovery of more complete manuscript sources.</meta>

<page-num>8</page-num>

superior to the Paris edition, they even copied the printing errors from it. After this Naples edition, which soon also became rare, another edition was repeated in Bologna similar to the previous ones, and another was published in Florence in the year 1792, in which, for the first time, the drawings copied from the original sketches by Leonardo appeared; therefore, this truncated part of the edition would not be despicable if it had been handled more accurately by the printer and the editor. Meanwhile, as taste grew among amateurs and craftsmen for this author, another edition was published again in the year 1804 in Milan, and another likewise came out in Perugia the following year; both of these editions exactly copied the old Parisian one, and only in this second one—to which various notes were added by the editor—were the drawings made on separate plates in unshaded outlines. While this Book appeared so truncated and mangled, it was nonetheless known to the editors themselves—from the citations of books and chapters frequently encountered in the work—that this Treatise was not entirely complete. This was demonstrated more clearly by a codex written on the first pages in the own hand of **Vincenzo Pinelli**, a man of letters who lived at the end of the 16th and the beginning of the 17th Century, in which it was titled: *Discourse on the Drawing of Leonardo da Vinci, Part Second.* Toward the middle of the past century, **Gori** <note>Anton Francesco Gori (1691–1757), a famous Florentine antiquarian.</note> had also affirmed in print that he had found among the codices of the **Etruscan Academy** a Manuscript with the following title: *Opinions of Leonardo da Vinci (containing) the method of painting perspectives, shadows, distances, heights, depths, from near and far, and other things, and precepts of painting.* And this, or one similar to it, is the very Book that **Benvenuto Cellini** <note>The famous Renaissance sculptor and goldsmith.</note> purchased for the price of fifteen gold scudi, and of which he makes honorable mention in his writings (1). Among the codices of the **Ambrosian Library** in Milan,

The first part of it seems not to have been unknown to Lomazzo, who, in addition to the Book of the <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: "notomìa," an archaic term for anatomy</note> of the horse—which he said was lost during the entry of the French into Milan—also affirmed that Leonardo had composed a Book in which he examined whether painting or sculpture is preferable. These, then, were the vague reports that existed regarding Vinci’s writings on painting, and only the history of them was known—which, to the great detriment of the arts, were lost almost immediately after the author's death (1); when through

---

(1) Notable for the history of these writings is the memoir left since the beginning of the 17th Century by Gianambrogio Mazzenta, which I report in its original form, hoping to do something pleasing to the lovers of such news. *“There came into my hands,” (he writes), “now 50 years ago, thirteen volumes by Leonardo da Vinci in folio and in quarto written in reverse <note>Leonardo’s famous "mirror writing"</note> and chance made them fall to me in the following manner. I was studying law at Pisa in the company of the young Aldo Manuzio, a great lover of books. A certain Lelio Gavardi of Asola, provost of San Zeno in Pavia and a close relative of Aldo, came to our house. He had been a master of polite letters in Milan in the house of the Melzi Lords, who are called 'of Vavero' (Vaprio) to distinguish this from other Melzi families of the same city. He had seen in their country house at Vaprio many drawings, instruments, and books by Leonardo. . . . . Francesco Melzi (his student and heir) had approached the manner of Vinci more than any other: he worked little because he was rich; but his paintings are well finished, and often confused with the works of the master. . . He, upon dying, left the works of Leonardo in his house at Vaprio to his sons, who, having different tastes and employments, neglected those treasures, and very soon dispersed them. Lelio Gavardi took from them what he pleased. He brought 13 volumes to Florence, hoping to obtain a good price for them from the Grand Duke Francesco, who was eager to acquire similar works; all the more so because Leonardo was highly esteemed in his homeland. But upon Gavardi's arrival in Florence, the prince died, wherefore he came to Pisa. I could not refrain from disapproving of his conduct: he blushed at it; and since I, having finished my studies there—”*

This Codex formerly belonged to the Library of the Dukes of Urbino, and passed with the rest of the Library of those Princes into this of the Vatican on the occasion—

<meta>The following block is the continuation of the Mazzenta memoir, detailing the specific fate of the thirteen volumes.</meta>

> *...of [Gavardi's] departure, as he had to return to Milan, he delivered the volumes of Vinci to me, praying me to restore them to the Melzi family. I loyally performed his commission, and returned everything to Dr. Orazio, head of the Melzi family, who was quite surprised that I had taken so much trouble; and he made me a gift of those books, telling me that he had many other drawings by the same author, neglected for a long time in a corner of his country house. Thus those books became mine, and later my brothers'. These brothers, boasting of such an acquisition made so easily, aroused the envy of other enthusiasts, who went to Dr. Orazio and obtained from him drawings, figures, anatomical preparations, and other precious remains from Leonardo's studio. One of those who obtained the most was Pompeo Aretino, son of the Knight Leoni, a pupil of Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo</note>, who was in the service of King Philip II of Spain, for whom he had made all the bronzes that are in the Escorial. Pompeo promised Dr. Melzi a seat in the Senate of Milan if he succeeded in recovering the thirteen volumes, wishing to offer them to King Philip, who was a lover of such curiosities. Flattered by this hope, Dr. Orazio went to my brother, begging him on his knees to return the gift he had made him; and since he was a colleague, friend, and benefactor, my brother returned seven of them. Of the other six that remained in the Mazzenta house, one was donated to Cardinal Federico Borromeo for the Ambrosian Library... Another was later given by my brother to Ambrogio Figini, who left it to his heir Ercole Bianchi with the rest of his studio. Due to the urgency expressed to me by the Duke of Savoy, I procured a third one for him as well. My brother having then died outside of Milan, the other three volumes also came into the hands of Pompeo Aretino, who joined other drawings and writings of Leonardo to them, and by separating the leaves, he formed a large volume <note>This refers to the famous Codex Atlanticus</note> which passed to his heir Polidoro Calchi, and was later sold to Mr. Galeazzo Arconati. This generous man still has it in his rich Library, having refused to sell it to the Duke of Savoy and to other princes who sought it.*

In this Barberini Library, under No. 3457, is preserved a neat Manuscript copied from Leonardo's originals with this title: *Leonardo da Vinci on the motion and measurement of waters.* (And at the end there is this note): *These are nine Books on the motion and measurement of water by Leonardo da Vinci, collected and ordered from various of his manuscripts by Friar Luigi Maria Arconati, Dominican Master of Sacred Theology, 1643.* This is perhaps a copy of the Originals generously donated by the Arconati Family to the Ambrosian Library as far back as the year 1637.

<page-num>II</page-num>
<header>II</header>

nor that by the death of Duke Francesco Maria della Rovere, the last of that family, those States were reunited with the Papal Domain <note>The Duchy of Urbino was incorporated into the Papal States in 1631</note>. It is written on paper in quarto format, and must be judged to be from the 16th Century. The handwriting is not bad, and only errs somewhat in spelling and in punctuation, which is entirely defective; the figures are drawn in pen and placed in their proper locations in the middle of the chapters. One encounters very rare little notes by the copyist, which I have placed in the present edition exactly as they stand in the Codex; I have not done this by chance, because from them one discerns his diligence and faithfulness. He must have been, without any doubt, a scholar of Vinci; and from the dialect he uses, it is evident that he was Lombard. Attributing the merit of this copy either to Francesco Melzi, or to Salai, or to another of his disciples, I believe we would not be far from the truth. However, whoever deserves such credit—for refinement of judgment, for diligence, and for excessive scrupulousness in not altering the author's mind in any point—deserves to be ranked alongside that much-celebrated Mannelli, thanks to whom we read Boccaccio correctly in his purity <note>A reference to the "Ottimo" manuscript of the Decameron copied by Francesco d'Amaretto Mannelli</note>. And it pleases me to prove this by reporting at the foot of the page a note that was not placed with the others in the Text, because it could have no place there, being a correction of an error made by the copyist himself (1). Furthermore, the drawings of this Codex, being copied from the author's original, must alone be held in high esteem and value; and it is a ridiculous thing that, for greater embellishment, these figures were given shading and invented by whim, as the painter Errard practiced in the Paris edition to the indignation of Poussin, who had drawn some of them, and where they were missing, imagined them from his own mind. When Poussin saw them so "dressed up," he affirmed that he no longer recognized those drawings because they had been spoiled by that painter (2). And <meta>catchword: And</meta>

When <term>Nicolas Poussin</term> resided in Rome, he often delighted in discussing painting with the Knight <term>Cassiano Dal Pozzo</term>, a man greatly devoted to Letters and the arts. Knowing of such a Manuscript in the <term>Barberini Library</term>, he had already taken a copy of it, and in their discussions, he communicated it to Poussin, who formed the sketches and drawings of the figures based upon it. In the year 1640, this copy was given by the Knight Dal Pozzo to Monsieur <term>Chanteloup</term>, who took it to France and granted it to <term>Du Fresne</term>, who also made use of another manuscript lent to him for that purpose by Monsieur <term>Thévenot</term>.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the new edition of Leonardo da Vinci's Treatise on Painting, specifically detailing the collaborative efforts of Giovanni Gherardo de Rossi and his son in preparing the text and illustrations from the Vatican Codex.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>

labor, the Magnificent Knight **Giovanni Gherardo de Rossi**, who, being a great lover of this author and competing with me to bring him to public light, has not only generously undertaken the present edition at his own expense, but has also wished to lend me his assistance in this matter. Furthermore, his son—a young man who joins the most refined manners with the knowledge of many noble disciplines—has faithfully highlighted the drawings within the **Codex**, and subsequently drew them on paper and organized them into plates according to my design. In order not to clutter the pages, which would have been marred by those copperplate prints, these have all been gathered together and are presented in a separate volume. To make this work even more useful and acceptable to students of this author and the fine arts, the aforementioned Mr. de Rossi, placing no limit on his courtesy, has added some of his own notes at the end. Because these were handled by a man who understands this subject so well, I believe they will be most welcome to every amateur and of great advantage to every craftsman. Other notes to clarify the text, which I had originally intended to include and which some might have desired, have been omitted. This was done not to avoid such a slight labor, but to prevent the volume from becoming excessively thick—being already sufficiently filled by the text—and also to avoid spoiling the clarity of the edition with the unsightly appearance of footnotes. I also considered that anyone reading this author should be sufficiently informed in his language to understand him, as he is neither so obscure nor so difficult that he cannot be understood by anyone with a basic knowledge of the <term>native tongue</term> <note>original: "patrio sermone," referring to the Italian language</note>.

And I here warn my readers that if they encounter any passage which seems somewhat obscure to them, or not conforming to regulated syntax according to some, it is written in that very form in the **Vatican Codex**. I have been extremely scrupulous in following the author's reading, not acting as an interpreter to make him speak in a modern fashion—as is the preference of some who, failing to comprehend concepts that are difficult for their dull wits, constantly croak against honest men who, for the benefit and splendor of **Italy**, setting aside every pastime and every joy, spend their lives without honors and without rich- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "ricchezze" or "riches" is implied.</note>

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface, shifting from the technical production of the plates to the biographical and editorial methodology used for this expanded edition of Leonardo da Vinci's work.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>

...dge, and with contempt for the common crowd, spend their lives among books, exercising themselves for the sole love of virtue in laborious and unprofitable pastimes. I have added hereafter the life of **Leonardo** <note>original: "Lionardo"</note> newly written by me; should anyone seek more minute details—such as knowing if, in his time, the winter was occasionally harsher than usual, or when a little glutton of a servant stole some household item from him, or how much he owed for house rent in some circumstance or other, or what color cloak and breeches he wore, and other similar trifles—he may profitably consult the memoirs written about the same **Leonardo** by **Amoretti** <note>Carlo Amoretti (1741–1816), a scholar who published a famous biography of Leonardo in 1804</note>. While Amoretti, with laudable study and effort, has given us much solid information regarding this artist, he has also added such trivialities, perhaps eager to meet the applause and approval of those who—contrary to the judgment of the ancients and our great modern writers—love to see the *Histories* and *Lives* of illustrious men written in the manner of **Commonplace Books** <term>Zibaldoni: miscellaneous notebooks or hodgepodge collections of facts and anecdotes</term>.

Since the past editions of this author are nothing in comparison to this greatly expanded one, it is not worth my while to discuss their quality or arrangement. I will only say that, besides having corrected infinite errors in the printed portion that distorted the meaning, there were also many chapters truncated at the end or in the middle, which have now been completed. I mention this because such growth will not be visible without a direct comparison, as I found no suitable way to distinguish them for the readers—as was done for the entire chapters, where those existing in the old editions are marked with an asterisk. This can be clearly seen in the **Index**, which shows at a glance the notable expansion of the work in the present edition. 

To ensure this edition was in no way inferior to previous ones, even in its adornment, we have added the **Portrait of Vinci** <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note> engraved by a capable artist after the original by the author's own hand which exists in the **Florence Gallery** <note>The Uffizi Gallery</note>. These, O most refined readers, have been the cares I have undertaken so that this edition might be corrected according to the text, leaving nothing to be desired, and being, in short, worthy of you and of its author—whose concepts, through my efforts, will for the first time be [presented] more completely and more purely...

<meta>The text continues the editor's justification for this new edition of Leonardo da Vinci's Treatise on Painting, specifically discussing the completeness of the Vatican Codex and the nature of Leonardo's writing process.</meta>

<page-num>15</page-num>

read by you than those that were in the first truncated editions. As for the question of whether this **Treatise** <note>The *Trattato della pittura*, a collection of Leonardo's notes on art theory and practice</note> can be called complete in this form, I would not know what to tell you; I can only affirm that, as far as I can conjecture, the copyist of the **Vatican Codex** <note>The *Codex Urbinas Latinus 1270*, the primary source for Leonardo's treatise</note> must have gathered everything the author ever wrote on painting. This is clearly proven by the quality of the text, which I explained to you above. Nevertheless, some books are cited in the work that do not exist here, and we must believe either that they were not written by the author, or they were drafts that he kept by him, or they are entirely lost. It is certain that such a great man would not have published his books in this form, but would have polished and ordered them; one perceives from the frequent repetitions encountered therein that this was a first form of the work he meditated upon, which he held as a collection of material he intended to use in a work he would have reorganized and corrected.

However, although these writings did not receive the final polishing from the author himself, they are greater in this subject than the most considered and polished writings of others. Even the repetitions with which they abound are advantageous rather than useless; by presenting things to us under different aspects, they are better imprinted on our memory, and they prove especially more profitable to youth. Indeed, it can be said of this man, as was once said of **Socrates**, that in whatever way and upon whatever subject his reasonings turned, they always resulted in the good and advantage of those who heard him.

Equal good and advantage will therefore be drawn from this golden **Treatise** by young painters; for from the diligent research that this **divine genius** <note>original: "divino ingegno"</note> knew how to extract from the nature of things, they will easily be able to learn in what way nature can be expressed and understood. This certainly cannot be provided by **practice** <term>Prattica: mechanical or repetitive execution without theoretical understanding</term>, which can serve no other purpose than—with the help of instruments and colors—to express what **genius** <note>original: "'ngegno"</note> dictates to us. This appears clearly in those who work only by practice; after having worked for an infinite time, they never produce a work of value or account. Then, by speculating on the doctrines that are enclosed in such great abundance in this book, and by each imitating what most suits his...

<summary>The editor discusses the editorial state of Leonardo's Treatise, arguing that while it is an unpolished collection of notes, its "divine genius" and observations on nature far surpass more refined works by other authors. He warns that mechanical practice without the guidance of such theoretical doctrines leads to mediocre art.</summary>

talent welcomes it, and by not following that which is contrary to one's own taste (for this is the principal reason why, through the stubbornness of masters, many remain confused and lose the good qualities that nature had granted them), this divine art <note>original: "arte divina"</note> will once again return to honor among us, and there will arise in our times craftsmen <note>original: "artefici"</note> not unworthy of being celebrated in the honored ranks of the most praised ancients and famous men.

<column-break/>

<term>Divine art (arte divina)</term>: A common Renaissance and Baroque descriptor for painting, implying that the artist's creativity mirrors the creative power of God.
<term>Masters (maestri)</term>: Established teachers or heads of workshops; the author critiques those who force a single style upon their pupils.
<term>Craftsmen (artefici)</term>: In this period, the term refers to skilled artists or practitioners of the visual arts, emphasizing their technical mastery.
<term>Nature (natura)</term>: Refers here to innate talent or the natural disposition of the student.
<term>Praised ancients (lodati antichi)</term>: The Greek and Roman artists (like Apelles or Zeuxis) who served as the ultimate benchmark for excellence during the Renaissance.

<summary>The author concludes his argument by stating that if students follow their natural inclinations rather than being forced into rigid styles by stubborn teachers, the art of painting will flourish again and rival the greatness of antiquity.</summary>

# THE LIFE OF LEONARDO
## DA VINCI.

---

*Keeping alive in the world's memory those men who were excellent, whether through virtue or other qualities, is undoubtedly of the greatest benefit to human life. For by portraying their remarkable appearances and manners upon paper, everyone is able to recognize and admire them; and the most elevated spirits, moved by their example, easily become desirous of virtue and set themselves to follow the path that these well-born souls have already traveled. Induced by such reasons, and having had the good fortune to publish more completely than what we previously had in print the Treatise of Leonardo da Vinci on Painting <note>original: "Trattato di Lionardo da Vinci in sulla Pittura"</note>, I have undertaken here to describe his life anew, in the best way I saw fit. And although I distrust myself not a little in this task, not being ignorant of the fact that Master Giorgio Vasari of Arezzo, that most diligent historian of the Lives of celebrated Painters <note>original: "Vite de' celebri Dipintori"</note>, has already done so with a display of supreme eloquence and learning, and that some modern authors also deserve praise for having narrated in greater detail many things concerning this supreme genius; nevertheless, seeing some things left silent by the first, and others discussed with too much tedious abundance by the second, I have resolved not to flee from this labor.*

*Leonardo da Vinci was born in Vinci, a small Tuscan land in the Val d'Arno, in the year 1452. His father was named*

Ser Pietro <note>A title of respect for a notary, equivalent to "Master" or "Sir"</note>; his mother is not known, which led some to judge that he was not born of a legitimate marriage. However, such a foundation has been criticized by others as unjust, and not a few have endeavored to defend him extensively with very strong arguments, making it appear that he was the son of the first of the three wives Ser Piero had. In the life of so great a man, however, this matters little or nothing, because since virtue is the true nobility of men, we can say that Leonardo, through his excellence in the arts, was of the most noble condition. He received from nature at his birth a most beautiful form of face and body, to which he added a robustness uncommon for his age; and he showed himself so charming in speech, and was endowed with such kindness, that he won the affection of whoever listened to him.

As he grew in age, it seemed right to Ser Piero to destine him for commerce <note>original: "mercanzia"</note>, a profession then practiced universally in his homeland, and which was the easiest way to acquire comforts and wealth. To this effect, he sent him to an abacus school <note>A school focusing on arithmetic and geometry for business</note>, where he proved so excellent that in the few months he attended, he continually raised doubts to the master, and in such a way that he very often confounded him. And not only in this sort of study, but he would have also made rapid progress in letters and philosophy, if his changeable inclination had not disgusted him with many things, which for a taste of variety he then abandoned. Nonetheless, he became most skilled in music, and singing extemporaneously, he sweetly accompanied his voice with the viola, which he played to perfection. Although he afterwards attended to these disciplines with profit, drawn nonetheless by natural instinct and following his most fortunate genius, drawing <note>original: "disegno"</note> was what most

And from his very first childhood, he delighted in making figures *in relief* <note>sculptural works that project from a flat background</note>, and drawing them from practice; far from these being like the *puppets* <note>original: "fantocci"</note> that other children usually make, they were figures corrected according to art. Wherefore his father—who was a worthy man, but poorly provided with the things of the world due to his too-large family—considering the elevation of his son's talents and knowing that one must not offer resistance to the forces of nature, settled him in the workshop of *Master Andrea da Verrocchio*, his friend, earnestly praying him to take care of the boy and to direct him in that study for which he showed himself so passionate. The *Master* was astonished when he recognized the genius of the youth, and took such wonder at it that he ingenuously confessed to *Ser Piero* that he would succeed most excellently in that profession. When *Leonardo* was born, although *Giotto*, *Masaccio*, and others of their followers had greatly refined painting with their works, nonetheless in this refinement of the art there was still much to be desired to make it reach perfection. He was, therefore, the first who gave the beginning and the extreme perfection to the third and final manner of painting, which is called *modern* <note>The "Maniera Moderna" or High Renaissance style</note>. Meanwhile, he did not limit his occupations in his youth to this art alone, but being endowed with a marvelous and divine intellect, he also made himself known as great in Sculpture; and we know that he assisted with his work *Francesco Rustici* in the casting of three bronze statues that still adorn the door of *St. John in Florence* <note>The Florence Baptistery</note>, and he also formed for his own studies many heads of children and women that were marvelous to whoever saw them. There he represented the **Last Supper** of Christ with the Apostles, and in this painting he chose to display his invention in a sovereign manner, expressing the moment in which Christ, turned toward his disciples, exclaims: *one of you must betray me*. At such a saying, the Apostles shake with horror, and one sees vividly depicted in their various faces love, fear, sorrow, and indignation; and so great was the genius of this artisan in this most admirable painting, that he knew how to express in the Apostles that suspicion of wanting to know who was betraying the master, masterfully making some of those further away rise to their feet, anxiously asking their companions the meaning of Christ's words. There is then a marvelous contrast between the two faces of ***St. John*** and ***Judas***, seeing portrayed in the first a pure and celestial ingenuity, and on the contrary, hatred, betrayal, and obstinacy in the second, who, unalterable and with a grim eye, listens to the divine sentence. Some maintain that he did not finish the head of Christ, because, finding no way to surpass that of ***St. John***, he left it be, advised also in this by ***Bernardo Zenale***, a Milanese Architect and his friend. But whatever they may say on this, others assure us they have seen it completed, and the means to do so could not have been lacking to such a divine genius, who we know placed into this painting all his knowledge and the entire excellence of the art; and as was wisely said by ***Luigi Lanzi*** <note>An influential 18th-century Italian art historian</note>, this was the compendium not only of what ***Leonardo*** taught in his books, but also of what he understood in his studies. And seeing that the Master gave only words in response to his entreaties, he went to complain to the Duke, and importuned him so much that the Duke was forced to send for Leonardo. When Leonardo arrived before him, the Duke urged him to finish the work, but did so in a manner that made it seem he was acting at the instigation of the Prior. Because of this, Leonardo—recognizing that it was not so much the Duke’s own desire to see the end of the work, but that he acted on the impulse of the Friar—spoke to him at length about the difficulty of art. He made him understand that great geniuses achieve more by searching with the intellect than by working with their hands, and added that he still lacked two heads to paint: namely, that of Christ and that of Judas. He explained that for the first, he would have to seek it in heaven, for he could not conceive of such divine beauty on earth; but for the second, in which he had to depict the face of a wretch who had betrayed his divine Master after receiving so many benefits, he hoped to find it among men. However, he added that if this hope of his should fail, he intended to use the face of that indiscreet Prior. The Duke laughed at Leonardo’s wit, and having humanely dismissed him, recommended the work to him, leaving him to work according to his own talent. Leonardo indeed undertook this, and it turned out to be of such great scale that no equal by any other modern artist would be admired as much, had it been finished; but it never reached completion. For this reason, some of his rivals sought to accuse him, saying that he made it so large on purpose so that it would never be finished; however, as *Vasari* <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists.</note> justly observes, one should not believe these trifles, but rather that his most grand soul—being too eager in desiring, as was his custom, excellence upon excellence and perfection upon perfection—was hindered by time. Or, what is more helpful to believe, he did not complete it because the Duke could not supply sufficient funds for such a vast work, being exhausted at that time by the immense expenses he had incurred and by the wars that his restless spirit was constantly stirring up in Italy. Anyone who saw the clay model <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive equestrian monument intended to honor Francesco Sforza.</note> assured that they had never seen anything like it, and everyone judged it a marvelous and superb thing. The young Duke *Gian Galeazzo* having died shortly before these occupations of Leonardo, *Ludovico il Moro* <note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), Leonardo’s patron in Milan.</note> had united the title of *Duke* to his power. Honorable commissions to practice his art were not lacking for Leonardo in Florence. Leonardo was venerable in his speech and appearance, endowed by nature with a strong and robust body, and proportioned in all his limbs; he possessed such strength that with his right hand he could twist a horseshoe <note>original: "ferro di cavallo"</note> as if it were lead. In his dress he was sumptuous and exceedingly refined, loving to appear well-groomed and adorned. Furthermore, he was very hospitable and entertained and welcomed friends, both poor and rich, most humanely in his house, provided they showed some sign of talent <note>original: "virtù," here meaning skill or intellectual merit</note>; and his liberal and magnificent soul always took pleasure in doing good and in appreciating those with talent. Thus, then, lived and died *Leonardo da Vinci*: from him, craftsmen may learn that perfection is not so easily acquired, and that one cannot reach it without a most fervent study of every discipline that concerns art. Fading is the fame of those who, by not following nature and by disdaining philosophical studies, bring shame upon themselves and the arts together; until every image of virtue and beauty is extinguished, the glory of *Leonardo* shall remain eternal in the memory of men.

# BOOK ONE.

## COMPARISON

### OF PAINTING, POETRY, MUSIC, AND SCULPTURE.

---

->*Whether Painting is a Science or not.*<-

**S**cience is the name given to that mental discourse which has its origin in its ultimate principles, beyond which nothing else can be found in nature that is part of that science. For example, in continuous quantity—that is, the science of Geometry—which, beginning from the surface of bodies, is found to have its origin in the line, the boundary of that surface. Yet in this we are not fully satisfied, because we know the line has its limit in the point, and the point is that of which nothing else can be smaller. Therefore, the point is the first principle of Geometry; and there can be no other thing, neither in nature nor in the human mind, that can give rise to the point. For if you say that the contact made upon a surface by the extreme sharpness of the tip of a stylus is the creation of a point, this is not true; rather, we shall say that such a contact is a surface that surrounds its center, and in that center is the residence of the point. Such a point is not made of the matter of that surface; neither it, nor all the points of the universe, have any power <note>original: "in potenza" — referring to Aristotelian potentiality; they lack physical dimension</note> even if they were joined together, nor, granted they could be joined, would they compose any part of a surface. And granted that you imagined a whole being composed of a thousand points, here, by dividing any part from that quantity of a thousand, it can be very well said that such

or nothing, that is, the tenth figure of Arithmetic, for

the unit, will make it say ten, and if you place two after such a unit
it will say one hundred, and thus infinitely the number where it is added

single nothing in terms of their substance and value <note>original: "valetudine" — meaning the inherent strength or capacity of the number</note>. No
human investigation can be called true science if it

### *Example and difference between Painting and Poetry.*

**S**UCH proportion exists from the imagination to the effect as
exists from the shadow to the shaded body, and the same proportion
exists from poetry to painting, because poetry places its things
in the imagination through letters, and painting gives them reality
outside the eye, from which eye it receives the likenesses, no
differently than if they were natural; whereas poetry gives them
without that likeness, and they do not pass to the impressionable faculty <note>original: "impressiva" — the part of the brain believed to receive sensory images</note> by
way of the visual power as painting does.

## Of the *Sciences* that can be imitated, and how *Painting*
## is inimitable, yet is a *Science*.

**T**hose sciences which are imitable are of such a nature that through them the disciple becomes equal to the author, and produces the same fruit; these are useful to the imitator, but they are not of such excellence as those which cannot be left as an inheritance, like other material goods. Among these, painting is the first. This cannot be taught to one whom nature has not granted the gift, as is done with the mathematical sciences <note>original: "mattematiche"</note>, of which the disciple takes as much as the master reads to him. This cannot be copied like letters <note>referring here to the written word or literature</note>, where the copy is worth as much as the original. This cannot be cast from a mold, as is done with sculpture, where the impression is the same as the original in terms of the merit of the work. This does not produce infinite offspring as printed books do. This alone remains noble; this alone honors its author and remains precious and unique, and never gives birth to children equal to itself. And such singularity makes it more excellent than those sciences which are published everywhere. Now, do we not see the greatest Kings of the East go about veiled and covered, believing they would diminish their fame by making their presence public and common? Now, is it not seen that paintings representing the images of the Saints are continually kept covered with coverings of very great price? And when they are uncovered, first great ecclesiastical solemnities are performed with various chants and diverse sounds. And at the uncovering, the great multitude of people who gather there immediately throw themselves to the ground, venerating and praying to that which such a painting figures <note>represents</note>, for the recovery of lost health and for eternal salvation, no differently than if such a divine idea were there present and alive. This does not happen in any other scien—

### *How painting embraces all the surfaces of bodies, and extends itself into them.*

**P**ainting extends only to the surfaces of bodies, and its perspective extends to the increase and decrease of bodies and of their colors; because an object that moves away from the eye loses as much in size and color as it gains in distance <note>original: "remozione"</note>. Therefore, painting is philosophy, because philosophy treats of augmentative and diminutive motion, which is found in the aforementioned proposition; of which we shall make the converse, and say: the thing seen by the eye acquires as much size, clarity <note>original: "notizia"</note>, and color, as the space interposed between it and the eye that sees it diminishes.

He who blames painting blames nature, because the works of the painter represent the works of nature itself, and for this reason, the said critic suffers from a poverty of feeling <note>original: "carestia di sentimento"; implying a lack of sensory perception or aesthetic soul</note>.

It is proved that painting is philosophy because it treats of the motion of bodies in the promptness of their actions, and philosophy also extends itself into motion. All sciences that end in words have as quick a death as they have life, except for their manual part—that is, writing, which is the mechanical part.

*How painting embraces the surfaces, shapes, and colors*
*of natural bodies, and philosophy only extends*
*into their natural virtues.*

**P**ainting extends into the surfaces, colors, and shapes of whatever thing is created by nature, and philosophy penetrates inside those same bodies, considering in them their own inherent virtues <note>original: "virtù"; here meaning essential properties or powers</note>. But philosophy does not remain satisfied with that truth which the painter achieves, who embraces in himself the primary truth of such bodies, because the eye is less deceived.

*How the eye is less deceived in its exercises*
*than any other sense. Luminous, or transparent,*
*and uniform, and mediums.*

The eye, at the proper distances and through the proper mediums <note>original: "mezzi"; the substance, like air or water, through which light travels</note>, is less deceived in its office than any other sense, because it sees only by straight lines which compose the pyramid <note>a reference to the "visual pyramid," a core concept in Renaissance perspective where light rays travel from an object to a point in the eye</note> that takes the object as its base and conducts it to the eye, as I intend to prove. But the ear is greatly deceived regarding the locations and distances of its objects, because the species <note>original: "specie"; a philosophical term for the sensory image or "likeness" of a thing traveling through space</note> do not come to it by straight lines, like those of the eye, but by tortuous and reflected lines; and many are the times that remote sounds seem nearer than those close by, by means of the passages of...

## *How he who despises painting loves neither philosophy,*
## *nor nature.*

**I**f you despise painting, which is the sole imitator of all the visible works of nature, you certainly despise a subtle invention, which with philosophical and subtle speculation considers all the qualities of forms: seas, sites, plants, animals, grasses, and flowers, all of which are encompassed by shadow and light. And truly, this is a science, and the legitimate daughter of nature; for painting is born of nature itself. But to be more accurate, we shall call it the grandchild of nature, because all visible things have been born of nature, and from these things painting is born. Therefore, we rightly call it the grandchild of nature and a work of God.

## *How the painter is Lord of every kind of people,*
## *and of all things.*

**T**he painter is master of all things that can fall within human thought, because if he has a desire to see beauties that would make him fall in love, he is the Lord capable of generating them; and if he wishes to see monstrous things that terrify, or those that are buffoonish and laughable, or truly compassionate, he is their Lord and creator. And if he wishes to generate desert sites, shady or dark places in hot weather, he depicts them for himself, and likewise warm places in cold weather. If he wants valleys, the same,

## Of the poet, and of the painter.

**P**ainting serves a worthier sense than poetry, and represents the figures of the works of nature with more truth than the poet. The works of nature are much worthier than words, which are the works of man; for there is the same proportion between the works of men and those of nature as there is between man and God. Therefore, it is a worthier thing to imitate the things of nature—which are the true likenesses in fact—than to imitate in words the deeds and words of men. And if you, poet, wish to describe the works of nature by your simple profession, feigning diverse locations and the forms of various things, you are surpassed by the painter with an infinite proportion of power. But if you wish to clothe yourself in other sciences separate from poetry itself, they are not yours—such as Astrology <note>In Leonardo's time, this included what we now call Astronomy</note>, Rhetoric, Theology, Philosophy, Geometry, Arithmetic, and the like—then you are no longer a poet; you transform yourself and are no longer the one of whom we speak here. Now, do you not see that if you wish to go to nature, you go there by means of sciences made by others based on the effects of nature? Whereas the painter, by himself and without the aid of science or other means, goes immediately to the imitation of these works of nature. By this <note>meaning painting</note>, lovers are moved

->*Which is of greater harm to the human species,*<-
->*to lose the eye, or the ear?*<-

**A**nimals receive greater harm through the loss of sight than of hearing for several reasons; first, because by means of sight, food is found, by which one must be nourished, which is necessary to all animals. <meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s "Paragone," specifically his defense of the eye as the superior organ for both scientific inquiry and aesthetic appreciation, responding to the philosophical anecdote of Democritus blinding himself.</meta>

<page-num>II</page-num>

to a philosopher depriving himself of sight, to this I respond, that such an eye, as the lord of the senses, does its duty in providing an impediment to those confused and lying—not sciences, but discourses—through which men always dispute with great shouting and waving of hands; and the same should be done by the sense of hearing, which is even more offended by this, because it desires harmony, in which all the senses are entwined. And if such a philosopher <note>Leonardo refers to the legend of Democritus, who was said to have blinded himself to avoid distractions from his meditations.</note> plucked out his eyes to remove the impediment to his discourses, consider now that such an act was a companion to his brain and his discourses, for it was entirely madness; now, could he not have simply closed his eyes when he entered into such a frenzy, and kept them closed until such fury consumed itself? But the man was mad, and the discourse was mad, and the plucking out of his eyes was the height of folly.

### *How the science of Astronomy <note>original: "Astrologia." In Leonardo's time, the term often encompassed both what we now call astronomy and astrology, though here he refers to the mathematical study of celestial bodies.</note> is born from the eye, because it is generated by means of it.*

**N**o part of Astronomy exists that is not the function of visual lines and of perspective—the daughter of painting; for it is the painter who, by the necessity of his art, has given birth to this perspective, and it cannot be done by itself without lines, within which lines are enclosed all the various figures of bodies generated by nature, without which the art of the Geometer is blind. And if the Geometer reduces every surface surrounded by lines to the figure of a square, and every body to the figure of a cube; and arithmetic does the same with its square and cube roots—these two sciences extend only to the knowledge of continuous and discontinuous quantity <note>A classical distinction: "continuous quantity" refers to geometry (space), while "discontinuous quantity" refers to arithmetic (numbers).</note>, but they do not concern themselves with quality, which is the beauty of the works of nature and the ornament of the world.

### The Painter who disputes with the Poet.

**W**hat poet with words will place before you, O lover, the true effigy of your ideal with as much truth as the painter will do? Who will be the one to show you the sites of rivers, woods, valleys, and fields, where your past pleasures are represented, with more truth than the painter? And if you say that painting is a "mute poetry" <note>original: "poesìa muta." A famous aphorism attributed to Simonides of Ceos: "Painting is mute poetry, and poetry is speaking picture."</note> in itself, unless there is someone to say or speak for what it represents, do you not see that your book is in a worse state? Because even though it has a man to speak for it, nothing is seen of the thing being spoken of, as will be seen of the one who speaks for paintings. If the actions in these paintings are well-proportioned to their mental states <note>original: "accidenti mentali." Leonardo refers to the outward physical expression of internal emotions or thoughts.</note>, they will be understood as if they were speaking.

If you call painting "mute poetry," the painter can also call poetry "blind painting." Now consider which is the more damaging monster: the blind or the mute? ...be mechanical because it is done for a price? Who falls into this error—if error it can be called—more than you? If you read for your studies, do you not go to whoever rewards you most? Do you perform any work without some reward? Although I do not say this to blame such actions, because every labor expects a reward. If the former describes the operations of the mind, the latter considers what the mind operates through movements. If poetry terrifies peoples with hellish fictions, painting does the same with those same things in action. Let the poet set himself to figure a beauty, a ferocity, or something foul, ugly, or monstrous along with the painter; let him transform forms in his own way as he wishes, and the painter will still satisfy more. Have we not seen paintings possess such conformity with the thing imitated that they have deceived both men and animals?

### *The difference between painting and poetry.*

**P**ainting is a poetry that is seen and not heard, and poetry is a painting that is heard and not seen. Therefore, these two poetries—or, if you prefer, two paintings—have exchanged the senses through which they ought to penetrate the intellect. Because if both must pass to the common sense <note>The "sensus communis," a theoretical part of the brain where the five senses were thought to be processed and integrated.</note> through...

the most noble sense, which is the eye; and if the one and the other [poetry and music] are poetry, they must pass through the less noble sense, which is hearing. Therefore, let us give a painting to the judgment of a man born deaf, and poetry shall be judged by a man born blind. The painting will be depicted with the movements appropriate to the mental states <note>original: "accidenti mentali." Leonardo believed that physical gestures must reveal the internal thoughts and emotions of the figure.</note> of the figures who act in any given situation. Without doubt, the man born deaf will understand the actions and intentions of the actors, but the man born blind will never understand anything demonstrated by the poet which might bring honor to that poetry. This is because among its noble parts is the depicting of gestures, the compositions of Histories <note>The "Istoria" or History Painting was considered the highest genre of art, depicting a narrative scene with multiple figures.</note>, and ornate and delightful places with transparent waters, through which one sees the greening depths of their courses, the waves playing over bridges and tiny pebbles <note>original: "giarre," likely a variant of "ghiaie."</note> with the grasses that mix with them, together with the darting fish and similar subtleties. These things might as well be told to a stone as to a man born blind, because he never saw any of the things of which the beauty of the world is composed: namely light, darkness, color, body, figure, location, distance <note>original: "remozione."</note>, proximity, motion, and rest. These are the **ten ornaments of nature**. But the deaf man, having lost the less noble sense—even though he has also lost speech, because having never heard anyone speak he could never learn a language—will nonetheless understand every state belonging to human bodies better than one who speaks and has hearing; and similarly, he will know the works of painters and what is represented in them, and the nature of such figures.

**P**ainting is a mute poetry, and poetry is a blind painting, and both go about imitating nature as far as is pos—

<page-num>16</page-num>

accessible to their powers, and through both one can demonstrate many moral customs, as <term>Apelles</term> <note>A celebrated painter of ancient Greece, famous for his lost work "Calumny," which Leonardo references here as an example of art conveying complex moral allegories.</note> did with his *Calumny*. But from **painting**, because it serves the eye—a sense more noble than the ear, which is the object of **poetry**—there results a **harmonic proportion**; that is to say, just as a harmony results from many various voices joined together at the same time, which so pleases the sense of hearing that the listeners remain in stunned admiration, almost half-alive. But much greater will be the proportional beauties of an angelic face set in a painting, from which proportionality there results a harmonic <term>concord</term> <note>original: "concento." A musical term for voices singing in unison or harmony, used here to describe the visual "music" of a well-proportioned face.</note>, which serves the eye in the same moment that music serves the ear. And if such a harmony of beauties is shown to the lover of the one whose beauty is imitated, without doubt he will remain in stupendous admiration and incomparable joy, superior to all other senses. 

But from poetry, which must extend itself to the figuration of a perfect beauty by describing each part of which the aforementioned harmony is composed in painting, no other grace results than what would happen in music if each voice were heard by itself at different times, from which no concord would be composed; as if we wished to show a face part by part, always covering those which were shown first. In such demonstrations, forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivione."</note> does not allow any proportionality of harmony to be composed, because the eye does not embrace them all at once with its <term>visual power</term> <note>original: "virtù visiva." In Renaissance optics, this referred to the active capacity of the eye to perceive and process light and form.</note>. At the same time, the same thing happens with the beauties of whatever thing is imagined by the poet; because its parts are described separately at separate times, the memory receives no harmony from them.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to poetry because it presents all parts of a beautiful subject simultaneously, creating a visual harmony similar to musical chords, whereas poetry's sequential nature causes the viewer to forget the whole.</summary>

## The Difference between Poetry and Painting.

**PAINTING** represents itself to you immediately with the same demonstration for which its maker generated it; it gives that pleasure to the highest sense <note>Leonardo considers sight the "highest" or "maximum" sense because it perceives reality directly.</note> which any thing created by nature can give. In this case the poet, who sends the same things to the common sense <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was believed in the Renaissance to be the part of the brain where all sensory inputs—sight, sound, etc.—were gathered and processed.</note> by way of the hearing (a lesser sense), gives no more pleasure to the eye than if one were to hear a thing recounted. Now see what a difference there is between hearing a thing recounted—which gives pleasure to the eye only over a long period of time—and seeing it with that swiftness with which natural things are seen. And even though the works of poets are read over a long interval of time, it is often the case that they are not understood, and it becomes necessary to make various commentaries upon them. It is very rare that such commentators understand what was truly in the mind of the poet; and many times readers only read a small part of their works due to lack of time. But the work of the painter is understood immediately by its viewers.

### Of the difference and also the similarity that painting has with poetry.

**PAINTING** represents its essence to you in an instant through the visual faculty, and through the very medium by which the <term>impressive faculty</term> <note>original: "impressiva." Leonardo's term for the part of the mind that receives and "imprints" sensory images.</note> receives natural objects. It does this at the same moment in which the <term>harmonic proportionality</term> <note>The mathematical arrangement of parts that creates beauty, similar to how notes create a chord in music.</note> of the parts is composed—those parts which make up the whole that satisfies the sense. Poetry reports the same thing, but through a medium less worthy than the eye, which carries the figures of the named things to the impressive faculty more confusedly and with more slowness than the eye does. The eye is the true medium between the object and the impressive faculty, which...

## *Dispute between the poet and painter, and what the difference is between poetry and painting.*

**T**he poet says that his <term>science</term> is <term>invention</term> <note>original: "invenzione." The creative capacity to conceive of a subject or story.</note> and <term>measure</term> <note>original: "misura." Referring to the meter and rhythm of verse.</note>, and this is the simple body of poetry: the invention of subject matter and the measure of the verses, and that she then clothes herself in all the other sciences. To which the painter responds that he has the same obligations in the science of <term>painting</term>, namely invention and measure; invention in the subject matter, which he must imagine, and measure in the things painted, so that they are not disproportionate. But he does not merely clothe himself in these three sciences; rather, the others for the most part clothe themselves in painting—such as <term>astrology</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "astrology" often included what we now call astronomy.</note>, which can do nothing without <term>perspective</term>, which is a principal member of painting itself; that is, mathematical astrology—I do not speak of the fallacious judicial— <note>The author is distinguishing between mathematical astronomy and "judicial astrology," which attempted to predict the future and was often dismissed as superstitious or fraudulent.</note>

...painting, and may those who live off the labor of fools forgive me. The poet says he must describe a thing that represents another, full of beautiful sentiments. The painter says he has the freedom to do the same, and in this regard, he too is a poet. And if the poet says he can kindle men to love—which is the primary drive of all animal species—the painter has the power to do the same, and even more so, because he places before the lover the actual likeness of the beloved. The lover often interacts with this image, kissing it and speaking to it, which he would not do with the same beauties if they were merely placed before him by a writer. Furthermore, painting so overcomes the minds of men that it leads them to love and fall in love with a picture that does not represent any living woman.

It once happened to me that I made a painting representing a divine subject <note>Likely a Madonna or a female Saint.</note>, which, once bought by a lover, he wished to have the representation of such a Deity removed so that he could kiss it without suspicion. But in the end, his conscience overcame his sighs and lust, and he was forced to remove it from his house.

Now you go, poet, and describe a beauty without the representation of a living thing, and try to awaken men to such desires with that. If you say, "I will describe hell to you, or paradise, and other delights or terrors," the painter surpasses you, because he will place before you things that, while remaining silent, will express such delights or will terrify you and move your soul to flee. Painting moves the senses more quickly than poetry. And if you say that with words you can move a crowd to tears or laughter, I will tell you that it is not you who moves them, but the **Orator**; that is a <term>science</term> <note>A formal discipline of rhetoric.</note> which is not poetry. But the painter will move one to laughter, though not to tears, because weeping is a more profound physical state than laughter. A painter once made a picture that caused anyone who saw it to immediately yawn, and this accident was repeated as long as one kept their eyes on the painting...

### *The poet's argument against the painter.*

**Y**ou say, O painter, that your art is adored, but do not credit yourself with such virtue, but rather the thing which such a painting represents. Here the painter responds: O you, poet, who also make yourself an imitator, why do you not represent things with your words so that your letters—the containers of those words—are also adored? But nature has favored the painter more than the poet; and deservedly, the works of the favored one should be more honored than those of the one who is not in favor. Therefore, let us praise him who satisfies the hearing with words, and him who satisfies the joy of seeing with painting. But the praise for the one of words is much less, insofar as words are accidental <note>In the Aristotelian sense: secondary or non-essential qualities.</note> and created by a lesser author than the works of nature, of which the painter is the imitator; which nature is contained within the figures upon their surfaces.

There is no judgment so foolish that, if proposed with the choice of whether to remain in perpetual darkness or to lose one's hearing, would not immediately say they would rather lose their hearing, along with their sense of smell, before remaining blind. Because he who loses his sight loses the beauty of the world with all the forms of created things, while the deaf man only loses the sound made by the movement of struck air, which is the smallest thing in the world. You, who say that a science is all the more noble as it extends to a more worthy subject, and for this reason a false imagination of the essence of God is worth more than an imagination of a less worthy thing—for this reason we shall say that painting, which only extends to the works of God, is more worthy than poetry, which only extends to the lying fictions of human works. With rightful lamentation, painting grieves for being cast out from the number of the **liberal arts** <note>The "Artes Liberales" were the traditional academic disciplines (like Grammar or Logic) considered worthy of a free person; Leonardo argues painting belongs among them due to its scientific basis.</note>; seeing as she is the true daughter of nature, and operated by the most worthy sense. But why must I extend myself in such a high and long discourse? What is that thing which is not done through it? It moves men from the East to the West; this has discovered **navigation**, and in this it surpasses nature; for simple natural things are finite, but the works that the eye commands to the hands are infinite, as the painter demonstrates in the inventions of infinite forms of animals, and herbs, plants, and places.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci presents a passionate defense of the eye as the supreme sensory organ, crediting it as the foundation of all sciences, from astronomy to painting. He argues that sight is what makes life in the "prison" of the body bearable and allows for the infinite creativity of the artist.</summary>

# How Music should be called the younger sister of Painting.

**M**usic is not to be called anything other than the sister of painting (3) <note>Leonardo often uses familial metaphors to rank the arts; "sister" implies a shared origin in proportion, but "younger" implies a lower status.</note>, since it is the subject of hearing—the second sense after the eye. Music composes harmony through the joining of its proportional parts, which are operated at the same time <note>original: "medesimo tempo" — referring to the simultaneous sounding of notes in a chord.</note>, and are forced to be born and die in one or more harmonic intervals. These intervals surround the proportionality of the members of which such harmony is composed, no differently than the circumferential line surrounds the limbs from which human beauty is generated. But painting excels and reigns over music because it does not die immediately after its creation, as unfortunate music does; rather, it remains in existence, and shows you as still living that which is, in fact, a single surface. O marvelous science! You preserve in life the fleeting beauties of mortals, which have more permanence than the works of nature; for nature's works are continually changed by time, which leads them to their inevitable old age. Such a science <note>Painting.</note> has the same proportion to divine nature as its works have to the works of nature itself, and for this reason, it is adored.

## The Musician speaks with the Painter.

**T**he musician says that his science should be equated to that of the painter, because music composes a body of many members, of which the observer contemplates all its grace in as many harmonic intervals as there are moments in which it is born and dies; and with those moments, it gracefully entertains the soul that resides in the body of the observer. But the painter responds and says: that the body composed of hu-

<summary>Leonardo argues that while Music and Painting both rely on mathematical proportion, Painting is superior because it is permanent, whereas Music "dies" as soon as it is performed.</summary>
