...of its members. It <note>Painting</note> does not provide pleasure to harmonic rhythms in which beauty must vary itself by taking on a new shape, nor does it have to be born and die within those rhythms; rather, it makes beauty permanent for many, many years. It is of such excellence that it preserves in life that harmony of proportioned limbs which nature, with all its strength, could not conserve. How many paintings have preserved the image of a divine beauty, whose natural original has been destroyed in a short time by age or death? Thus, the work of the painter has remained more worthy than that of nature, its mistress.

### *The Painter provides the degrees of things presented to the eye, just as the musician provides those of the voices presented to the ear.*

**A**lthough the things presented to the eye touch one another successively, I will nonetheless establish my rule in intervals of 20 to 20 cubits <note>original: "braccia" — a Florentine measure of length, roughly 23 inches.</note>, just as the musician has done with voices. For although the voice is united and joined together, he has nonetheless established a few degrees from voice to voice, calling them first, second, third, fourth, and fifth; and so, degree by degree, he has given names to the variety of the rising and falling of the voice. If you, O musician, say that painting is mechanical because it is operated by the exercise of the hands, and music is operated by the mouth (which is a human organ, though not for the sake of the sense of taste, just as the hand is not for the sense of touch), then words are even less worthy than deeds. But you, writer of sciences, do you not copy with your hand, writing what is in your mind just as the painter does? And if you should say that music is composed of proportion, I have followed that same path in painting, as you shall see.

### That thing is more worthy which satisfies a better sense.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to music because it immortalizes beauty that nature allows to wither, and he asserts that painting follows mathematical proportions (perspective) just as music follows harmonic scales.</summary>

Therefore, painting, which satisfies the sense of sight, is more noble than music, which only satisfies hearing. That thing is more noble which possesses more eternity; therefore music, which goes on consuming itself even as it is born, is less worthy than painting, which can be made eternal with glass <note>Likely referring to mosaic or enamel work, which Leonardo considered the most permanent form of painting.</note>. That thing which contains within itself more universality and variety of things shall be called of greater excellence; therefore, painting is to be preferred above all other operations, because it contains all the forms that exist, and even those that do not exist in nature. It is more to be magnified and exalted than music, which attends only to the voice. With painting, the likenesses of the Gods are made; around painting, divine worship is conducted, which is adorned by music serving it. With this <insert>art</insert>, lovers are given the likeness of the cause of their loves; with this, beauties are preserved which time and nature make fleeting; with this, we preserve the likenesses of famous men. And if you should say that music is made eternal by writing it down, we do the same here with letters. Therefore, since you have placed music among the liberal arts <note>The traditional medieval curriculum of the seven "Liberal Arts" included music but excluded painting as a "mechanical" craft.</note>, you must either place painting there as well, or remove music. And if you should say that base men practice it <note>painting</note>, music is likewise spoiled by those who do not know it. If you say that the non-mechanical sciences are those of the mind, I say that painting is mental, and that just as music and geometry consider the proportions of continuous quantities, and arithmetic those of discontinuous ones, painting considers all continuous quantities, as well as the qualities of the proportions of shadows, lights, and distances within its perspective.

### *Which science is mechanical and which is not mechanical.*

**T**hey say that knowledge is "mechanical" if it is born from experience, and "scientific" if it begins and ends in the mind; and they call "semi-mechanical" that which is born from science and ends in manual operation. But to me, it seems that those sciences are vain and full of errors which are not born from Experience, the mother of all certainty, and which do not terminate in a known experience—that is, those whose origin, middle, or end does not pass through any of the five senses. And if we doubt the certainty of every thing that passes through the senses, how much more ought we to doubt those things rebellious to the senses, about which philosophers dispute and contend. And truly <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the argument that true science must be verifiable by the eyes and hands.</note>

### *Why painting is not numbered among the sciences.*

**B**ecause writers have had no knowledge of the science of painting, they have been unable to describe its degrees and parts. And since painting itself does not demonstrate its final purpose through words, it has remained behind the aforementioned sciences due to ignorance, though it does not lack for this its own divinity <margin>5</margin>. And truly, it is not without reason that they have not ennobled it, because it ennobles itself by itself without the aid of others' tongues, no differently than the excellent works of nature do. And if painters have not described it in writing and reduced it to a science, it is not the fault of painting; and it is not, for this reason, less noble than poetry. For few painters make a profession of letters, because their lives are not long enough to understand them. For this reason, shall we say that the virtues of herbs, stones, and plants do not exist because men have not known them? Certainly not; but we shall say that these herbs remain noble in themselves without the aid of human tongues or letters.

### *Beginning on sculpture, and whether it is a science or not.*

**S**culpture is not a science but a most mechanical art <note>term: "mechanical art" (Italian: *arte meccanicissima*). In the Renaissance, mechanical arts were associated with manual labor and trade, whereas "liberal arts" or "sciences" were associated with the intellect.</note>, because it produces sweat and physical exhaustion for its practitioner; the simple measurements of the limbs and the nature of movements and poses are sufficient for such an artist. Thus, it ends in itself, showing to the eye only what is physically there, and it provides no sense of wonder to its observer in the way that painting does—which, on a flat surface, by force of science, demonstrates vast landscapes with distant horizons. <margin>6</margin>

---

### *The difference between painting and sculpture.*

**B**etween painting and sculpture I find no other difference than this: the sculptor carries out his works with greater physical exertion than the painter, and the painter carries out his works with greater mental exertion. This is proven to be true because the sculptor, in making his work, uses the strength of his arms and percussion to consume the marble or other surplus stone that exceeds the figure enclosed within it. This is a most mechanical exercise, often accompanied by great sweat composed of dust and turned into mud; his face is pasted and all floured with marble dust—looking like a baker <note>original: "fornajo"</note>—and he is covered in tiny chips, as if it had snowed on him, and his dwelling is filthy and full of stone chips and dust. The exact opposite happens to the painter—speaking of excellent painters and sculptors—for the painter sits with great ease before his work, well-dressed, and moves the lightest brush with lovely colors, adorned in garments as he pleases. His dwelling is full of lovely paintings and clean...

<summary>Leonardo argues that sculpture is a lowly "mechanical" craft defined by physical labor and filth, whereas painting is an intellectual science practiced in comfort and elegance.</summary>

The painter has ten various discourses <note>The "ten discourses" or "ten attributes of sight" are a recurring theme in Leonardo's theory, representing the complete visual world.</note> with which he brings his works to completion: namely, light, darkness, color, body, figure, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. The sculptor only has to consider body, figure, location, motion, and rest. With darkness or light he does not concern himself, because nature generates these for him in his sculptures; of color, nothing; of distance or proximity, he concerns himself only moderately—that is, he employs nothing but linear perspective, but not the perspective of colors, which vary at different distances from the eye in their hue and in the clarity of their boundaries and shapes. Therefore, sculpture involves less discourse, and consequently, it requires less labor of the mind <note>term: "labor of the mind" (Italian: *fatica d'ingegno*). ### *How sculpture requires*
greater genius, difficulty, and perfection than the other. First, sculpture is subject to certain lights, namely from above, while painting carries both light and shadow with it everywhere. Light and shadow are of such importance, then, to sculpture; the sculptor in this case is aided by the nature of the <term>relief</term> <note>the physical projection of the material</note>, which it generates by itself. But the painter, through accidental art, creates it in the places where nature would reasonably do so. The sculptor cannot diversify his work with the various natures of the colors of things; painting lacks nothing in any part. The perspectives of sculptors do not appear at all true; those of the painter appear to be hundreds of miles beyond the work itself. <term>Aerial perspective</term> <note>the technique of representing distance by modifying tone and color to simulate the effect of the atmosphere</note> is far removed from their work; they cannot represent transparent bodies, they cannot represent luminous ones, nor reflected lines, nor shiny bodies like mirrors and similar lustrous things, nor mists, nor dark weather, and infinite other things that are not mentioned so as not to be tedious. 

What sculpture does have is that it is more resistant to time; although, regarding similar resistance, a painting made upon thick copper covered with white <term>enamel</term> <note>original: "smalto"</note>, and painted upon that with enamel colors, and put back into the fire and baked—this, for eternity, surpasses sculpture. The sculptor might say that where he makes an error, it is not easy for him to repair it; this is a weak argument to try to prove that an irremediable <term>forgetfulness</term> <note>original: "ismemorataggine"; implying a lapse in judgment or physical slip</note> makes the work more worthy. But I will say indeed that the genius of the master who makes such errors will be more difficult to repair. We know well that he who is a practitioner will not make such errors; rather, with good rules, he will proceed by removing so little at a time that he will bring his work to a good conclusion. Furthermore, if the sculptor works in clay or wax, he can remove and add, and when it is finished, it is easily cast in <term>bronze</term>; and this is the final operation and the most permanent that sculpture has. And if the sculptor says he cannot repair the material once too much has been removed from his work, whereas the painter can, the answer is this: he who removes too much understands little and is no master; because if he has mastery over the measurements, he will not remove what he should not. Therefore, we shall say such a defect belongs to the operator and not to the material. But painting is of marvelous artifice, entirely composed of the most subtle speculations, of which <term>sculpture</term> is entirely deprived because it requires very little reasoning. One responds to the sculptor who says that his science is more permanent than painting, that such permanence is a virtue of the sculpted material and not of the sculptor; and in this regard, the sculptor should not attribute it to his own glory, but leave it to nature, the creator of such material.

## Of the sculptor and painter.

**T**he sculptor performs his art with greater physical labor than the painter—that is, it is mechanical—and with less mental labor; which is to say it requires little reasoning compared to painting, because the sculptor only removes material, while the painter is always adding various substances. The sculptor only seeks the outlines that surround the sculpted material, whereas the painter seeks those same outlines and, beyond those, seeks shadow, light, color, and <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scorto"; the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has to create the illusion of three-dimensionality</note>. In these matters, nature continually assists the sculptor—namely with shadow, light, and <term>perspective</term>—which are elements the painter must acquire through the force of his own genius, transforming himself into nature itself, while the sculptor finds them already made. And if you should say there is some sculptor who understands what the painter understands, I answer you: that insofar as the sculptor understands the parts of the painter, he is a painter, and where he does not understand them, he is a simple sculptor. But the painter always needs to understand sculpture—that is, the natural world—which possesses <term>relief</term> <note>the quality of standing out from a surface</note> that by itself generates <term>light and dark</term> <note>original: "chiaro, e scuro"</note> and <term>foreshortening</term>. And for this reason, many return to nature because they are not learned in such reasoning regarding shadows, light, and perspective; and thus they portray the natural world, because only such portrayal has been put into practice without any other science or reasoning of nature in that regard. And among these, there are some who, through glass and other papers or transparent veils, look at things made by nature, and there on the surface of the transparencies they outline them; and with the rules of proportionality, they surround them with profiles, sometimes increasing them within such profiles, and they occupy them with light and dark, noting the location, quantity, and shape of shadows and lights. But this is to be praised in those who know how to create from their imagination afterwards

# BOOK SECOND.

## PRECEPTS FOR THE PAINTER.

### *On the first principle of the science of painting.*

**T**he principle of the science of painting is the point; the second is the line; the third is the surface; the fourth is the body <note>In this context, "body" refers to a three-dimensional solid or volume.</note> which is clothed by such a surface. And this pertains to that which is simulated—that is, the body itself which is represented; because in truth, painting does not extend further than the surface, by which the body, the form of any visible thing, is simulated.

### *Principle of the science of painting.*

**A** flat surface has its entire image <note>original: "simulacro"</note> reflected in every part of another flat surface placed opposite to it. This is proven: let *r. s.* be the first flat surface, and *o. q.* be the second flat surface placed opposite the first. I say: that the first surface *r. s.* is entirely in surface *o. q.*, and entirely in *o.*, and entirely in *q.*, and entirely in *p.*, because *r. s.* is perceived from angle *o.* and from angle *p.*, and likewise from infinite angles made in *o. q.* (*Fig. 1. Plate I.*) <note>Leonardo is describing the optical principle that light rays from an object reach every point of an opposing area, the foundation of perspective and the camera obscura.</note>

### *On the second principle of painting.*

**T**he second principle of painting is the shadow of the body, through which the body is simulated. Regarding this shadow, we shall provide its principles, and with those, we shall proceed in "sculpting" <note>original: "isculpir." Leonardo uses this term metaphorically to describe how a painter uses light and shadow to give a flat surface the illusion of three-dimensional relief.</note> the aforementioned surface.

<sig>g</sig> <note>This is a printer's signature mark, used to help binders assemble the book pages in the correct order.</note>

## *To what the science of painting extends.*

**T**he science of painting extends to all the colors of surfaces, and the shapes of the bodies clothed by them, and to their proximity and distance with the proper degrees of diminution according to the degrees of distance; and this science is the mother of perspective, that is, of visual lines. This perspective is divided into three parts: of these, the first contains only the outlines of bodies; the second, the diminution of colors at various distances; the third, the loss of definition <note>original: "cognizione," referring to the loss of detail or clarity as an object recedes.</note> of bodies at various distances. But the first, which extends to the outlines and boundaries of bodies, is called drawing <note>original: "disegno," which in the Renaissance encompassed both the act of drawing and the conceptual design or underlying structure of a work.</note>, that is, the figuration of any body. From this emerges another science that extends to shadow and light, or if you prefer, <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>; this science requires great discourse. However, the science of visual lines has given birth to the science of astronomy, which is simple perspective, because it consists entirely of lines and intersected pyramids <note>Leonardo views the eye as the apex of a pyramid of light rays; astronomy is the study of these "pyramids" extending to the stars.</note>.

## *What the young student should learn first.*

**T**he youth should first learn perspective; then the measurements of every thing; then, step by step, learn from a good master to become accustomed to graceful limbs; then from nature, to confirm the reasoning of the things learned; then for a time to view the works of various masters; and finally, to acquire the habit of putting the art into practice and operation (10).

**T**he study of the youth who desire to perfect themselves

## *What rule should be given to young painters.*

We clearly know that sight is among the swiftest operations that exist, and in one instant it sees infinite forms; nevertheless, it only comprehends one thing at a time. Let us suppose that you, reader, look at this entire written page in one glance, and you will immediately judge it to be full of various letters; but you will not know in that moment what those letters are, nor what they mean; therefore, you must go word by word, line by line, if you wish to gain knowledge of these letters. Furthermore, if you wish to climb to the top of a building, you must ascend step by step, otherwise it will be impossible to reach its height. And so I say to you, whom nature turns toward this art: if you wish to have true knowledge of the forms of things, you shall begin with their smallest parts, and do not move to the second until you first have the first well-fixed in your memory and in your practice. If you do otherwise, you will throw away your time, or truly prolong your study. And I remind you to learn diligence before speed.

you will be alone, you will be entirely your own master; and if you are accompanied by even a single companion, you will be only half your own, and even less so in proportion to the indiscretion of his behavior. And if you should say, "I will do it my way, I will withdraw to one side so that I may better contemplate <term>speculare: the act of deep mental observation and analysis</term> the forms of natural things," I say this is difficult to do well, because it is impossible not to frequently lend an ear to their chatter. One cannot serve two masters; you would perform the duty of a companion poorly, and the effect of your artistic contemplation even worse. And if you say, "I will withdraw so far away that their words will not reach me and will not hinder me," I tell you that in this case you would be considered a madman; but see, that by doing so, you would still be alone (11) <note>Leonardo emphasizes that true intellectual work requires total isolation from social distractions.</note>.

### *Notice of the youth disposed toward painting.*

**M**any are the men who have a desire and love for drawing, but no natural disposition; and this may be recognized in children who lack diligence and never finish their works with shadows.

### *Precept for the painter.*

**I**t is not praiseworthy for a painter to do only one thing well, such as a nude, a head, drapery, animals, landscapes, or similar particulars; for there is no mind so dull that, having turned itself to one single thing and practicing it constantly, would not eventually do it well (12) <note>Leonardo argues for a universal mastery rather than specialization, which he views as a sign of limited intellect.</note>.

<summary>Leonardo argues that a painter must work in solitude to maintain mental focus and asserts that true artistic talent is marked by diligence and a mastery of all subjects rather than specializing in just one.</summary>

## *In what way the* youth *should proceed in his* study.

**T**he mind of the painter must continually transform itself into as many reflections as there are figures of notable objects appearing before him; he should pause at these, observe them, and create rules based upon them, considering the location, the circumstances, the lights, and the shadows.

### *On the method of* studying.

**S**tudy the science first, and then follow the practice born from that science <note>Leonardo emphasizes that "science" (the underlying principles of nature and optics) must precede "practice" (the manual execution).</note>. The painter must study with a system, leaving nothing that is not committed to memory, and observing what differences exist between the limbs of animals and their joints.

### *To what likeness the* genius *of the* painter *should be.*

**T**he genius <note>original: "ingegno" – referring to the painter's innate creative intellect and talent.</note> of the painter should be like a mirror, which always transforms itself into the color of whatever object it faces, and fills itself with as many likenesses as there are things placed before it. Therefore, knowing that you, the painter, cannot be good unless you are a universal master of imitating with your art all the qualities of forms produced by nature—which you will not know how to do unless you see them and represent them in your mind—ensure that when you walk through the countryside, your judgment turns to various objects. From one moment to the next, look now at this thing, now at that, making a bundle <note>original: "fascio" – a collection or gathering of observations.</note> of various things selected and chosen from among those that are less good. And do not act like some painters who, tired in their imagination, set aside their work and take exercise with...

<summary>Leonardo advises the young painter to maintain a mind like a mirror, constantly observing and cataloging the variety of nature to achieve universal mastery. He stresses that artistic practice must always be rooted in scientific understanding and disciplined observation of the world.</summary>

<keywords>artistic education, observation, science and practice, universal mastery, imitation of nature, painter's mind, anatomy, light and shadow</keywords>

### *On the judgment of the painter.*

## *Discourse on the precepts of the painter.*

**I** have observed universally among all those who make a profession of portraying faces from life, that he who achieves the greatest likeness is a poorer composer of Histories <term>Istorie: complex narrative paintings featuring multiple figures, considered the highest form of art</term> than any other painter. And this arises because it is manifest that nature has more disposed him toward that specific thing than toward another; for this reason, he has held more love for it, and that greater love has made him more diligent. And all the love that is placed upon a part is lacking from the whole, because all his delight has been united in that single thing, abandoning the universal for the particular. Since the power of such a genius <note>original: "ingegno"</note> is reduced to a small space, it has no power in expansion. This genius acts in the likeness of a concave mirror, which, catching the rays of the Sun, reflects that quantity of rays with a milder warmth when it reflects them across a greater expansion; but when it reflects them all into a smaller place, then such rays are of immense heat, yet applied only to a small area. So do...

These such painters, loving no other part of painting than the human face alone. And what is worse is that they recognize no other part of the art which they might esteem, or upon which they might have judgment; their works being without movement, and because they themselves are lazy and of little motion, they blame that thing which has greater and more prompt movements than those made by them; saying that such figures appear possessed <note>original: "spiritati"</note>, and masters of Moorish dances <term>Moresche: a lively, rhythmic dance often involving exaggerated gestures</term>. It is true that one must observe decorum, that is, that the movements must be announcers of the motion of the mind of the mover <note>Leonardo’s famous principle that physical gestures must reveal the internal emotional state (moto dell' animo).</note>; that is, if one has to figure someone who must demonstrate a fearful reverence, that it should not be made with such audacity and presumption <note>original: "prosonzione"</note> that such an affection appears as desperation, or as if giving a command.

As I saw in recent days an angel who appeared, in his Annunciation, as if he wanted to chase Our Lady out of her room, with movements that demonstrated as much insult as could possibly be done to a most vile enemy. And Our Lady appeared as if she wanted, in desperation, to throw herself out of a window. Therefore, keep it in mind not to fall into such defects.

Of this matter I will make no excuse to anyone, because if one believes that I am speaking to him, it is because everyone who acts in his own way condemns himself, and thinks he does well; and this you will recognize in those who follow a practice without ever taking counsel from the works of nature, and are only turned toward doing much, and for a penny more of daily gain they would sooner sew shoes than paint. But of these I do not extend into a longer discourse, because I do not accept them into the art that is the daughter of nature. But to speak of painters and their judgments, I say that to him who moves his figures too much, it seems that he who moves them as much as is appropriate makes figures that are asleep; and to him who moves them little, it seems...

### Precept of the painter.

**I**f you, painter, will strive to please the leading painters, you will make your painting well, because they alone are those who can judge you with truth. But if you wish to please those who are not masters, your paintings will have few foreshortenings <term>scorti: the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth</term>, and little relief, or prompt movement. And for this reason, you will fail in that part for which painting is held to be an excellent art—that is, in making that which has no relief appear to be in relief. And here the painter surpasses the sculptor, who provides no wonder of himself in such relief, since that which the painter acquires through his art is made by nature for the sculptor.

## *On being universal.*

### *On the practitioner of painting and his precepts.*

**I** remind you, painter, that when by your own judgment or by the advice of others you discover some errors in your works, you should correct them, so that in publishing such a work you do not publish your own shortcomings <note>original: "materia tua" (14) — literally "your material," implying one's own flaws or lack of skill</note> along with it. Do not excuse yourself by persuading yourself that you will restore your reputation in your next work, because painting does not die immediately upon its creation as music does; rather, for a long time it will bear witness to your ignorance. And if you say that correcting takes time which, if spent on another work, would earn you much more, you must understand that the money earned in excess of what is needed for our living is not worth much. If you desire it in abundance, you will never finish working, and it is not truly yours. All treasure that is not used is "ours" only in name; and what you earn that does not serve your life is in the hands of others without your benefit. But if you study and polish your works well with the discourse of the two perspectives <note>Leonardo likely refers to linear perspective (geometry) and aerial perspective (the effect of atmosphere on color and clarity).</note>, you will leave behind such works that will give you more honor than money. Nothing deceives us more than our own judgment if it acts in passing sentence upon our own works; yet it is effective in judging the things of enemies and friends, because hatred and friendship are two of the most powerful influences <note>original: "accidenti" — in Renaissance philosophy, these are non-essential qualities or conditions that affect a subject</note> found among living beings. And for this reason, you, O painter, should be eager to hear what your adversaries say of your works no less willingly than what your friends say; for hatred is more powerful than love, because hatred ruins and destroys love. Since a true friend is like another self, he may be deceived in his judgment. There is then a third kind of judgment: those moved by envy who give birth to flattery, praising the beginning of good works so that the lie may blind the practitioner.

### *A way to increase and awaken the mind*
### *to various inventions.*

**I** shall not refrain from including among these precepts a new method of speculation <note>original: "speculazione" — deep observation or theoretical study</note> which, although it may seem small and almost ridiculous, is nonetheless of great utility in awakening the mind to various inventions. And this is: if you look at certain walls stained with various spots, or stones of mixed colors. If you have to invent some setting, you will be able to see there the likenesses of diverse landscapes, adorned with mountains, rivers, rocks, trees, great plains, valleys, and hills in various arrangements. Furthermore, you will be able to see there different battles and the lively actions of strange figures, expressions of faces, and costumes, and infinite things which you can then reduce into complete and good form. It happens with such walls and mixtures just as it does with the sound of bells: in their ringing, you will find every name and word that you can imagine.

### *On studying even when you wake, or before you sleep in bed in the dark.*

I have also experienced it to be of no small utility, when you find yourself in the dark in bed, to go about repeating with the imagination the superficial outlines of the forms previously studied, or other notable things understood through subtle speculations <note>original: "speculazioni" — intellectual observations or theoretical inquiries</note>; and this is truly a laudable act and useful for confirming things in the memory.

some useful amusement, one should always use things relevant to your profession—that is, to develop a good "judgment of the eye" <note>original: "giudizio d’occhio"; the ability to estimate proportions and distances accurately by sight alone</note> in knowing how to judge the truth of the widths and lengths of things. Also, see who can best draw a line of one cubit, and let it be tested with a pulled thread. Such games are the cause of developing a good judgment of the eye, which is the principal act of painting.

## *Whether it is better to draw in company or not.*

**I** say and confirm that drawing in company is much better than drawing alone, for many reasons. The first is that you will be ashamed to be seen among the number of draftsmen if you are insufficient, and this shame will be the cause of good study. Secondly, a "good envy" <note>a healthy sense of competition or emulation</note> will stimulate you to be among those more praised than yourself, for the praise of others will spur you on. Another reason is that you will learn from the gestures of those who do better than you; and if you are better than the others, you will profit by avoiding their flaws, and the praise of others will increase your virtue.

## *The way to learn well by heart.*

**W**hen you wish to know a thing you have studied well by heart, follow this method: that is, when you have drawn the same thing so many times that you seem to have it in your mind, try to do it without the model. Then, have your model traced <note>original: "lucidato"; the process of making a transparent tracing</note> upon a thin, flat piece of glass, and place this over the thing you have made without the model. Note well where the tracing does not match your drawing. And where you find you have erred, keep it in mind not to err again in the future. Return to the model to redraw that mistaken part as many times as necessary until you have it well in your imaginative faculty. And if you cannot obtain a flat glass to trace a thing, take a piece of thin kidskin parchment <note>original: "carta di capretto"; a very fine, translucent vellum used for tracing</note>—

## *How the painter is not praiseworthy if he is not universal.*

**I**t can be clearly said that some are deceived who call that painter a good master who only does a head or a figure well. Certainly, it is no great feat that by studying a single thing for the whole of one's life, one should reach some perfection in it; but knowing that painting embraces and contains within itself all things produced by nature, and those brought about by the accidental actions of men—and ultimately whatever can be comprehended by the eyes—it seems to me a poor master who only does one figure well. Now, do you not see how many and what kind of actions are performed by men? Do you not see how many different animals there are, as well as trees, herbs, and flowers; the variety of mountainous and level sites, springs, rivers, cities, public and private buildings, tools suitable for human use, various garments, ornaments, and arts? All these things ought to be practiced with equal skill and goodness by the one you wish to call a good painter.

These men, with the utmost foolishness, allege that they do not produce good work because of poor payment, and that they...

### *How the painter should be eager to hear everyone's judgment while creating a work.*

**C**ertainly, while a man is painting, he should not refuse the judgment of anyone. For we clearly know that a man, even if he is not a painter, will have knowledge of the form of another man, and will judge well if he is hunchbacked, or if he has one shoulder high or low, or if he has a large mouth or nose, or other defects <term>mancamenti: physical flaws or errors in anatomical proportion</term>. If we know that men can truly judge the works of nature, how much more must we confess that they can judge our errors, knowing how much a man deceives himself in his own works. And if you do not recognize this in yourself, consider it in others, and you will profit from their mistakes. Therefore, be eager to listen patiently to the opinions of others; consider well, and think deeply whether the critic has cause or not to blame you. And if you find that he is right, correct it; and if you find he is not, act as though you have not heard him. And if he is a man you esteem, show him by reason how he is mistaken.

### *Of the variety of figures.*

**T**he painter must seek to be universal, because he lacks much dignity if he does one thing well and another poorly: like many who only study the measured and proportioned nude <note>original: "ignudo" - the standard term for the naked human form in Renaissance art theory</note>, and do not seek its variety. For a man may be well-proportioned and yet be fat and short, or long and thin, or medium; and he who does not take account of this variety always makes his figures according to a template <note>original: "in stampa" - literally 'in print' or 'from a stamp,' meaning repetitive or formulaic</note>, so that they all appear to be sisters, which deserves great rebuke.

->*Of those who use practice without diligence, or rather, science.*<-

Those who fall in love with practice without diligence, or rather science, to put it better, are like mariners who take to the sea in a ship without a rudder or a compass, who never have certainty of where they are going. ->*On not imitating another painter.*<-

->*On drawing from nature.*<-

When you have to draw from nature, stand at a distance three times the size of the object you are portraying; and ensure that when you draw, or when you begin any line, you look throughout the entire body you are portraying, noting whatever aligns with the direction of the principal line.

## *Advice to the Painter.*

Note well in your portraying, how among the shadows there are shadows insensible in their darkness and shape; and this is proven by the third [proposition], which says that globular surfaces possess as many varieties of darkness and light as there are varieties of darkness and light in the objects surrounding them <note>Leonardo is referring to his theory of reflections, where a rounded object "mirrors" the light and dark of its environment within its own shadows</note>.

->*How high the light should be for portraying*<-
->*from nature.*<-

The light for portraying from nature should be from the north <note>original: "tramontana"</note>, so that it does not change; and if you use a southern light, keep the windows covered with cloth <note>original: "impannate" - windows covered with oiled linen or paper to diffuse sunlight</note>, so that the sun, shining all day, does not cause the lighting to shift. The height of the light should be situated in such a way that every body casts a shadow on the ground as long as the body is high.

->*Which lights should be chosen for portraying*<-
->*the forms of bodies.*<-

The forms of any body are compelled to take on that light in which you imagine those figures to be; that is, if you imagine such figures in the countryside, they are surrounded by a great amount of light when the sun is not visible; and if the sun sees said figures <note>meaning if they are in direct sunlight</note>, their shadows will be very dark compared to the illuminated parts, and they will be shadows with sharp edges <note>original: "termini espediti"</note>, both the primary and the derivative shadows. Such shadows will harmonize little with the lights, because from one side the blue of the air illuminates and tints with its own color the part that it sees; and this is very evident in white objects: and that part...

<summary>Leonardo provides technical instructions on the behavior of light and shadow on curved surfaces and advises painters to use stable, diffused northern light for consistent portraiture.</summary>

<page-num>71</page-num>

that is illuminated by the sun, is shown to participate in the color of the sun. You will see this very clearly when the sun sinks to the horizon among the redness of the clouds, so that those clouds are tinted with the color that illuminates them. This redness of the clouds, together with the redness of the sun, makes everything that takes light from them turn reddish; and the part of the bodies that does not see this redness remains the color of the air. Anyone seeing such bodies judges them to be of two colors. From this you cannot escape: once you have shown the cause of such shadows and lights, you must make them participate in the aforementioned causes; otherwise, your work is vain and false. 

And if your figure is in a dark house and you see it from the outside, such a figure will have soft, smoky shadows <note>original: "ombre sfumate" — the famous Leonardo technique of blurring edges to create depth</note> if you are standing in the line of the light. That figure will have grace and bring honor to its imitator <note>the artist</note> by having great relief and sweet, smoky shadows, especially in that part where you see the darkness of the dwelling the least; for there, the shadows are almost imperceptible. The reason for this shall be stated in its proper place.

### *On the qualities of light for portraying natural or artificial reliefs.*

**L**ight that is cut off from shadows with too much sharpness is highly criticized among painters. Therefore, to avoid such an inconvenience, if you are painting bodies in the open countryside, do not paint the figures illuminated by the sun. Instead, feign a certain quantity of mist or transparent clouds to be interposed between the object and the sun. Since the figure is not struck by direct sunlight, the boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note> of the shadows will not be sharply defined against the boundaries of the lights.

->*On portraying nudes.*<-

When you portray nudes, always ensure you sketch them in their entirety, and then finish that limb which seems best to you, and put that into practice with the other limbs; otherwise, you would fall into the habit of never joining the limbs together well. And never make the head turned in the same direction as the chest, nor the arm move in the same way as the leg. And if the head turns toward the right shoulder, make its parts lower on the left side than on the right; and if you make the chest protruding, ensure that as the head turns toward the left side, the parts of the right side are higher than the left <note>Leonardo is describing "contrapposto," the classical pose where the weight shift and counter-rotation of the body create a sense of dynamic balance and life.</note> (17).

->*On portraying from artificial relief, or from nature.*<-

He who portrays from relief <note>original: "di rilievo" — likely referring to plaster casts or sculptures used for practice</note> must arrange himself in such a way that the eye of the figure being portrayed is level with the eye of the one who is portraying it. And this should be done for a head which you have to portray from life <note>original: "di naturale"</note>, because universally, the figures or persons that you encounter in the streets all have their eyes at the same height as yours; and if you were to make them higher or lower, you would diminish the likeness of your portrait.

->*Method of portraying with glass.*<-

Take a piece of glass as large as a half-sheet of royal paper, and fix it firmly before your eyes—that is, between your eyes and the object you wish to portray. Then position yourself with your eye two-thirds of a "braccio" <note>A "braccio" or "arm's length" was a common Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches; two-thirds would be about 15 inches.</note> away from said glass, and steady your head with an instrument in such a way that you cannot move it at all. Afterward, close or cover one eye, and with a brush or a pencil <note>original: "lapis" — likely a leadpoint or graphite stylus</note>, mark on the glass that which...

### *How landscapes should be portrayed.*

**L**andscapes should be portrayed in such a way that the trees are half-lit and half-shadowed; but it is better to do them when the sun is partially obscured by clouds, for then the trees are illuminated by the universal light of the sky and the universal shadow of the earth; and these parts are darker the closer they are to the ground.

### *On portraying by candlelight.*

**T**o this light at night, let a frame <note>original: "telajo"</note> be interposed, either with oiled paper or without oiling it, but simply a whole sheet of thin chancery paper <note>original: "carta cancelleresca" — a high-quality, thin writing paper used in administrative offices.</note>, and you will see your shadows become smoky and without hard edges; and let the light, without the interposition of paper, provide illumination to the sheet where you are drawing.

### *The method of portraying simple and composite shadows.*

**D**o not portray a figure indoors with a specific light source <note>original: "lume particolare" — a concentrated light like a lamp or window</note> while pretending it is in the universal light of the countryside without sun; for the countryside creates a simple shadow <term>simple shadow: an even shadow cast by a broad, diffused light source</term>, while the specific light of a window or the sun creates a composite shadow <term>composite shadow: a shadow with varying degrees of darkness, often softened by reflected light</term>, that is, mixed with reflections.

### *On the light where one portrays the flesh tones of faces and nudes.*

**T**his dwelling should be open to the air, with the walls colored in flesh tones <note>original: "incarnato"</note>, and the portraits should be made in summer when the clouds cover the sun: or truly, you shall make the southern walls so high that the rays of the sun do not strike the northern wall, so that its reflected rays do not spoil the shadows.

### *On portraying figures for narrative paintings.*

**T**he painter must always consider, on the wall which he is to paint with a narrative <note>original: "istoriare" — to create a "history painting" or narrative scene</note>, the height of the site where he wishes to place his figures; and whatever he portrays from nature for said purpose, he should keep his eye as much lower than the thing he is portraying as that thing is to be placed higher than the eye of the viewer. Otherwise, his work will be blameworthy <note>original: "reprobabile" — technically incorrect or subject to criticism</note>.

### *On portraying a nude from life, or other subjects.*

**U**se the practice of holding a string with a hanging lead weight <note>original: "piombo pendente" — a plumb line</note> in your hand, so that you may see the alignments <note>original: "scontri" — the vertical correspondence of one part of the body to another</note> of the parts.

### *Measurements and divisions of the statue.*

**D**ivide the head into twelve degrees, and divide each degree into 12 points, and each point into 12 minutes, and the minutes into minimums, and the minimums into semi-minimums. <note>This reflects the Renaissance obsession with "harmonic" proportions, breaking the human form down into infinitesimal mathematical units.</note>

### *Method of portraying a relief at night.*

**E**nsure that you place a paper that is not too glossy between the relief <note>original: "rilievo" — a three-dimensional sculpture or model</note> and the light source, and you will have a good result in your drawing. <note>The paper acts as a diffuser to soften harsh candlelight.</note>

### *How the painter should position himself relative to the light and his relief.*

*a b* represents the window, *m* represents the point of the light source; I say that in whatever position the painter stands, he will be well-placed, provided that the eye remains between the shaded part and the illuminated part of the body being portrayed: which place you will find by positioning yourself between point *m* and the division that the shadow makes from the light upon the portrayed body. (*Fig. 2. Plate I.*)

### *On the quality of the light.*

**A** light that is large and high, but not too powerful, will be that which renders the details of the bodies very pleasing.

## *On the deception experienced in the judgment of limbs.*

**T**hat painter who has clumsy hands will make them similar in his works, and the same will happen to him with any limb, unless long study prevents it. Therefore, you, painter, look well at that part which is most ugly in your own person, and with all study provide a good remedy for it; because if you are brutish <note>original: "bestiale" — lacking refinement or acting on animal instinct</note>, your figures will appear the same, and if you have talent likewise, every part of good and of bad that you have in yourself will be demonstrated in part in your figures.

## *That one must know the internal form of man.*

**T**hat painter who has knowledge of the nature of the nerves, muscles, and tendons <note>original: "lacerti" — an archaic term for the fleshy part of the muscle</note>, will know well, in moving a limb, how many and which nerves are the cause of it, and which muscle by swelling is the cause of shortening that nerve, and which cords <note>original: "corde" — referring to tendons</note> converted into very thin cartilages wrap and surround the said muscle; and thus he will be a diverse and universal demonstrator of various muscles, by means of the various actions of the figures, and will not do as many, who in different acts always show those same things in arms, backs, chests, and other muscles, which things should not be counted among small errors.

## *On the defect of the painter.*

**I**t is a supreme defect in masters who are accustomed to repeating the same movements in the same stories near to one another, and similarly the beauties of the faces being always one and the same—

## *On the same defect of painters.*

**I**t is a supreme defect of painters to replicate the same motions, and the same faces, and the same styles of drapery in a single Narrative <note>original: "Istoria" — a technical term for a complex multi-figure composition depicting a historical, biblical, or mythological event</note>, and to make the majority of the faces resemble their master. This has many times caused me wonder, because I have known some who, in all their figures, seem to have portrayed themselves from life (18). And in those figures, one sees the acts and motions of their maker: if he is quick in speech and in his movements, his figures are similar in their quickness; and if the master is devout, the figures likewise appear with their necks bent <note>original: "colli torti" — a posture associated with religious humility or affectation</note>; and if the master is of little worth, his figures appear as laziness portrayed from life; and if the master is disproportionate, his figures are similar. And if he is foolish, it is demonstrated extensively in his Narratives, which are enemies of resolution and do not attend to their own actions; rather, some look here and others there as if they were dreaming; and thus every quality in the painting follows the specific quality of the painter. And having many times considered the cause of such a defect, it seems to me that one must judge that the soul which rules and governs each body is that which forms our judgment before it is even our own conscious judgment. Therefore, she <note>The soul (anima) is grammatically feminine in Italian</note> has constructed the whole figure of the man as she judged it to be right—whether with a long nose, or short, or snub-nosed <note>original: "camuffo"</note>—and thus she established the...

He argues that this lack of variety is a major flaw, as nature itself never repeats the same form exactly.</summary>

its height and form. And this judgment is of such power that it moves the painter's arms and makes him replicate himself, as it seems to that soul that such is the true way to represent a man, and whoever does not do as she <note>The soul is referred to as "she" (Italian: "anima"), a feminine noun.</note> does is in error. And if she finds anyone who resembles the body she has composed, she loves them and often falls in love with them. And for this reason, many fall in love and take a wife who resembles themselves, and often the children born of such unions resemble their parents.

### *Precept so that the painter does not deceive himself in the choice of the figure he depicts.*

**T**he painter ought to create his figure based on the rule of a natural body, which is commonly of praiseworthy proportion; beyond this, he should have himself measured and see in what parts his own person varies much or little from that aforementioned praiseworthy standard. Once this knowledge is gained, he must strive with all his study to avoid falling into the same defects in the figures he creates that he finds in his own person. You must fight against this vice with the utmost effort, since it is a defect born together with judgment; because the soul, the mistress of your body, is that which is your own judgment, and she willingly delights in works similar to that which she performed in the composing of her own body. From this it arises that there is no female figure so ugly that she does not find some lover, unless she be monstrous; so remember to understand the defects that are in your own person, and guard against them in the figures that are composed by you.

<note>Leonardo is warning against "automorphism"—the tendency of an artist to project their own physical characteristics onto their subjects. He suggests that the soul acts as a blueprint for the body, and unless the artist is consciously aware of their own proportions, they will instinctively recreate their own likeness in every painting.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains that the soul's innate preference for its own physical form leads painters to replicate their own likeness and defects in their art. He advises artists to measure their own bodies to identify personal deviations from ideal proportions so they can consciously avoid projecting these traits onto their figures.</summary>

### *The defect of painters who portray a thing in relief*
### *indoors by one light, and then place it*
### *in the countryside by another light.*

**I**t is a great error of those painters who portray a thing in relief <note>A three-dimensional object or model.</note> by a particular light <note>A focused, directional light source like a lamp or window.</note> in their houses, and then put such a portrait into a work set in the universal light of the air in the countryside, where such air embraces and illuminates all parts of the views in the same manner. In doing so, the painter creates dark shadows where there can be no shadow; or if there is indeed one there, it is of such brightness that it is almost imperceptible. Likewise, they create reflections where it is impossible for them to be seen.

#### *On painting and its division.*

**P**ainting is divided into two principal parts, of which the first is figure—that is, the line that distinguishes the shape of bodies and their particles—and the second is the color contained within those boundaries.

#### *Figure, and its division.*

**T**he figure of bodies is divided into two other parts: namely, the proportionality of the parts among themselves, which must correspond to the whole; and the movement appropriate to the mental state <term>accidente mentale: the internal emotion or thought process that triggers a physical action</term> of the living thing that moves.

### *That errors are not seen in small things as they are in large ones.*

### *Why painting can never appear in relief,*
### *like natural things.*

Painters often fall into despair regarding their imitation of nature, seeing that their paintings do not have that relief and that vivacity which things seen in a mirror possess, alleging that they have colors which by far exceed—in clarity and in darkness—the quality of the lights and shadows of the thing seen in the mirror; in this case, they accuse their own ignorance and not the reason, because they do not know it. ### *Why the arrangement of figures one above the other is a thing to be avoided.*

This universal practice used by painters on the walls of chapels is greatly and reasonably to be blamed, because they place a narrative <note>original: "istoria"; referring to a narrative scene or history painting</note> on one level with its landscape and buildings, then they rise another degree and make another narrative, changing the point of view from the first, and then a third and a fourth, so that a single facade is seen made with four points of view; this is the utmost foolishness of such masters. We know that the point is placed at the eye of the spectator of the narrative: and if you should say: "How am I to depict the life of a Saint divided into many scenes on the same wall?" To this I answer you, that you should place the first foreground with the point at the height of the eye of those viewing the narrative, and on said plane depict the first narrative on a large scale, and then, by degrees, diminishing the figures and buildings upon various hills and plains, you shall create the entire setting of that story. For the rest of the wall, in its upper part, you shall make trees that are large in comparison to the figures, or angels, if they suit the subject of the narrative, or birds, or clouds, or similar things: otherwise, do not trouble yourself with it, for all your work will be false (19). <note>Leonardo is criticizing the medieval and early Renaissance "stacked" perspective, advocating instead for a unified atmospheric perspective where distance is suggested by height and scale within a single coherent space.</note>

### *Which requires more reasoning and utility: the light and shadow of bodies, or their outlines.*

The boundaries of bodies <note>original: "termini de’ corpi"</note> require greater reasoning and ingenuity than shadows and lights, because the outlines of the limbs, which are not bendable, are immutable and are always the same; but the positions, quality, and quantity of shadows are infinite.

### *Which is of greater importance: that a figure abounds in the beauty of colors, or in the demonstration of great relief.*

**O**nly painting presents itself to its observers by making that which is nothing <note>referring to the flat surface of the wall or canvas</note> appear in relief and detached from the walls; and colors only bring honor to the masters who created them <note>referring to the color-makers or chemists, rather than the artist</note>, because they cause no other wonder in themselves than beauty. This beauty is not the virtue of the painter, but of the one who generated those colors. A thing can be clothed in ugly colors and yet cause wonder in its observers by appearing to be in <term>relief</term> <note>the illusion of three-dimensionality on a flat surface</note>.

### *Which is more difficult: shadows and lights, or indeed good drawing.*

**I** say that a thing which is constrained by a limit is more difficult than that which is free. Shadows have their limits at certain degrees, and he who is ignorant of them will find his works lack relief, which relief is the importance and the soul of painting. Drawing <note>original: "disegno"; encompassing both line-work and the underlying design</note> is free, in that one will see infinite faces, all of which will be different. One will have a long nose, another a short one. Therefore, the painter can also take this liberty, and where there is liberty, there is no fixed rule.

### Memorandum for the painter.

**D**escribe which are the muscles, and which are the <term>tendons</term> <note>original: "corde"; literally "cords," the common Renaissance term for tendons or sinews</note>, that through the various movements of each limb are revealed, or hidden, or do neither one nor the other: and remember that such an action is of the utmost importance among painters and sculptors who make a profession of studying muscles. ### *Precepts of painting.*

The painter who wishes to gain honor from his works must always seek out the readiness of natural actions performed by men spontaneously, born from the powerful influence of their emotions. He should make brief sketches of these in his little notebooks <note>original: "libretti"; Leonardo famously carried small notebooks at his belt to capture life in motion</note> and later apply them to his purposes by having a man stand in that same pose, in order to observe the quality and appearance of the limbs that are employed in such an action.

### *Precepts of painting.*

An object, or the figure of it, will reveal itself with more distinct and clear boundaries the closer it is to the eye. Therefore, you, painter—who under the title of "practitioner" <note>original: "prattico"; likely referring to a craftsman who relies on habit rather than scientific theory</note> fakes the view of a head seen from a close distance with finished brushstrokes and harsh, crude hatching—know that you deceive yourself. For at whatever distance you imagine your figure to be, it is always depicted at that specific degree where it is found, even if at a long distance the knowledge of its boundaries is lost. Despite this, it does not fail to be seen in a finished, <term>smoky</term> <note>original: "fumoso"; related to "sfumato," the technique of blurring edges to create depth and atmosphere</note> manner, rather than with clear and crude outlines. 

Therefore, one must conclude that in a work which the eye of the viewer can approach closely, all parts of that painting must be finished in their respective degrees with the utmost diligence. Furthermore, the foremost parts should be defined with known and clear boundaries against their background, while those more distant should be well-finished but with "smokier" boundaries—that is, more confused, or one might say, less distinct the further away they are. Successively observe what was said above: first the less distinct boundaries, then the limbs, and finally the whole figure and color becoming less distinct.

<summary>Leonardo advises painters to capture spontaneous human emotions in sketches and explains the principle of atmospheric perspective, where edges must become softer and less distinct as they recede from the viewer.</summary>
<keywords>observation, notebooks, natural action, sfumato, perspective, edges, finish, artistic practice</keywords>

<header>On the first painting.</header>

**T**he first painting consisted only of a single line, which surrounded the shadow of a man cast by the sun upon the walls.

### *How painting must be viewed from a single window.*

**P**ainting must be viewed from a single window <note>In this context, "window" refers to a single, fixed point of view or aperture, essential for the mathematical consistency of linear perspective</note>, as is evident by the nature of bodies shaped in such a way. And if you wish to depict a round ball at a great height, you will need to make it elongated in the likeness of an egg, and stand back so far that, through <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scorciando"; the visual effect where an object appears shorter or compressed when viewed at an angle</note>, it appears round.

### *On the primary parts into which painting is divided.*

**D**arkness, light, body, figure, location, distance, and proximity. To these, two others can be added: namely, motion and rest; for it is necessary to represent such things in the movements of the subjects that are imagined in painting.

### *How painting is divided into five parts.*

**T**he parts of painting are five: namely, surface, figure, color, shadow and light, proximity and distance—or, if you prefer, increase and decrease. These constitute the two types of perspective: the decrease in the clarity of things seen at a long distance, and the decrease of colors; and which color it is that first diminishes at equal distances, and which one maintains itself the longest.

### *Painting is divided into two principal parts.*

**P**ainting is divided into two principal parts: namely, the outlines which surround the shapes of finished bodies, which outlines are called drawing <note>original: "disegno"; in the Italian Renaissance, this term encompasses both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept of design or intent</note>. The second is called shadow. But this drawing is of such excellence that it not only investigates the works of nature, but infinitely more than those that nature produces. This commands the sculptor to finish his statues <note>original: "simulacri"; images or representations</note>, and it teaches the perfect end to all manual arts, even if they were infinite in number. And for this reason, we shall conclude that it is not only a science, but a deity <note>original: "deità"</note> to be remembered by its rightful name, which deity repeats all the visible works created by the highest God.

### *Considerations to be had in establishing figures, or of linear painting.*

**L**et the boundaries of any body be considered with the utmost diligence, as well as the manner of their winding <note>original: "serpeggiare"; literally "snaking," referring to the graceful, S-shaped curves often sought in Renaissance composition</note>; and let it be judged whether the turns of these windings partake of circular curvature or angular concavity.

### *Of shadows.*

**T**he shadows which you discern with difficulty, and whose boundaries you cannot know—but rather perceive and transfer into your work with a confused judgment—you shall not make finished or truly defined, so that your work may have an ingenious result <note>original: "risultazione"; likely referring to the "sfumato" effect where edges blur into one another to create a sense of depth and realism</note>.

<header>Of the parts and qualities of painting.</header>

**T**he first part of painting is that the bodies figured therein demonstrate themselves in relief, and that the fields surrounding them, with their distances, demonstrate themselves as receding into the wall where such painting is generated, by means of the three perspectives: that is, the diminution of the figures of the bodies, the diminution of their magnitudes, and the diminution of their colors. And of these three perspectives, the first has its origin in the eye; the other two are derived from the air interposed between the eye and the object seen by that eye. The second part of painting consists of the appropriate and varied actions in the figures, so that men do not appear to be brothers <note>Leonardo emphasizes variety (varietà) to avoid the "monotony" of figures looking too similar to one another.</note>.

## *Of the selection of beautiful faces.*

**I**t seems to me no small grace in that painter who gives good expressions <note>original: "arie"; literally "airs," referring to the overall character, mood, or "look" of a face.</note> to his figures. He who does not possess this grace by nature may acquire it through accidental study in this manner: Look to take the good parts of many beautiful faces, which beautiful parts are confirmed more by public fame than by your own judgment; for you might deceive yourself by choosing faces that have a conformity with your own. Because it often seems that such conformities please us; and if you were ugly, you would choose faces that were not beautiful, and you would create ugly faces, as many painters do, whose figures often resemble the master. Therefore, take beauties, as I tell you, and fix them in your mind.

### *How one should depict <term>putti</term> <note>Italian for "little boys," often referring to the chubby, winged infants in Renaissance art.</note>.*

**T**he small children should be depicted with quick and twisting gestures when they sit, and when standing, with timid and fearful gestures.

### *How one should depict <term>old men</term>.*

**O**ld men should be made with lazy and slow movements, their legs bent at the knees when they stand still, and their feet parallel and distant from one another; they should be inclined downward, the head bowed forward, and the arms not too extended.

### *How one should depict <term>old women</term>.*

**O**ld women should be depicted as bold and quick, with angry movements, in the manner of infernal furies; and the movements should appear quicker in the arms and heads than in the legs.

### *How one should depict <term>women</term>.*

**W**omen should be depicted with modest gestures, their legs drawn close together, their arms gathered together, heads low, and tilted to the side.

**T**hat thing which is entirely deprived of light is all darkness; the night being in such a condition, if you wish to depict a <term>narrative scene</term> <note>original: "istoria"; a complex multi-figure composition representing a story.</note> within it, you shall ensure that, there being a great fire, that thing which is nearest to said fire is most colored by its—

### *On the method of depicting distant things in painting,*

**I**t is clearly seen that one layer of air is thicker than another, specifically that which borders the flat earth; and the higher it rises, the thinner and more transparent it becomes. Regarding high and large things that are far from you, their lower parts will be less visible, because you see them through a line which, although it begins at your eye in the thick air, nevertheless, by ending at the very summit of the object seen, ends in air much thinner than that of its base. For this reason, as this line moves further from you point by point, it constantly changes quality from thin to thinner air. Therefore, you, the painter, when you create mountains, ensure that from hill to hill the bases are always lighter; and when you make them more distant from one another, make the bases lighter, and the higher they rise, the more they should show the truth of their form and color. <note>This describes "aerial perspective," the technique of using color and clarity to show depth.</note>

### *How the air must be made clearer the lower*
### *you make it end.*

**B**ecause this air is thick near the earth, and the higher it rises, the thinner it becomes, when the sun is in the east you shall look toward the west, toward the south and north, and you will see that this thick air receives more light from the sun than the thin air, because the rays <note>original: "razzi"</note> find more resistance. And if the sky, to your sight, ends at a low plain, that furthest part of the sky will be seen through that thicker and whiter air, which will corrupt the truth of the color seen through it; and the sky will appear whiter there than it does above you, because the visual line passes through a smaller quantity of air corrupted by thick vapors. And if you look toward the east, the air will appear darker to you the lower it goes, because in said low air the luminous rays pass through less easily.

->Whether the light should be taken from the front or from the side, and which gives more grace.<-

Light taken from the front of faces placed against side walls that are dark will cause such faces to have great relief <note>The term "relief" (rilievo) refers to the three-dimensional quality or "popping" effect of a painted figure.</note>, especially when having the light from above. This relief occurs because the front parts of such a face are illuminated by the universal light of the air placed before it, whereby such illuminated parts have almost imperceptible shadows; and after these front parts of the face follow the side parts, darkened by the aforementioned side walls of the rooms, which darken the face all the more as that face enters between them with its parts. Besides this, it follows that the light descending from above deprives itself of all those parts for which a shield is made by the projections of the face—such as the eyebrows, which withdraw the light from the sockets of the eyes, and the nose, which takes it from a large part of the mouth, and the chin from the throat, and other similar projections.

->*Where there can be no luminous reverberation.*<-

All dense bodies are clothed on their surfaces with various qualities of light and shadow. Lights are of two natures: one is called original, and the other derivative. I say original light is that which derives from the flame of fire, or from the light of the sun, or the atmosphere. Derivative light will be reflected light. But to return to the promised definition, I say that luminous reverberation <note>original: "riverberazione luminosa"; the bouncing of light from one surface to another.</note> will not occur from that part of a body which is turned toward shadowy bodies, such as the dark spaces of roofs of various heights, or of grass, green or dry woods; for although the part of each branch turned toward the original light is clothed in the quality of that light, nevertheless there are so many shadows cast by each branch upon the other that, in short, such darkness results that the light there is as nothing. Therefore, such objects cannot give any reflected light to the bodies opposite them.

->*On reflections.*<-

Reflections participate more or less in the nature of the surface where they are produced, and in the nature of the object that produces them, according to whether the surface where they are produced is of a more polished quality than the object that produces them.

->*On the reflections of lights that surround shadows.*<-

The reflections of illuminated parts that bounce into the opposite shadows illuminate or lighten their darkness more or less, <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the following page.</note>

### *Where the reflections of lights are of greater or lesser clarity.*

**T**he reflections of lights possess lesser or greater clarity and evidence in proportion to whether they are seen against backgrounds of greater or lesser darkness. This happens because if the background is darker than the reflection, then that reflection will be strong and evident due to the great difference these colors have between them. But if the reflection is seen against a background lighter than itself, then such a reflection will appear dark in comparison to the whiteness with which it borders, and thus such a reflection will be imperceptible <note>original: "insensibile"; literally "insensible," meaning it cannot be detected by the eye.</note>.

### On the reflected colors of flesh.

The reflections of flesh that receive light from other flesh are redder and of a more excellent "incarnation" <note>original: "incarnazione"; a technical term in painting referring to the depiction of skin tones and flesh.</note> than any other part of flesh found on a man: and this happens because of the third rule of the second book, which says: the surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its object; and more so as such an object is closer to it, and less so as it is more remote, and as the opaque body is larger. Because if it is large, it blocks the appearances <note>original: "specie"; in Renaissance optics, these are the visual images or "species" emitted by objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> of surrounding objects, which are often of various colors that corrupt the primary, closer appearances when the bodies are small. However, it is still possible for a small, nearby color to tint a reflection more than a large, remote color, according to the sixth rule of perspective, which says: large things can be at such a distance that they will appear much smaller than small things nearby.

### *Where reflections are most noticeable.*

That reflection will be of more immediate clarity which is seen against a field of greater darkness, and that one will be less noticeable which is seen against a lighter field. This arises because when things of varying darkness are placed in contrast, the less dark one makes the darker one appear even more shadowy; and when things of varying whiteness are placed in contrast, the whitest one makes the other appear less white than it truly is.

### *On double and triple reflections.*

Double reflections are of greater power than single reflections, and the shadows that are placed between the incident light <note>The primary light falling directly onto a surface.</note> and these reflections are of little darkness. For example, let *a* be the light source; *a n* and *a s* are the direct rays; *s n* are the illuminated parts; *o b* are the parts of these bodies illuminated by reflections. The reflection *a n e* is a single reflection, while *a n o* and *a s o* is a double reflection. A single reflection is defined as that which is seen from only one illuminated source, and the double is seen from two illuminated bodies. The single reflection *e* is created by the illuminated part *b d*; the double reflection *o* is composed of the illuminated part *b d* and the illuminated part *d r*. Its shadow, which is placed between the incident light *n* and the reflected light *n o, s o*, is of little darkness. (*Fig. 6. Plate I.*)

No color that reflects onto the surface of another body tints that surface with its own pure color, but it will be <insert>mixed with the colors of the objects surrounding it.</insert>

Therefore you, painter, make sure to use in the reflections of the faces of your figures the color of the parts of the garments which are near the parts of the flesh closest to them; but do not separate them with too much definition unless necessary.

## *On the colors of reflections.*

**A**ll reflected colors are of less luminosity than direct light, and the proportion between the incident light <term>incident light: light falling directly onto a surface</term> and the reflected light is the same as the proportion between the luminosities of their causes.

## *On the boundaries of reflections in their field.*

**T**he boundary of reflections against a field lighter than the reflection itself will cause that reflection to end against a field darker than it, and then that reflection will be perceptible, and it will make itself more evident the darker that field is, and vice versa.
