Later, through the movement of the limbs, the skin grows over the folds of the joints, and thus when the limbs are extended, the skin that grew over the joints becomes wrinkled. Furthermore, as one grows in age, the muscles thin out, and the skin that covers them begins to grow and fill with wrinkles, sagging and separating from the muscles due to the fluids <note>original: "umori" — referring to the four humors or bodily fluids believed in Renaissance medicine to govern health and physical state</note> interposed between the muscles and the skin. The branching of the nerves, which connect the skin to the muscles and provide sensation, become stripped of the muscular parts that once covered them, and in place of those muscles, they are surrounded by poor fluids. Because of this, they are poorly and insufficiently nourished; hence, such a structure of limbs—partly due to the continuous weight of the skin and partly due to the excess fluid—becomes elongated, distancing the skin from the muscles and bones, and forming various sacks full of folds and wrinkles.

### *How it is necessary for the painter to know <term>anatomy</term>*

<note>original: "notomia" — a Renaissance spelling of anatomy</note>

**I**t is a necessary thing for the painter, in order to be a good composer of limbs in the attitudes and gestures that can be made by nude figures, to know the <term>anatomy</term> of nerves, bones, muscles, and sinews <note>original: "lacerti" — specifically the fleshy parts of the muscles</note>, so as to know in different movements and exertions which nerve or muscle is the cause of such a movement. And the artist should only make those specific ones evident and enlarged, and not all of them throughout the body, as many do; for to appear as great draftsmen, they make their nudes woody and without grace, so that they look more like a sack of walnuts than a human surface, or rather a bundle of radishes rather than muscular nudes.

**T**he muscle of the back of the thigh shows a greater variety in its extension and contraction than any other muscle in the human body. The second is that which composes the buttock. The third is that of the back. The fourth is that of the throat. The fifth is that of the shoulders. The sixth is that of the stomach, which originates below the <term>pomegranate</term> <note>original: "pomo granato" — a historical anatomical term for the xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone</note>, and ends below the <term>pubic bone</term> <note>original: "pettignone" — an archaic term for the pubic region</note>, as will be said of them all.

### *Where a cord is found in men without muscles.*

**W**here the arm ends at the palm of the hand, about four fingers' width away, there is a cord—the largest in man—which is without a muscle; it originates in the middle of one of the <term>focili</term> <note>original: "fucili del braccio" — referring to the two bones of the forearm, the radius and the ulna</note> of the arm, and ends in the middle of the other bone. It has a square shape, is about three fingers wide, and half a finger thick; this serves only to hold the two aforementioned bones of the arm tightly together so that they do not spread apart.

### *Of the eight pieces that originate in the middle of the cords in various joints of man*

**T**here originate in the joints of man certain pieces of bone, which are fixed in the middle of the cords <note>original: "corde" — here meaning tendons or ligaments</note> that bind certain joints, such as the kneecaps, and those of the shoulders and the feet. These are eight in total: there being one for each shoulder, one for each knee, and two for each foot under the first joint of the big toes toward the heel; and these become extremely hard as a man reaches old age.

### *Of the muscle that is between the pomegranate and the pubic bone.*

**A** muscle originates between the <term>pomegranate</term> <note>original: "pomo granato" — the xiphoid process at the base of the sternum</note> and the <term>pubic bone</term> <note>original: "pettignone" — the pubic region</note> (I say it ends in the pubic bone), which is of three powers, because it is divided in its length by three cords <note>original: "corde" — here referring to the tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis</note>. That is: first the upper muscle, then follows a cord as wide as the muscle itself; then follows the second muscle lower than this, to which the second cord is joined; finally follows the third muscle with the third cord, which cord is joined to the bone of the pubic region. These three repetitions of three muscles with three cords are made by Nature because of the great movement a man has in bending and extending himself with such a muscle. If it were made of a single piece, it would create too much variation in its stretching and contracting during the bending and extending of the man. It creates greater beauty in the man to have little variation in such a muscle during his actions; for if the muscle has to extend nine <term>fingers</term> <note>original: "dita" — a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to 3/4 of an inch</note> and then retract as many, it only amounts to three fingers for each muscle segment. These create little variation in their shape and do little to deform the beauty of the body. (*Fig. 14. Plate IV.*)

### *Of the extreme twisting that a man can do to see behind himself.*

**T**he extreme twisting that a man can perform will be in showing his heels behind him while his face is looking forward. This cannot be done without difficulty, and only if the leg is bent and the shoulder facing the <term>nape</term> <note>original: "nucca"</note> is lowered. The cause of such twisting shall be demonstrated in the anatomy, along with which muscles move first and which move last. (*Fig. 15. Plate IV.*)

### *How much one arm can be brought*
### *toward the other from behind.*

**O**f the arms that are sent behind the back, the elbows will never be closer together than the distance required for the longest fingers to pass the elbow of the opposite hand. That is to say, the closest the elbows can possibly be behind the small of the back <note>original: "reni" — literally "kidneys," but used here to refer to the lumbar region or lower back</note> is a space equal to the distance from one's elbow to the tip of the longest finger of that hand; these arms thus form a perfect square. And as for how much the arms can be crossed over the chest so that the elbows meet in the middle of the chest, these elbows, along with the shoulders and arms, form an equilateral triangle. *(Fig. 16. Plate IV.)*

---

### *Of the preparation of strength in a man*
### *who wishes to generate a great strike.*

**W**hen a man prepares himself to create motion with force, he bends and twists as much as he can in the direction opposite to where he intends to deliver the strike <note>original: "percussione" — a blow or impact</note>. There, he readies himself with all the strength possible, which he then directs and releases upon the object he strikes with a compound motion <note>original: "moto decomposto" — likely referring to a complex or multi-jointed movement where the stored energy is unleashed</note>.

### *Of the force composed by man, and first*
### *we shall speak of the arms.*

From the back originates the one that extends the arm, and from the front, the one that bends it.

<meta>This page continues the mechanical analysis of the human body, specifically focusing on the leverage of the arm and the distinction between simple and compound forces in pulling and pushing.</meta>

<page-num>182</page-num>

Whether a man is more powerful in pulling than in pushing is proven by the ninth proposition of *On Weights* <note>original: "de ponderibus" — likely referring to the medieval treatise *Liber de ponderibus* attributed to Jordanus de Nemore, which Leonardo and his contemporaries studied</note>, where it says: among weights of equal power, that one will prove more powerful which is more remote from the pole <note>the fulcrum or center of rotation</note> of their balance. It follows, therefore, that if **n b** is a muscle and **n c** is a muscle of equal power between them, the front muscle **n c** is more powerful than the back muscle **n b**, because it is fixed to the arm at site **c**, which is more remote from the pole of the elbow **a** than is **b**, which is on the other side of that pole; and thus the intent is concluded. But this is simple force, and not compound, as we propose to treat, and we must move further forward. For compound force is that when, in performing an operation with the arms, a second power is added from the weight of the person and the legs—as in pulling and pushing—where in addition to the power of the arms, the weight of the person is added, along with the strength of the back and the legs, which lies in the desire to extend oneself. This would be like two people at a column, where one pushes it and the other pulls it. *(Fig. 17. Plate IV.)*

### *Which is the greater power of man: that of pulling, or that of pushing.*

**M**an has much greater power in pulling than in pushing, because in pulling there is added the power of the muscles of the arms which are created only for pulling and not for pushing. This is because when the arm is straight, the muscles that move the elbow cannot have any action in pushing, any more than a man would have by leaning his shoulder against the thing he wishes to remove from its place; in that action, the nerves <note>In this period, "nerves" often referred generally to tendons, ligaments, or the "sinews" of the muscles</note> that straighten the curved back are employed, and those

<summary>This page uses the principles of levers to explain why the human arm is anatomically better suited for pulling than pushing, distinguishing between simple muscular force and compound force involving the whole body's weight.</summary>

### *Of the limbs that bend, and what function the flesh covering them performs during said bending.*

**T**he flesh that covers the joints of the bones, and the other parts near the bones, increases and decreases in thickness according to the bending or extension of the aforementioned limbs. That is, they increase on the inside of the angle generated by the bending of the limbs, and they thin and stretch on the side of the exterior angle. The middle area interposed between the convex <note>the outer curve</note> and concave <note>the inner curve</note> angles participates in such increase or decrease, but more or less so depending on whether the parts are closer to or further from the angles of the said bent joints.

Then, one returns the entire weight onto that planted foot, leaning the hand upon its knee, and at the same time extends the arm, which carries the chest and the head upward; and thus one extends and straightens the thigh with the chest, and stands upright upon that planted foot until the other leg has been lifted.

## *Of composite motion.*

**C**omposite motion is defined as that which occurs when an operation requires bending downward and sideways at the same time. Therefore, you, the painter, must create composite movements that are entirely consistent with their compositions; that is, if a figure performs a composite act necessitated by a specific action, ensure you do not imitate it incorrectly by making them perform a simple act, which would be further removed from the reality of that action.

## *Of motions appropriate to the effects of men.*

**T**he motions of your figures must be demonstrative of the amount of force appropriate for them to use in various actions; that is, you should not show the same force in one who lifts a small rod as would be appropriate for lifting a heavy beam. Therefore, make the demonstrations of force vary according to the quality of the weights being handled by them.

## *Of the motions of figures.*

**Y**ou should never make heads straight upon the shoulders, but turned sideways, to the right or to the left, even if they are looking up or down, or straight ahead; because it is necessary to make their movements show an alert vivacity <term>vivacità desta: a sense of being wide awake and full of life</term>, and not a sleepy one. And do not make the midpoints of the whole person—front or back—show their alignments <term>rettitudini: the vertical lines of the body's axis</term> directly above or below the other upper or lower midpoints. And if you must use such a pose, do it

## On the variety of faces.

Let the air <note>the general appearance or expression</note> of the faces be varied according to the accidents <note>temporary states or conditions</note> of the man: in fatigue, in rest, in weeping, in laughter, in shouting, in fear, and similar things; and furthermore, the limbs of the person, together with their entire attitude, must correspond to the altered expression of the face.

## On the membering of animals.

All the parts of any animal must be corresponding to the age of its whole; that is, the limbs of the young should not be rendered with pronounced muscles, tendons, or veins, as some do, who, in order to appear skillful and show great draftsmanship, spoil the whole by means of mismatched limbs. Others do the same, who, through a lack of draftsmanship, give the limbs of the young to the elderly.

### *How a figure is not praiseworthy if it does not show the passion of the soul.*

That figure will not be praiseworthy if it does not, as much as possible, express with its actions the passion of its soul <note>the internal emotional or mental state</note>.

### *How the hands and arms in all their operations must demonstrate the intention of their mover as much as possible.*

The hands and arms in all their operations must demonstrate the intention of their mover <note>the mind or soul that moves the body</note> as much as possible, because with these, anyone who possesses a refined judgment follows the mental intents in all their movements. And al-

### *On motion born from the mind by means of an object.*

**W**hen the motion of a man is caused by means of an object,
either such an object arises immediately, or not: if it arises immediately,
the one who moves first turns the most neces-
sary sense toward the object, which is the eye, leaving the feet in their original place,
and only moves the thighs together with the hips and knees
toward that part where the eye turns; and thus in such <term>accidenti</term> <note>temporary emotional or physical states</note>
a great discourse will be made.

### *On common motions.*

**T**he movements of men are as varied as are
the varieties of the <term>accidenti</term> that run through their minds:
and each state in itself moves these men more or less.

### *On the motion of animals.*

**E**very two-footed animal, in its motion, lowers that part which is above the foot it is lifting more than the part which is above the foot resting on the ground: and its highest part does the opposite; and this is seen in the hips and shoulders of a man when he walks, and the same in birds with their heads and their rumps.

### *That every limb should be proportioned to its whole body.*

**S**ee to it that every part of a whole is proportioned to its whole: as if a man is of a thick and short figure, see that every one of his limbs is the same in itself, that is, short and thick arms, wide and thick hands, and short fingers, with their joints in the manner mentioned above. And so with the rest. And I intend the same to be said of all animals and plants, as much in diminishing the proportions of their thicknesses as in increasing them.

### *That if figures do not express the mind, they are twice dead.*

**I**f figures do not perform prompt actions with their limbs that express the concept of their minds, those figures are twice dead. **O**bserve decorum—that is, the suitability of action, clothing, setting, and circumstances to the dignity or lowliness of the things you wish to represent. ### *On the age of figures.*

**D**o not mix a quantity of children with as many old men, nor young men with infants, nor women with men, unless the subject you wish to depict necessitates they be bound together in a mixture.

### *The quality of men in historical compositions.*

**O**rdinarily, in common historical compositions <term>historical compositions: "istorie," the highest genre of painting involving narrative scenes from the Bible, mythology, or history</term>, make old men rare and separated from the young, because old men are rare, and their habits do not suit the habits of the young; and where there is no conformity of habits, friendship is not made, and where there is no friendship, there is separation. And where you make historical compositions appearing of gravity and counsel, make few young men in them, because young men willingly flee from counsel and other noble things.

### *On depicting one who speaks to many people.*

**Y**ou shall make the one whom you wish to speak among many people in the act of considering the matter he has to treat, and adapt to him the actions belonging to that matter; that is, if the matter is persuasive, let the actions be similar to the purpose, and if the matter is an explanation of various reasons, make the one who speaks take one finger of the left hand with two fingers of the right hand, having closed the two smaller ones <note>original: "i due minori". ### How an angry figure should be made.

**T**o the angry figure, you shall make him hold someone by the hair with his head twisted to the ground, and with one of his knees on the victim's ribs, and with the right arm raising his fist high. This man should have his hair standing up, his eyebrows low and narrow, and his teeth clenched at the corners of his arched mouth; the neck should be thick, and in front—due to his leaning over the enemy—full of wrinkles.

### How a desperate man is depicted.

**T**o the desperate man, you shall make him striking himself with a knife, and with his hands having torn his garments; let one of these hands be in the act of tearing at the wound, and you shall make him with his feet standing firm, and the legs somewhat bent, and the body similarly inclined toward the ground with his hair torn and scattered. <header>On the suitability of the limbs.</header>

**A**nd I remind you again to take great care in assigning limbs to your figures, so that they appear—beyond being consistent with the size of the body—similarly consistent with age; that is, the young with few muscles and veins in their limbs, and of a delicate surface, with rounded limbs of a pleasing color. For men, let them be sinewy and full of muscles. For the old, let them have wrinkled, rough, and veiny surfaces, with the tendons <note>original: "nervi," which in this period often referred to tendons or sinews rather than the modern neurological sense</note> very evident.

### *On laughing and crying and their differences.*

**B**etween the one who laughs and the one who cries, there is no variation in the eyes, nor the mouth, nor the cheeks, but only in the rigidity of the eyebrows, which are lowered <note>original: "s’aggiungono," implying the brows are drawn together and down</note> in the one who cries, and raised in the one who laughs. To the one who cries is added, furthermore, the tearing of clothes and hair with the hands, and the scratching of the skin of the face with the fingernails, which does not happen to the one who laughs. For the same reason, do not make the face of one who cries with the same movements as one who laughs, because they often resemble each other; the true method is to vary them just as the cause <note>original: "accidente," a philosophical term for a non-essential or external circumstance</note> of crying is varied from the cause of laughing. Because in crying, the eyebrows and the mouth vary according to the various causes of the weeping: for one cries with anger, another with fear, another out of tenderness and joy, another out of suspicion, and another out of pain and torment, another out of pity and grief for the loss of relatives or friends. Among these mourners, some appear desperate, some moderate; some weep, some scream; some stand with their face toward the sky and their hands held low, having their fingers woven together; others, fearful, with their shoulders raised.

<header>On those who jump.</header>

### On those who jump.

**N**ature operates and teaches without any conscious reasoning from the jumper <term>saltatore</term>, who, when he wishes to jump, raises his arms and shoulders with great force <term>impeto</term>. These, following that force, move together with a large part of the body and lift themselves upward until their momentum is consumed. This momentum is accompanied by the sudden extension <term>estensione</term> of the body, which had been curved in the back and in the joints of the hips, the knees, and the feet. This extension is performed diagonally—that is, forward and upward—and thus the motion dedicated to moving forward carries the jumper's body, while the upward motion lifts the body, causing it to describe a great arc and increasing the distance of the jump.

### *On the motion of figures in pushing and pulling.*

**P**ushing <term>spingere</term> and pulling <term>tirare</term> are of the same action; for pushing is simply an extension of the limbs, and pulling is a contraction of those same limbs. To both powers is added the weight of the mover <term>motore</term> against the object being pushed or pulled. There is no difference between them except that one pushes and the other pulls. He who pushes while standing has the movable object pushed in front of him, and he who pulls has it behind him. Pushing and pulling can be performed along various lines around the center of the mover's power. Regarding the arms, this center will be in the place where the nerve of the humerus <term>omero</term> of the shoulder, that of the breast <term>poppa</term>, and that of the shoulder blade <term>patella</term> <note>original: "patella dell’opposita alla poppa," referring here to the scapula or shoulder blade opposite the chest</note> join with the upper shoulder bone <term>osso della spalla</term>.

<summary>Leonardo explains the biomechanics of jumping as a combination of arm momentum and leg extension, followed by an analysis of pushing and pulling as reciprocal forces involving body weight and shoulder anatomy.</summary>
<keywords>jumping, biomechanics, momentum, pushing and pulling, anatomy of the shoulder, physics of motion</keywords>

### *On the man who wishes to throw something away from himself with great force.*

**T**he man who wishes to throw a dart, or a stone, or another object with impetuous motion <term>impetuoso moto</term>, can be depicted in two principal ways: that is, he may be depicted when the man prepares for the creation of the motion, or truly when the motion itself is finished. But if you represent him during the creation of the motion, then the inner side of the foot will be on the same line as the chest, but he will have the opposite shoulder over that foot; that is, if the right foot is under the weight of the man, the left shoulder will be over the tip of that same right foot. (*Fig. 19. Plate IV.*)

### *Why he who wishes to throw, or to drive a tool into the ground by pulling, raises the opposite leg in a curve.*

**H**e who, by pulling, wishes to drive or thrust a tool <note>original: "il cannone," likely referring here to a heavy iron bar or rod rather than a piece of artillery</note> into the ground, raises the leg opposite to the arm that pulls, and bends that leg at the knee; and he does this to balance himself <term>bilicarsi</term> over the foot that rests on the ground, without which bending or twisting of the legs he could not perform the action, nor could he pull, if that leg did not then extend itself.

### *The weighting of bodies that move.*

**T**he weightings <term>ponderazioni</term> or balances <term>bilichi</term> of men are divided into two parts: that is, simple and composite. Simple is that which is performed by a man upon his immobile feet, over which the man, by opening his arms at various distances...

### *Of the man who rests upon two feet, and who gives*
### *more of his weight to one than to the other.*

**W**hen, through long standing, a man has tired the leg upon which he rests, he sends part of the weight onto the other leg: but such a way of resting is to be used for decrepit age, or in infancy, or truly in one who is weary, because it shows tiredness or a lack of health <term>valetudine</term> in the limbs; and therefore one always sees a young man who is healthy and vigorous resting upon one of his legs, and if he gives some weight to the other leg, he uses it when he wishes to give the necessary beginning to his movement, without which all motion is denied, because motion is generated by inequality <note>Leonardo's physical principle that movement requires a loss of equilibrium or "inequality" of weight</note>.

### *Of the counterpoises of a man when standing upon his feet.*

**A** man who stands upon his feet will either load himself equally upon those feet, or he will load himself with unequal weights. If he loads himself equally upon those feet, he will be loaded with natural weight mixed with accidental weight <note>Natural weight refers to the body itself; accidental weight refers to an external load being carried</note>, or he will be loaded with simple natural weight. If he is loaded with natural weight mixed with accidental weight, then the opposite extremities of the limbs are not equally distant from the poles of the joints of the feet; but if he is loaded with simple natural weight, then such extremities of opposite limbs will be equally distant from the joints of the feet. And thus, a specific book shall be made regarding this counterpoise <term>ponderazione</term>.

### *Of four-footed animals, and how they move.*

**T**he maximum height of four-footed animals <note>quadrupeds</note> varies more in animals that are walking than in those that stand still: and this is more or less the case depending on whether the animals are of greater or lesser size. This is caused by the obliquity <note>the slanted or diagonal positioning</note> of the legs that touch the ground, which raise the figure of said animal when those legs undo their obliquity and place themselves perpendicularly over the earth.

### *Of the correspondence that one half of a man has with the other half.*

**O**ne half of the thickness and width of a man will be equal to the other, provided that the limbs joined to it do not perform unequal and dissimilar movements.

### *That it is impossible for a memory to preserve all the aspects and mutations of the limbs.*

**I**t is impossible for any memory to be able to retain all the aspects or mutations <note>changes in appearance or position</note> of any limb of whatever animal it may be. We shall exemplify this case with the demonstration of a hand. And because every continuous quantity is infinitely divisible, the motion of the eye that regards the hand, and moves from *a* to *b*, moves through a space *a b* which is itself also a continuous quantity, and consequently infinitely divisible; and in every part of that motion, the aspect and figure of the hand varies in its sight, and it will do the same moving through the whole circle; and the hand will do the same as it raises itself in its motion, that is, it will pass through space which is a quantity.
(*Fig. 22. Plate IV.*)

### *Of the first four parts that are required for the figure.*

**A**ttitude <note>term: attitude; here meaning the specific pose, gesture, or "disposition" of a figure that conveys action or emotion</note> is the first and most noble part of the figure; not only does a well-painted figure in a poor attitude have a lack of grace, but even a living person of the highest beauty loses reputation when their actions are not suited to the task they have to perform. Certainly, without any doubt, this attitude is of greater speculation <note>intellectual study or theoretical depth</note> than the goodness of the painted figure itself; for such goodness of the figure can be achieved by the imitation of a living model, but the movement of such a figure must be born from great discre- <note>The text breaks off mid-word, likely "discretion" or "discernment," referring to the artist's judgment.</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues that the infinite variations of a moving limb cannot be fully memorized and asserts that a figure's "attitude" or pose is more important than its physical beauty.</summary>

### *Discourse on the practical.*

**A**nd you, painter, study to make your works such that they have the power to draw their viewers to them, and hold them there with great admiration and delight; do not draw them in and then drive them away, as the air does to one who, in the nighttime, leaps naked from his bed to contemplate the quality of that air, whether cloudy or serene; for being immediately driven away by the cold, he returns to the bed from which he first rose. Instead, make your works similar to that air which, in warm weather, draws men from their beds and retains them with delight to possess the summer coolness. Do not wish to be a practitioner before you are a scholar, nor let greed overcome the glory which is deservedly acquired from such an art. Do not you see that among human beauties, it is the most beautiful face that stops the wayfarers, and not their rich ornaments? And I say this to you who adorn your figures with gold or other rich trimmings <insert>friezes</insert>. Do you not see the shining beauties of youth diminish in their excellence because of excessive and overly cultivated ornaments? Have you not seen mountain women wrapped in uncultivated and poor clothes acquire greater beauty than those who are adorned? Do not use affected hairstyles or arrangements of heads, where—among those of dull wit—a single hair placed more to one side than the other makes the one who wears it fear great infamy, believing that those around him will abandon every other thought and speak only of that, and only criticize that. Such people always have the mirror and the comb as their counselor, and the wind is their chief enemy

### *Of the practice sought with great diligence*
### *by the painter.*

**A**nd you, painter, who desire the greatest practice <note>term: practice; here meaning technical proficiency or 'praxis'</note>, you must understand that if you do not build it upon a good foundation of natural things, you will produce works with very little honor and less profit; but if you build it well, your works will be many and good, to your great honor and utility.

### *Of the painter judging his own works*
### *and those of others.*

**W**hen the work is equal to the judgment <note>term: judgment; the artist's intellectual capacity to perceive perfection and flaws</note>, that is a poor sign for such judgment; and when the work surpasses such judgment, that is the worst case, as happens to one who marvels at having performed so well; but when the judgment surpasses the work, this is a perfect sign. And if a young man is in such a disposition, without doubt he will be an excellent practitioner, though he will be a composer of few works—yet they will be of such quality that they will stop men in admiration to contemplate their perfections.

<summary>Leonardo advises painters to depict hair with natural movement rather than stiff artifice and emphasizes that an artist's critical judgment must always exceed their technical execution to achieve true excellence.</summary>
<keywords>hair movement, naturalism, artistic judgment, foundation of nature, self-criticism, painter's practice</keywords>

## *On the painter judging his own painting.*

**W**e know that errors are more easily recognized in the works of others than in one's own; therefore, ensure that you are first a good master of perspective, then possess a complete knowledge of the measurements of man, and be a good architect—that is, in what pertains to the form of buildings and other things. Where you lack practical experience, do not refuse to draw them from nature. Furthermore, you should hold a flat mirror while you paint, and frequently look at your work within it; there it will be seen in reverse and will appear as if by the hand of another master, allowing you to better judge your errors. It will also be good to stand up often and take some recreation, because upon returning, your judgment will be improved; whereas staying fixed upon the work will cause you to be greatly deceived. It is also beneficial to move far away, because the work appears smaller and more can be understood in a single glance; the discordant and disproportionate limbs and the colors of things are better recognized than from up close.

## *How the mirror is the master of painters.*

**W**hen you wish to see if your painting as a whole conforms with the things portrayed from nature, take a mirror and have it reflect the living subject; then compare the reflected thing with your painting, and consider your subject well in both. You see a flat mirror demonstrate things that appear in relief <note>term: relief; the illusion of three-dimensionality on a flat surface</note>, and painting does the same. Painting has only a single surface, and the mirror is the same. Both the mirror and the painting show the likeness of things surrounded by shadow and light, and both appear to be far beyond their actual surface. And if you...

### *Which painting is most praiseworthy.*

**T**hat painting is most praiseworthy which has the most conformity with the thing imitated. This comparison is to the confusion of those painters who wish to "correct" the things of nature, such as those who imitate a little child of one year, whose head fits five times into his height, yet they make it fit eight times; and while the width of the shoulders is equal to the head, they make it double, thus reducing a small child of one year to the proportions of a man of thirty years. They have practiced and seen this error practiced so many times that they have turned it into a habit; this habit has so deeply penetrated and established itself in their corrupt judgment that they make themselves believe that nature—or whoever imitates nature—makes great errors by not doing as they do.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painters can surpass the mirror's depth if they master light and shadow, and he critiques artists who ignore natural proportions in favor of stylized habits.</summary>

### *What is the primary object and intention of the painter.*
The first intention of the painter is to make a simple flat surface appear as a body in relief and detached from that plane: and he who exceeds others in such an art deserves the greatest praise. This investigation—or rather, the crowning achievement of such a science—is born from shadows and lights, or what you might call <term>chiaro e oscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro e oscuro"; the technique of using strong contrasts between light and dark to model three-dimensional forms</note>. Therefore, if you avoid shadows, you avoid the glory of the art among noble minds, and you acquire it only among the ignorant common folk, who desire nothing more than the beauty of colors, entirely forgetting the beauty and wonder of showing a flat thing in relief.

### *Which is more important in painting: the shadow, or its outlines.*
Shadows in painting require much greater investigation and speculation than their outlines. The proof of this is shown by the fact that outlines can be traced <note>original: "lucidare"; to trace or copy through a transparent medium</note> using veils or flat glass placed between the eye and the thing to be traced; but shadows are not governed by such a rule, because of the "insensibility" <note>meaning the softness or lack of a hard edge</note> of their boundaries, which are most often blurred, as is demonstrated in the *Book of Shadow and Light* <note>Leonardo refers here to his own specialized treatise on the physics of light</note>.

### *How one must give light to figures.*
Light must be used according to the natural site where you imagine your figure to be: that is, if you imagine it in the sun, make the shadows dark and the areas of light expansive, and let the shadows of all surrounding bodies be imprinted upon the ground. And if the figure is in gloomy weather, make little difference between the lights and the sha—

->*Where the viewer of a painting ought to stand.*<-

Let us suppose that *a b* is the painting being viewed, and that *d* is the light. I say that if you place yourself between *c* and *e*, you will perceive the painting poorly, especially if it is done in oil or truly varnished, because it will have a luster and will be almost like a mirror. For these reasons, the closer you approach point *c*, the less you will see, because that is where the rays of light sent from the window to the painting bounce back. But if you place yourself between *e* and *d*, your vision will be well-served, especially the closer you approach point *d*, because that location participates less in the said percussion of reflected rays.

### *How high the vanishing point should be placed.*

The point <note>The "point" refers to the central vanishing point in linear perspective.</note> must be at the height of the eye of an ordinary man, and the furthest edge of the plain that borders the sky must be placed at the height of that boundary where the flat earth meets the sky, except that mountains are exempt from this rule <note>meaning the horizon line is determined by the flat earth, while mountains naturally rise above it</note>.

### *That small figures should not, by reason, be finished.*

I say that when things appear to be of minute form, it arises from said things being far from the eye; this being the case, it is necessary that there be much air between the eye and the object. This great quantity of air hinders the clarity of the forms of that object, whereby the minute parts of those bodies become indiscernible and unrecognizable. Therefore you, painter, shall make small figures only sketched <note>original: "accennate"; suggested or indicated rather than detailed</note> and not finished; if you do otherwise, it will be against the effects of Nature, your mistress. A thing remains small because of the great distance between the eye and the object; a great distance encloses within itself much air; and much air creates in itself a thick body which obstructs and takes away the minute details of objects from the eye.

### *What background the painter should use for his figures.*

Since it is seen through experience that all bodies are surrounded by shadows and lights, I desire that you, painter, arrange the part that is illuminated so that it ends against something dark, and likewise, let the shadowed part of the body end against light things. This rule will be of great help in giving relief <note>the illusion of three-dimensionality</note> to your figures.

And if you want to see what kind of shadow is required for your flesh, make a shadow there with your finger, and according to whether you want it lighter or darker, hold your finger closer or further from your painting, and imitate that.

### *On depicting a wild place .*

**T**he trees and grasses that are more branched with thin limbs should have less depth of shadow, and those trees and grasses that have larger leaves will be the cause of larger shadows.

### *How one must make an imaginary animal appear natural .*

**Y**ou know that it is impossible to create any animal which does not have its own limbs, and that each limb by itself must bear a resemblance to those of some other animal. Therefore, if you want to make an imaginary animal appear natural—let us say, for example, a serpent—take for the head that of a mastiff or a hound <note>original: "bracco"; a type of Italian pointing dog</note>, and give it the eyes of a cat, the ears of a porcupine, the nose of a greyhound <note>original: "veltro"</note>, the eyebrows of a lion, the temples of an old rooster, and the neck of a water turtle.

### On faces that should be made to have relief with grace.

**I**n streets facing west, when the sun is at midday, let the walls be so high that the one facing the sun does not reflect light onto the bodies in shadow. It would be ideal to have air without glare, at which time the sides of the faces are seen to share in the darkness of the walls opposite them; and thus the sides of the nose, and the whole face turned toward the opening of the street, will be illuminated. For this reason, the eye positioned in the middle of the street's opening will see such a face with all the parts turned toward it being illuminated, and those sides turned toward the walls of the buildings being in shadow.

To this will be added the grace of shadows with a pleasing softness <note>original: "perdimento"; literally "losing" or "fading," referring to the gradual disappearance of edges</note>, entirely deprived of any sharp boundaries <note>original: "termine spedito"</note>. This will arise because of the length of the light that passes between the roofs of the houses and penetrates between the walls, ending upon the pavement of the street; it then bounces back by reflected motion <note>term: "moto riflesso" - the principle of light bouncing off one surface to illuminate the shadowed side of another object</note> into the shaded parts of the faces, brightening them somewhat. And the length of the aforementioned light from the sky, shaped by the edges of the roofs with its front which stays above the mouth of the street, illuminates almost down to the beginning of the shadows <note>original: "nascimento dell' ombre"</note> that are beneath the features of the face. And so, step by step, it changes into brightness until it ends upon the chin with an imperceptible darkness from every direction. As if such light were *a e*, see the line *f e* of the light that illuminates as far as under the nose, and the line *c f* only illuminates as far as under the lip, and the line *a h* extends as far as under the chin; and here the nose remains strongly luminous because it is seen by the entirety of the light *a b c d e*.
(*Fig. 24. Plate IV.*)

<note>This passage reflects Leonardo da Vinci's obsession with "sfumato" and the way light behaves in urban environments to create "relief" (the illusion of 3D depth) and "grace" (aesthetic beauty).</note>

### *On separating and distinguishing figures from their backgrounds.*

**Y**ou must place your figure against a light background if the figure is dark; and if the figure is light, place it against a dark background; and if the figure is both light and dark, place the dark part against the light background, and the light part against the dark background. <note>This is the fundamental principle of "chiaroscuro" contrast to ensure the subject remains legible to the viewer.</note>

### *On the difference of lights placed in various positions.*

**A** small light source creates large and sharply defined shadows upon shaded bodies. Large light sources create small shadows with blurred edges upon shaded bodies. When a small and powerful light is enclosed within a large and less powerful one—as the sun is within the atmosphere—then the less powerful light will remain in the place of shadow upon the bodies illuminated by it. <note>Leonardo is observing how the ambient light of the sky acts as a secondary, softer light source compared to the direct, concentrated light of the sun.</note>

### *On avoiding the disproportion of surroundings.*

**A** very great vice is demonstrated by many painters: that is, making the dwellings of men and other surroundings in such a way that the doors do not even reach the knees of their inhabitants, even though the doors are closer to the eye of the viewer than the man who shows he wishes to enter therein. We have seen porticos crowded with men, where one of the supporting columns is held in the fist of a man who leans against it as if it were a slender walking stick; such things are to be avoided with every effort. Bodies should correspond both in size and in function to the subject being treated. This proposition is defined before it is proposed; therefore, you shall read above. <note>Leonardo refers to the "above" likely meaning earlier sections of his notebooks where he establishes the mathematical rules of perspective and scale.</note>

## *On the boundaries of bodies called outlines, or contours.*

**T**he boundaries of bodies are of such minute visibility that at even a small distance between the object and the eye, the eye cannot perceive the features of a friend or relative; one does not recognize them except by their clothing, and thus the mind receives knowledge of the whole through the combination of the whole and its parts. <note>Leonardo argues that "lines" do not exist in nature; rather, our eyes perceive shapes as masses that lose detail as they recede.</note>

### *On the surface qualities that are first lost as shaded bodies move away.*

**T**he first things lost as shaded bodies move away are their boundaries. Secondly, at a greater distance, the shadows that divide the parts of bodies that touch one another are lost. Third, the thickness of the legs and feet is lost, and so successively the smaller parts disappear, so that at a long distance there remains only a mass of confused shape.

### *On the surface qualities that are first lost in distances.*

**T**he first thing among colors to be lost in the distance is the luster <note>original: "lustro"</note>, which is their smallest part and the "light of lights" <note>The specular highlight or the brightest point of reflection on a surface.</note>. The second is the light, because it is smaller than the shadow. Third are the principal shadows, and in the end there remains only a moderate, confused darkness.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the optical degradation of forms and colors over distance, noting that fine outlines and highlights vanish first, eventually leaving only a blurred silhouette.</summary>
<keywords>optics, perspective of disappearance, contours, highlights, shadows, visual perception, distance</keywords>

## *How to make a figure that appears to be 40 cubits high in a space of 20 cubits, and has corresponding limbs, and stands upright on its feet.*

**I**n this and in every other case, it should not trouble the painter how the wall stands where he is painting, especially if the eye that looks at such a painting is to see it from a window or from another opening <note>original: "spiracolo," literally a breathing hole or small aperture</note>: because the eye does not have to attend to the flatness or the curvature of those parts, but only to the things that are to be shown beyond that wall in various places of the feigned landscape <term>finta campagna: a painted or "faked" countryside used as a background in perspective</term>. But such a figure would be better made in the curvature *f r g*, because in it there are no angles. (*Fig. 29. Plate V.*)

### *Painting and its members and components.*

**L**ight, darkness, color, body, figure, position, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. Of these ten parts of the office of the eye <note>the "office of the eye" refers to the functions or capabilities of sight</note>, painting possesses seven, which are: light, darkness, color, figure, position, distance, and proximity. I remove "body," "motion," and "rest." Thus, there remain light and darkness—which mean shadow and light, or if you prefer, clear and obscure—and color. I do not include "body" because painting is in itself a superficial thing <note>original: "cosa superficiale," meaning existing only on a surface</note>, and a surface has no body, as is defined in geometry. To put it better, whatever is visible is counted within the science of painting. Therefore, the ten categories of the eye mentioned above are reasonably the ten books into which I divide my painting; but light and darkness are a single book treating of light and shadow, and they are made into the same book because shadow is surrounded by, or rather in contact with, light. And the same happens with light and shadow (32).

## *Warning regarding shadows and lights.*

**L**ight and shadow are always mixed at the boundaries of shadows: and the derivative shadow <note>shadow cast by an object onto another surface, as opposed to the "attached" shadow on the object itself</note> mixes with light more as it becomes more distant from the shaded body. However, color will never be seen in its pure state. This is proven by the ninth [proposition], which says: the surface of every body partakes of the color of its object <note>meaning the color of the things surrounding it</note>, even if it is the surface of a transparent body, such as air, water, and the like; because the air takes its light from the sun, and darkness arises from the deprivation of that sun. Therefore, the air is tinted in as many various colors as there are things placed between it and the eye, because the air in itself has no more color than water has. But the moisture that mixes with it from the middle region downward is what thickens it; and as it thickens, the solar rays that strike it illuminate it, while the air from the middle region upward remains dark. And because light and darkness together compose the color blue, this is the blue with which the air is tinted, with greater or lesser darkness as the air is mixed with greater or lesser humidity.

## *Painting and its definition.*

**P**ainting is a composition of light and darkness mixed together with the diverse qualities of all simple and compound colors.

### *Why the same landscape appears*
### *at times larger or smaller*
### *than it actually is.*

**L**andscapes appear at times larger or smaller than they are due to the interposition of air that is thicker or thinner than usual, which comes between the horizon and the eye that sees it.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Between horizons at an equal distance from the eye, that one will appear more remote which is seen through thicker air, and that one will appear closer which is seen in thinner air. And if an object is seen at a distance of one hundred miles, which miles consist of uniform and thin air, and the same object is seen at the same distance of one hundred miles consisting of uniform and thick air—with a thickness relative to the aforementioned air—without doubt the same things seen first in the thin air, and then seen in the thick, will appear four times as large as they did in the thin.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Unequal things seen at equal distances will appear equal if the thickness of the air interposed between the eye and those things is unequal—that is, with the thick air placed before the smaller object. And this is proven by means of the perspective of colors <note>term: "perspective of colors" (prospettiva de' colori); Leonardo's theory that the atmosphere changes the color and clarity of objects based on distance</note>, which makes a great mountain, appearing small by measurement, seem larger than a small object near the eye; just as one sees that a finger near the eye covers a great mountain far from the eye.

## *Of things which the eye sees below itself mixed within fog and thick air.*

**T**he closer the air is to the water or the earth, the thicker it becomes. This is proven by the 19th [proposition] of the second [book], which says: that thing which has in itself greater weight rises the least; from which it follows that the lighter thing rises higher than the heavy one; therefore, our proposition is concluded.

### *Of buildings seen in thick air.*

**T**hat part of the building will be less evident which is seen in air of greater thickness; and conversely, that part which is seen in thinner air will be better known <note>original: "nota"; meaning clearly perceived or distinct</note>. Therefore the eye *n*, seeing the tower *a d*, will see in every degree of lowliness a part less known and lighter, and in every degree of height a part more known and less light. (*Fig. 33. Plate V.*)

### *Of the thing that shows itself from a distance.*

**T**hat dark thing will show itself lighter which is more remote from the eye. It follows by the converse that the dark thing will show itself with greater darkness which is found closer to the eye. Therefore, the lower parts of any thing placed in thick air will appear more remote from the feet than their summits; and for this reason, the low root of the mountain will appear further away than the peak of the same mountain, which in itself is actually more remote. (*Fig. 34. Plate VI.*)

## *Of the lower boundaries of remote things.*

**T**he lower boundaries <note>original: "termini"; the edges or outlines</note> of remote things will be less perceptible than their upper boundaries. This happens frequently with mountains and hills, the peaks of which are set against the sides of other mountains located behind them. On these, the upper edges are seen more clearly than their bases, because the upper edge is darker, being less obscured by the thick air that settles in low places. It is this air that blurs the boundaries of the bases of hills. The same occurs with trees, buildings, and other things that rise up through the air. From this it arises that tall towers seen from a distance often appear thick at the top and thin at the bottom; this is because the upper part reveals the angle of the sides where they meet the front, as the thin air does not hide them from you as the thick air does. This happens according to the seventh [proposition] of the first [book], which states that the thick air interposed between the eye and the sun is brighter at the bottom than at the top; and where the air is whiter, it obscures dark objects from the eye more than if such air were blue. ### *Of the blue color that appears in distant landscapes.*

**O**f remote things seen by the eye, whatever their actual color may be, that which possesses the greatest darkness—whether natural or accidental—will appear to be the most blue. Natural darkness is that which is dark in itself; accidental darkness is that which is dark because of the shadow cast upon it by other objects.

### *Which parts of bodies are lost to view due to distance.*

**T**hose parts of bodies that are smallest in size will be the first to be lost to view over a long distance. This happens because the images <note>original: "spezie"; the visual species or rays carrying the likeness of the object</note> of smaller things, at an equal distance, reach the eye at a smaller angle than larger things; and the recognition of remote things diminishes as their size diminishes. It follows, therefore, that when a larger mass at a great distance reaches the eye at a minimal angle and is almost lost to view, the smaller parts will completely lack any recognition.

### *Why things are less recognizable the further they are removed from the eye.*

**T**hat thing will be less known which is more remote from the eye. This happens because those parts that are most minute are lost first; then, the second-most minute parts are also lost at a greater distance, and so on, following in succession. As the parts are consumed little by little, the knowledge of the remote thing is consumed, so that in the end all the parts are lost along with the whole. Furthermore, the color fails because of the thickness of the air that is interposed between the eye and the thing seen <note>Leonardo refers here to "atmospheric perspective," where the density of the air acts like a veil, obscuring both detail and true color.</note>.

### *Why parallel towers in the fog appear narrower at the base than at the top.*

**P**arallel towers in the fog, at a long distance, show themselves to be thinner at the base than at the top. This is because the fog that serves as their background <note>original: "campo"; the field or background against which an object is silhouetted</note> is thicker and whiter at the bottom than at the top. Therefore, by the third rule of this [science] which says: a dark object placed against a white background diminishes its size to the eye. And the converse says: a white object placed against a dark background shows itself to be thicker. It follows that the lower part of the dark tower, having for its background the whiteness of the low and thick fog, causes that fog to appear to grow over the lower boundaries of said tower and diminish them. This the fog cannot do to the upper boundaries of the tower, where the fog is thinner <note>This optical illusion occurs because the bright light of the fog "bleeds" into the dark edges of the tower, a phenomenon known as irradiation.</note>.

## *Why faces appear dark from a distance.*

**W**e see clearly that all the images <note>original: "similitudini"; the visual species or likenesses emitted by objects according to Renaissance optical theory</note> of evident things that serve as our objects, whether they be large or small, enter the sense through the small light of the eye <note>The pupil, which Leonardo often calls the "light" or "pupilla."</note>. If the image of the vastness of the heaven and the earth passes through such a small entrance, and the face of a man being almost nothing among such large images of things, it occupies so little of that light—due to the distance that diminishes it—that it remains incomprehensible. Furthermore, having to pass from the surface to the receptive faculty <term>impressiva: the part of the brain where Leonardo believed sensory images were processed</term> through a dark medium, namely the hollow nerve <note>original: "nervo voto"; the optic nerve, which was then believed to be a hollow tube for the passage of visual spirits</note> which appears dark, that image, not being of a powerful color, is tinged by that darkness of the passage, and having reached the receptive faculty, it appears dark. No other cause can in any way be taught regarding that point and the nerve that stands in the light; and because it is full of a transparent humor like air, it performs the same function as a hole made in a board, which appears black when looked at, and things seen through clear and dark air become confused in the darkness.

## *Why a man seen at a certain distance is not recognized.*

**D**iminishing perspective <term>prospettiva diminutiva: the mathematical reduction of an object's size as it recedes</term> demonstrates to us that the further away a thing is, the smaller it becomes. And if you look at a man who is a crossbow-shot <note>original: "balestrata"; a common Renaissance unit of distance, roughly 200-300 yards</note> distant from you, and you place the eye of a small needle <note>original: "gucchia"; an archaic term for "ago" (needle)</note> close to your eye, you will be able to see through it many men sending their images to the eye, and at one and the same time they will all fit within said window. Therefore, if a man a crossbow-shot away sends his image to the eye, which occupies a small part—

### *Which parts of bodies moving away from the eye are lost to notice first, and which are preserved longer.*

### *On linear perspective.*

**L**inear perspective <term>prospettiva lineare: the mathematical system of projecting three-dimensional space onto a two-dimensional surface using vanishing points and converging lines</term> functions through the office of visual lines to prove by measurement how much the second object is smaller than the first, and the third smaller than the second, and so on by degrees until the end of the things seen. I find by experience that if the second object is as far from the first as the first is from the eye, even though they are of equal size, the second will be half the size of the first; and if the third object is of equal distance beyond the second, it will be two-thirds smaller, and so on <note>Leonardo is describing the harmonic progression of size reduction in perspective, where the perceived size is inversely proportional to the distance.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains how the smallest details and outlines of an object vanish first as distance increases and introduces the mathematical rules of linear perspective regarding size reduction.</summary>

step by step at equal distances, they will always make a proportionate diminution, provided that the interval does not exceed the number of 20 <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly equivalent to 23 inches or 58 centimeters</term>. Within these twenty braccia, a figure of your same size will lose two-quarters of its magnitude; within 40, it will lose three-quarters; and then five-sixths at 60 braccia; and so, hand in hand, it will continue its diminution. This assumes the wall <note>The "wall" refers to the vertical plane of the painting or the observer's station point</note> is at a distance from you equal to twice your height, for placing it at only one height's distance creates a great difference between the first braccia and the second.

## *Of bodies seen in the fog.*

**T**hose things which are seen in the fog will appear much larger than their true size. This is because such fog is similar to the hazy air interposed between the eye and the horizon in clear weather; thus, a body near the eye seen through the proximity of the fog appears to be at the distance of the horizon, where a very large tower would appear smaller than the aforementioned man standing nearby.

### *Of cities and other buildings seen in the evening or the morning in the fog.*

**I**n buildings seen at a long distance in the evening or morning in the fog, or thick air, only the brightness of those parts illuminated by the sun is revealed, which are found toward the horizon; and the parts of said buildings that are not seen by the sun remain almost the color of the medium darkness of the fog.

### *Why things higher up in the distance are darker than the low ones, even if the fog is uniform in thickness.*

**O**f things placed in the fog, or other thick air, or in vapor, or in smoke, or at a distance, that one will be so much more noticeable which is higher up: and of things of equal height, that one appears darker which stands out against darker fog. This is what happens to the eye *h*, which, seeing towers *a b c* of equal height among themselves, sees the summit *c* of the first tower at *r*, a depth of two degrees of thickness in the fog; and it sees the summit of the middle tower *b* in only one degree of fog; therefore, the summit *c* shows itself to be darker than the summit of tower *b*. (*Fig. 35. Plate VI.*)

<note>Leonardo is explaining "aerial perspective," where the atmosphere acts as a filter. ### *Of the patches of shadows that appear on bodies from a distance.*

**T**he throat, or any other perpendicular straightness that has some projection above it, will always be darker than the perpendicular face of that projection itself. It follows that a body will appear more illuminated when it is seen by a greater amount of the same light. See in *a* <note>Referring to the accompanying diagram, Fig. 36</note> that no part of the sky *f k* illuminates it; and in *b* the sky *h k* illuminates it; and in *c* the sky *g k*; and in *d* the sky *f k* entirely. Therefore, the chest will be of equal brightness to the forehead, nose, and chin. 

But what I have to remind you regarding faces is that you should consider how, at different distances, different qualities of shadows are lost, and only those primary patches remain—namely, the hollows of the eye <note>original: "incassature dell' occhio"</note> and other similar features. Ultimately, the face remains dark because the highlights are consumed, which are small things compared to the middle shadows <term>middle shadows: the transitional tones between deep shadow and bright light</term>. For this reason, over a long distance, the quality and quantity of the primary lights and shadows are consumed, and every quality blends into a middle shadow. 

And this is the cause why trees, and every body, at a certain distance appear to become darker in themselves than those same objects would be when near the eye. But then the air that is interposed between the eye and the object causes that object to brighten and lean toward blue; however, it turns blue in the shadows rather than in the luminous parts, where the truth of the colors is more visible.

### *Why at the approach of evening the shadows of bodies cast upon a white wall are blue.*

**T**he shadows of bodies generated by the redness of the sun near the horizon will always be blue. This arises from the eleventh principle, which states: the surface of every opaque body partakes of the color of its object <note>In Leonardo's optics, an "object" refers to whatever is facing or illuminating a surface</note>. Therefore, since the whiteness of the wall is entirely deprived of any color of its own, it is stained by the color of its objects, which in this case are the sun and the sky. And because the sun grows red toward evening, and the sky appears blue, the place where the shadow is—which does not "see" the sun, according to the eighth principle of shadow, which says: no luminous body ever saw the shadows of the body it illuminates—that place will be seen by the sky. Therefore, by the aforementioned eleventh principle, the derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow: the shadow cast onto a surface, as opposed to the "attached shadow" on the object itself</term> striking the white wall will be blue in color, and the field surrounding that shadow, being seen by the redness of the sun, will partake of the color red. (->*Fig. 37. Plate VI.*<-)

#### *Where smoke is brightest.*

**S**moke seen between the sun and the eye will be brighter and more lucid than in any other part of the landscape where it originates. The same occurs with dust and mist, which, if you are positioned between them and the sun, will appear dark to you.

#### *Of dust.*

**D**ust that is raised by the running of any animal: the higher it rises, the brighter it is; and it is darker the less it is raised, provided it stands between the sun and the eye.

<header>Of smoke.</header>

**S**moke is more transparent and darker toward the edges of its billows <note>original: "globulenze," referring to the rounded, cloud-like shapes of smoke</note> than toward its centers.

Smoke moves with much greater obliquity <note>slant or angle</note> as the wind that drives it is more powerful.

Smokes are of as many various colors as there are varieties of things that generate them.

Smokes will not produce defined shadows, and their boundaries are less distinct the further they are from their causes; and things placed behind them are less evident as the globes of smoke are denser; and they are whiter the closer they are to their beginning, and bluer toward their end.

Fire will appear darker to us the greater the amount of smoke that is interposed between the eye and said fire.

Where the smoke is more remote, objects are less obscured by it.

Depict the landscape with smoke in the manner of a thick mist, in which one sees smoke in various places with their flames at the beginnings illuminating the densest billows of said smokes; and let the highest mountains be more evident than their bases, as is seen to happen in mists (*).

### On backgrounds.

**T**he most principal part of painting is the backgrounds <term>campi: literally "fields," referring to the negative space or backdrop against which a subject is painted</term> of the things depicted. In these backgrounds, the boundaries of natural things that possess a convex curvature are always recognizable, as are the shapes of such bodies within those backgrounds, even if the colors of the bodies are the same color as the aforementioned background. This arises because the convex boundaries of bodies are not illuminated in the same way that the background is illuminated by the same light; for such a boundary will often be lighter or darker than that background. But if such a boundary is the same color as the background, without a doubt that part of the painting will prevent the recognition of the shapes of that boundary. Such a choice in painting is to be avoided by the minds of good painters, since the intention of the painter is to make his bodies appear to stand forward from their backgrounds; and in the aforementioned case the opposite happens, not only in painting, but even in things in relief <note>original: "rilievo" – referring to three-dimensional sculpture</note>.

### *On the judgment that must be made regarding the work of a painter.*

**F**irst, you must consider the figures, whether they have the relief required by their position and the light that illuminates them; that the shadows are not the same at the edges of the narrative <term>istoria: a "history" or narrative painting, the highest genre of art which depicts a story</term> as they are in the middle, because it is one thing to be surrounded by shadow, and another to have shadow on only one side. Those figures are surrounded by shadow which are toward the middle of the narrative—

### *On the relief of figures remote from the eye.*

**T**hat opaque body will show itself to be of lesser relief <note>original: "rilievo" — the illusion of three-dimensionality</note> which is more distant from the eye; and this happens because the air placed between the eye and that opaque body—being a thing brighter than the shadow of such a body—corrupts that shadow and brightens it, and takes away the power of its darkness, which is the cause of making it lose its relief.

### *On the boundaries of illuminated members.*

**T**he boundary of that illuminated member <note>original: "membro" — a limb or part of the body</note> will appear darker when seen against a lighter background, and likewise it will appear lighter when seen against a darker background. And if such a boundary is flat, and seen against a light background similar to its own brightness, the boundary will be imperceptible.

### *On boundaries.*

**T**he boundaries of secondary objects will never be as distinct as the primary ones. Therefore you, painter, do not define the boundaries of the fourth-distance objects with the fifth as sharply as you do the first with the second; because the boundary of one thing against another is of the nature of a mathematical line, but is not a line; for the boundary of one color is the beginning of another color, and it should not be called a line, because nothing intervenes between the boundary of one color placed before another color except the boundary itself, which is a thing imperceptible even from up close; therefore you, painter, do not emphasize it in distant things.

## *On flesh tones, and things remote from the eye.*

**T**he painter should place in figures and things remote from the eye only spots <note>original: "macchie" — refers to broad areas of color or tone without fine detail</note> that are not defined, but have blurred boundaries; and let the choice of such figures be made when it is cloudy, or towards evening. Above all, take care, as I have said, to avoid defined lights and shadows, because they appear like mere tints when seen from afar, and the resulting works are difficult and without grace. And you must remember that shadows should never be of such a quality that, through their darkness, you lose the color where they are produced, unless the place where the bodies are situated is already pitch dark. Do not make profiles, do not pick out individual hairs, and do not apply white highlights except on white things; and let those highlights demonstrate the primary beauty of the color where they are placed.

The <term>perspective</term> <note>In this context, Leonardo refers to the entire science of representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface.</note> that is applied in painting is divided into three principal parts. The first of these concerns the diminution of the size of bodies at various distances. The second part is that which treats the diminution of the colors of such bodies. The third is that which diminishes the clarity of the figures and the boundaries of these bodies at various distances.

The **blue of the atmosphere** is a color composed of light and darkness. I say light because of the air illuminated within the particles of moisture infused within said air. By darkness, I mean the pure air which is not divided into atoms—that is, particles of moisture—upon which the solar rays might strike. An example of this is seen in the air that lies between the eye and shaded mountains, darkened by the great abundance of trees found upon them, or shaded in those parts not struck by the solar rays; this air becomes blue, but it does not become blue in its luminous part, and much less so in the part covered by snow.

Among things equally dark and at an equal distance, that which is set against a whiter field will appear darker, and vice versa.

That object which is painted with the greatest contrast of white and black will appear to have better <term>relief</term> <note>original: "rilievo" — the illusion of three-dimensionality and physical presence on a flat surface.</note> than any other. Therefore remember, painter, to dress your figures in the lightest colors you can; for if you make them of a dark color, they will have little relief and little visibility from a distance. This is because the shadows of all things are dark; if you make a dark garment, there will be little variation between the light and the shadow, whereas in light colors there will be a great difference.

### *Why, of two things of equal size, the painted one will appear larger than the one in relief.*

**T**his reasoning will not be easy to demonstrate, as many others are, but nonetheless I will strive to satisfy you, if not entirely, then at least as much as I am able. Diminishing <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical method of representing three-dimensional objects on a plane surface so that they appear smaller as they recede.</note> shows us by logic that the further things are from the eye, the more they diminish, and these reasons are well confirmed by experience. Therefore, the visual lines that exist between the object and the eye, when they extend to the surface of the painting, are all cut at the same boundary; however, the lines that exist between the eye and a sculpture have various boundaries and lengths. That line which is longer extends to a limb further away than the others, and therefore that limb appears smaller. Since there are many lines longer than others—and by the logic that among many parts, each further away than the next, those being further away must necessarily appear smaller—by appearing smaller, their diminution causes the entire sum of the object to appear smaller. This does not happen in painting, because the lines terminate at one and the same distance, so they must remain without such diminution. Therefore, the parts that do not diminish do not reduce the sum of the object, and for this reason, a painting does not diminish in the way a sculpture does.

### *Why things portrayed perfectly from nature do not appear to have the same relief as nature itself.*

**I**t is impossible that a painting, even if imitated with the highest perfection of outlines, shadows, lights, and color, could appear to have the same...

**THINGS** will show much more relief in a light and illuminated field than in a dark one. The reason for what is proposed is that if you want to give relief to your figure, you make it so that the part of the body which is most remote from the light participates less in that light, whereby it remains darker; and ending then against a dark field, it comes to fall into confused boundaries. For this reason, if a reflected light <note>original: "riflesso"</note> does not reach it, the work remains without grace, and from a distance nothing appears except the luminous parts; thus it happens that the dark parts appear to be of the same field, and so things appear cut off, and relieved so much less than they ought to be, as the field is dark.

### *How figures often resemble their masters.*

**T**his happens because our judgment is that which moves the hand to the creation of the outlines <term>lineamenti: the defining features or contours of a face or body</term> of these figures in various aspects until it is satisfied; and because this judgment is one of the powers of our soul <note>original: "potenze dell'anima"</note>, with which the soul composed the form of the body where it dwells according to its will; therefore, having to remake a human body with the hands, it willingly remakes that body of which it was the first inventor. ### *Of the shadows made by bridges upon their waters.*

**T**he shadows of bridges will never be seen upon their waters unless the water first loses its function of mirroring on account of turbidity. And this is proven because clear water has a lustrous and clean surface, and it mirrors the bridge in all the places interposed within equal angles between the eye and the bridge; and it mirrors the air beneath the bridge, where the shadow of such a bridge ought to be. This the turbid water cannot do, because it does not mirror, but indeed receives the shadow, just as a dusty road would do. <note>Leonardo distinguishes between a reflection (which requires a mirror-like surface) and a shadow (which requires a matte surface to be visible). In clear water, you see the reflection of the underside of the bridge, not the shadow cast upon the water's surface.</note> (*Fig. 45. Plate VII.*)

### *beyond the surface.*

**T**he water that allows the bottom to be seen through its transparency will show that bottom more clearly the slower the water's motion. ### Of the statue.

**I**f you wish to make a figure of marble, first make one of clay; once it is finished and dry, place it in a crate that is large enough—after the figure is removed from that place—to receive the marble you wish to carve therein in the likeness of that clay model. Then, having placed the clay figure inside this crate, take small rods that fit exactly through holes in the crate, and push them into each hole until each white rod touches the figure in various places. Dye the part of these rods that remains outside the crate black, and make a mark on the rod and its corresponding hole so that they match at your will. Then you shall remove the clay figure from the crate and place your piece of marble in it, and remove so much from the marble that all your rods are hidden up to their marks in said holes. To be able to do this better, arrange it so that the entire crate can be lifted up, while the bottom of said crate remains always under the marble; in this way, you will be able to remove the stone with your tools with great ease (35).
