### *On the smoke of Cities.*

**S**moke is seen better and more clearly in the eastern parts than in the western ones when the sun is in the east. And this 
arises from two causes. The first is that the sun shines through the particles of such smoke with its rays, brightening them and making them 
evident. The second is that the roofs of the houses seen to the east at such a time are in shadow, because their slant 
cannot be illuminated by the sun. And the same happens with 
dust; and both are more luminous the 
denser they are, and they are densest toward the middle.

### *On smoke and dust.*

**W**hen the sun is in the east, the smoke of cities will not be 
seen to the west, because it is not seen penetrated by the 
solar rays, nor seen against a dark field, because the roofs of the 
houses show the eye that same part which is 
shown to the sun, and because of this light field such smoke is little seen. 
But dust in a similar aspect appears darker 
than smoke, because it is of a denser matter than smoke, 
which is a moist matter.

### *The eye placed on high, which sees low objects.*

**W**hen the eye, placed in a high position, sees the high peaks of mountains together with their bases, then the colors of the mountain peaks will seem more distant than the colors of their base. This is proved by the fourth [rule] of this [treatise] which says: among colors of equal nature, the most remote is tinged more by the color of the medium interposed between it and the eye that sees it. It follows that since the bases of the mountains are seen through thicker air than their peaks, these bases will appear more remote from the eye than those peaks, which are seen by the same eye through thinner air. Let the eye then be placed at height *a*, which sees the summit of the mountain *b* after the interposition of the air *a b*, and sees the base *d* of the same mountain after the air *a d*, a shorter space than *a b*; because this air *a d* is thicker than the air *a b*, the base of the mountain, as has been said, will appear more distant than its summit. (*Fig. 49. Plate VII.*)

<note>Leonardo is describing "aerial perspective," where the density of the atmosphere (the "medium") changes the appearance of objects. Counter-intuitively, he argues that because the air is denser at lower altitudes, the base of a mountain might appear more obscured—and thus more distant—than the peak, even if the peak is physically further away.</note>

### *The eye placed low which sees low and high objects.*

**B**ut when the eye is placed in a low position and sees the base of the mountains and their peaks, then the colors of that mountain will be much less distinct than those of the preceding examples. And this happens because the peak and the base of the mountain are seen through a much greater thickness <note>Leonardo uses "grossezza" (thickness/density) to refer to the volume of atmosphere the light must travel through.</note> than the aforementioned ones, insofar as the eye that sees them is situated in a lower place. Let the eye be *n* and the peak and base of the mountain be *o p*. Therefore, the visual line *p n* in the second figure being lower than the visual line of the second figure *a* <note>Leonardo is comparing the diagrams in his manuscript; "a" refers to the high vantage point from the previous page.</note>, it is necessary that the color of the base in the second demonstration be more varied from its natural color than the base in the first demonstration; and the same is understood to have been said of the mountain peaks. (*Fig. 50. Plate VII.*)

### *Why all the species that come to the eye converge at a single point.*

**O**f things of equal size situated at various distances, the most remote will be seen under a smaller angle. *b d* is equal to *c e*, but *c e* comes to the eye through an angle so much smaller than *b d* as it is more remote from point *a*, as shown by the angle *c a e* in respect to the angle *b a d*. <note>The "species" (spezie) refers to the visual images or "simulacra" that Leonardo believed radiated from objects to the eye.</note> (*Fig. 51. Plate VII.*)

### *Of things mirrored in water.*

**O**f things mirrored in water, that one will be most similar in color to the object mirrored which is reflected in clearer water.

### *Of the nature of the medium interposed between the eye and the object.*

**T**he medium <term>medium: the substance (like air or water) through which light travels</term> interposed between the eye and the object is of two types: that is, either it has a surface, such as water and crystal or another transparent thing, or it is without a common surface, such as the air that rests against the surface of the bodies enclosed within it, which air has no continuous surface in itself except at its lower and upper boundaries.

### *Effects of the medium surrounded by a common surface.*

# BOOK FOUR.

## ON DRAPERY, AND THE METHOD OF CLOTHING FIGURES WITH GRACE, AND ON THE TYPES AND NATURES OF FABRICS.

---

### *On the fabrics that clothe figures.*

The fabrics <note>original: "panni" — refers to drapery or cloth used in painting</note> that clothe figures must show that they are inhabited by those figures. With a brief contour, they should show the posture <note>original: "attitudine"</note> and motion of such a figure, and avoid the confusion of many folds, especially over the highlights, so that the forms remain recognizable.

### *On the broken and solid styles of drapery clothing the figures.*

The fabrics that clothe the figures <note>corrected from "figur"</note> must have folds that are either solid or broken <note>original: "salde o rotte" — "solid" refers to continuous, flowing folds, while "broken" refers to sharp, angular changes in the cloth's direction</note> according to the quality of the thin or thick cloth that you wish to represent. And you may use both styles in the compositions of your Narrative Paintings <term>Storie: large-scale compositions depicting a specific historical, biblical, or mythological event</term> to satisfy different artistic judgments.

### *On clothing figures with grace.*

In your drapery, use that part <note>corrected from "pa"</note> which surrounds the figure to show the manner of its posture <note>corrected from "attitine"</note>; and those parts that remain outside of that, adorn <note>corrected from "adorn"</note> in a flying and scattered manner, as will be described.

<header>On the fabrics that clothe figures, and their folds.</header>

->*On the fabrics that clothe figures, and their folds.*<-

**T**he fabrics that clothe figures must have their folds arranged to encircle the limbs they cover in such a way that, in the illuminated parts, no folds of dark shadow are placed, and in the shaded parts, no folds of excessive brightness are made. The outlines of these folds should, in some places, go around the limbs they cover, and not with lines that "cut" across the limbs, nor with shadows that appear to sink deeper than the actual surface of the clothed body. In effect, the cloth should be adapted in such a way that it does not appear "uninhabited"—that is, it should not look like a bundle of cloth stripped from a man, as many are seen to do. These artists fall so in love with various groupings of diverse folds that they fill an entire figure with them, forgetting the purpose for which such cloth is made: namely, to clothe and surround with grace the limbs where they rest, and not to fill everything with "bellies" or deflated bladders <note>The author uses "vessiche sgonfiate" (deflated bladders) to criticize bulky, hollow-looking drapery that lacks the sense of a body underneath.</note> over the illuminated highlights of the limbs. I do not deny that one should make some beautiful folds <note>original: "falda" — a decorative fold or drape of fabric</term>, but let them be made in parts of the figure where the limbs and the body naturally gather and collect such cloth. Above all, use a variety of fabrics in your narrative paintings <term>Storie: complex historical or biblical scenes</term>; for instance, making folds with "facing breaks" <note>original: "rotture affacciate" — sharp, angular folds where the fabric meets itself</note> in dense fabrics, while other fabrics should have soft folds with turns that are curved rather than sharp. This occurs in serges <term>Saje: a durable twilled woolen fabric</term>, satins <term>Rasse: a type of smooth, silken fabric</term>, and other rare fabrics like linens, veils, and the like. You shall also make drapery with few and large folds for thick fabrics, as seen in felts, coarse woolens <term>Schiavine: heavy, rough blankets or garments often worn by pilgrims</term>, and other bed covers. These reminders I do not give to the masters, but to those who do not wish to teach, <margin>The text cuts off here, likely transitioning to a critique of those who hoard artistic knowledge or fail to apply these principles.</margin>

Certainly, these are not masters; for he who does not teach for fear that his profit might be taken from him abandons the study of nature—the true teacher of painters—wherein those things already learned are forgotten, and those not yet learned are never acquired.

### *On the manner of clothing figures.*

**O**bserve the decorum <note>original: "decoro" — the suitability of style and dress to the character's status and the scene's gravity</note> with which you clothe figures according to their rank and age; and above all, ensure that the cloths do not obstruct the movement—that is, the limbs—and that said limbs are not "cut" by the folds nor by the shadows of the garments. And imitate as much as you can the Greeks and Latins <note>Refers to classical Greco-Roman sculpture, known for "wet drapery" that reveals the anatomy</note> in the manner of revealing the limbs when the wind presses the cloth against them. And make few folds, except in old men wearing togas and men of authority, where many are appropriate. <margin>37</margin>

### *On garments.*

**G**arments must be diversified with various types of folds according to the quality of the fabrics; that is, if it is a thick and coarse cloth, it will make "macaroni-like" <note>original: "maccaronesche" — thick, tubular, and simplified folds resembling pasta</note> and sparse folds; and if it is of medium thickness and dense, it will make folds that are flat-faced and with small angles. And above all, remember in every quality of cloth to make the folds between one break and another thick in the middle and thin at the sides; and the least thickness of such a fold shall be in the middle of the rounded angle of the fold.

### *On the nature of the folds of cloths.*

**T**hat part of the fold which is found furthest from its constrained ends will return most to its original nature.
Naturally, every thing desires to maintain itself in its own being. Cloth, because it is of equal density and thickness both on its reverse and on its right side, desires to stay flat; therefore, when it is constrained by some fold or crease to leave that flatness, it observes the nature of the force in that part of itself where it is most constrained, and that part which is furthest from those constraints, you will find returning most to its original nature—that is, of being extended and wide. For example, let *a b c* be the fold of the cloth mentioned above; let *a b* be the place where said cloth is folded and constrained. I proposed to you that the part of the cloth furthest from the constrained ends would return most to its original nature. Therefore, *c* being found furthest from *a b*, the fold at *c* will be wider than in any other of its places. (*Fig. 2. Plate VIII.*)

### *How one ought to give folds to cloths.*

**O**ne should not give a cloth a confusion of many folds; rather, make them only where they are held by the hands or arms; the rest should be left to fall simply where its nature pulls it, and the figure should not be traversed by too many lines or breakages of folds.
Cloths should be drawn from nature; that is, if you wish

## On the fewness of folds in garments.

**T**he figures, being dressed in a mantle, should not show so much of the naked form that the mantle appears to be directly upon the flesh—unless, of course, you intend for the mantle to be against the skin. For you must consider that between the mantle and the flesh there are other garments which prevent the form of the limbs from being revealed through the mantle. And that form of the limbs which you do allow to be revealed, make it sufficiently thick so that other garments appear to be beneath the mantle. You should only reveal the nearly true thickness of the limbs on a nymph or an angel, who are depicted dressed in thin garments pushed and pressed against them by the blowing of the winds. To these and similar figures, one may very well reveal the form of their limbs.

## On the folds of garments in foreshortening.

**W**here the figure is <term>foreshortened</term> <note>original: "scorta"; the artistic technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has to create the illusion of three-dimensional space</note>, show a greater number of folds than where it is not foreshortened, and let its limbs be surrounded by thick folds that circle around said limbs. Let *a* be where the eye is placed; *m n* sends the middle of each circle further from the eye than their ends; *n o* shows them straight because they are directly opposite; *p q* sends them in the contrary direction. Thus, use this discretion in the folds that surround the arms, legs, or other parts. (Fig. 3. *Plate VIII.*)

## On the ways of dressing figures, and diverse habits.

**T**he garments of figures should be suited to their age and to <term>decorum</term> <note>original: "decoro"; the artistic principle of appropriateness, ensuring a figure's appearance matches their social standing and character</note>; that is, let the old man be <term>togated</term> <note>original: "togato"; dressed in a long, dignified robe or toga</note>, and the young man adorned in a habit that occupies less of the neck from the tops of the shoulders upward, except for those who make a profession in religion. And avoid as much as possible the fashions of one's own age, except when they happen to be of the types mentioned above <note>original: "(38)"; likely a cross-reference to a specific rule in the original manuscript regarding timeless or classical dress</note>. Such contemporary fashions should not be used except for figures that are meant to resemble those buried in churches <note>referring to funerary monuments or effigies where historical accuracy of the deceased's era is required</note>; this is so that we do not provide cause for laughter in our successors regarding the foolish inventions of men, or rather, so that we leave them with admiration for their dignity and beauty. 

And I remember in my own days, seeing in my childhood men both small and great having all the edges of their garments <term>slashed</term> <note>original: "frappati"; a fashion of cutting decorative slits or jagged edges into the fabric</note> in every part, as much at the head as at the feet and the sides. And indeed, such an invention seemed so beautiful to that age that they even slashed the slashes themselves, and they wore hoods in a similar fashion, and shoes, and slashed crests that emerged from the principal seams of the garments in various colors. 

Afterward, I saw shoes, caps, <term>purses</term> <note>original: "scarselle"; small pouches or bags worn at the belt</note>, weapons carried for offense, the collars of garments, the lower edges of <term>doublets</term> <note>original: "giuponi"; a man's close-fitting jacket</note>, the cords of the clothing—and in effect, even the mouths of those who wished to appear handsome were pointed with long and sharp tips. In the next age, the sleeves began to grow, and they were so large that each one by itself was greater than the vest. Then they began to raise the garments around the neck so much that at last they covered the whole head; then they began to strip it in such a way that the clothes could not be supported at the shoulders, because they did not rest upon them. Then

### *Of the eye that sees the folds of garments surrounding a man.*

**T**he shadows interposed between the folds of garments surrounding human bodies will be darker the more they are directly opposite the eye within the concavities where such shadows are generated. And I mean this to be the case when the eye is situated between the shaded part and the luminous part of the aforementioned figure.

### *Of the folds of garments.*

**T**he folds of garments placed upon figures in any pose must always show the action of that figure with their outlines, in such a way that they do not create ambiguity or confusion regarding the true attitude to anyone who considers them. Furthermore, no fold should, by the shadow of its depth, appear to "cut" through any limb; that is, the depth of the fold should not appear to go deeper than the surface of the clothed limb itself. And if you represent figures dressed in multiple layers of clothing, it should not appear that the outermost garment encloses only the simple bones of the figure, but rather the flesh together with the bones, and the garments covering that flesh, with a thickness appropriate to the multiplication of its layers.

## On the folds

The experience of folds, which is rarely retained in the memory, must be added to that side where the limb, through its curvature, diminishes <note>original: "diminuisce"; referring to the compression of fabric on the inner side of a bent joint</note>, in contrast to the opposite side of said bend.

### On the quality of the cloths

The folds of the cloths should always express the quality of the flesh of the figure's body <note>original: "carne della figura"; the physical substance and volume of the person beneath the clothing</note> where we are working; let them be joined one to another by their conformity, like fingers; and let the arrangement of their habit <note>original: "habitudine"; the characteristic way the fabric hangs or settles</note> serve our understanding, so that no fold goes through the middle of the waist in a way that cuts across other limbs; that is, that it goes into the depth of the fold, which the surface should not see, and that it goes around the figure to emerge from the two poles <note>original: "poli"; likely referring to the points of tension or the outer boundaries of a limb's volume</note> so that the final view echoes within through the surmounting of such a figure, but the flesh is seen through that which makes the garment of the flesh with all the depth which is required by the multiplication of the <unclear>garment</unclear> ...

# BOOK FIVE.

## ON SHADOW AND LIGHT, AND ON PERSPECTIVE.

---

->*What shadow is.*<-

**S**hadow, designated by its proper name, should be called an alleviation of light applied to the surface of bodies; its beginning is at the end of light, and its end is in darkness. <note>The author defines shadow not as a "thing" in itself, but as a reduction or "alleviation" of light intensity.</note>

->*What the difference is between shadow and darkness.*<-

**T**he difference that exists between shadows and darkness is this: that shadow is the alleviation of light, and darkness is the integral deprivation of that light. <note>original: "tenebre"; total darkness or the complete absence of photons, whereas shadow still contains some reflected light.</note>

->*From what shadow derives.*<-

**S**hadow derives from two things dissimilar to one another, because one is corporeal and the other is spiritual. The corporeal is the shading body <note>the physical object blocking the light</note>; the spiritual is the light. Therefore, light and body are the cause of shadow.

->*On the nature of shadow in itself.*<-

**S**hadow is of the nature of universal things, which are all more powerful at the beginning and weaken toward the end. I say this of the beginning of every evident form and quality,

## Of shadow, and its division.

**S**hadows on bodies are generated by dark objects placed before those bodies, and they are divided into two parts, of which one is called primitive and the other derivative.

->*Of two species of shadows and into how many parts they are divided.*<-

**T**he species of shadows are divided into two parts, one of which is called simple, and the other composite. Simple is that which is caused by a single light and a single body; composite is that which is generated by multiple lights upon the same body, or by multiple lights upon multiple bodies. Simple shadow is divided into two parts, namely primitive and derivative. Primitive is that which is joined to the surface of the shaded body; derivative is that shadow which separates from the aforementioned body and travels through the air, and if it finds resistance, it stops at the place where it strikes with the shape of its own base; and the same is said of composite shadows.

The primitive shadow always forms the base of the derivative shadow.

The boundaries of derivative shadows are straight lines.

The darkness of the derivative shadow diminishes the more it is remote from the primitive shadow.

That shadow will show itself to be darker which is surrounded by a more splendid whiteness; or on the contrary, it will be less evident where it is generated against a darker field. <note>39: This refers to the principle of simultaneous contrast, where the perceived intensity of a shadow depends on the brightness of its surroundings.</note>

### *Which is darker: the primitive shadow,*
### *or the derivative shadow?*

**T**he primitive shadow <note>The shadow attached directly to the object itself.</note> is always darker than the derivative shadow <note>The shadow cast by the object onto another surface or through the air.</note>, because it is not corrupted by the strike of a reflected light, which instead acts upon the field where that derivative shadow strikes. Let *b c d e* be the shaded body, and *a* be the light that causes the primitive shadow *b e c* and creates the derivative shadow *b e c h i*. I say that if there is no reflected illumination *f h e i g* to reflect and corrupt <note>In this context, "corrupt" means to dilute or weaken the darkness of the shadow by adding light.</note> the primitive shadow at *b e* with *f h* and at *c e* with *i g*, then such primitive shadow will remain darker than the strike of the derivative shadow; provided that both shadows are formed on surfaces of equal darkness of color, or equal clarity of shadow. (*Fig. 1. Plate IX.*)

The shadow will appear darker the closer it is to the light.

All shadows are of the same color, and that which is found against a more luminous field appears to be of greater darkness.

Among shadows of equal quality, that which is closer to the eye will appear to be of lesser darkness.

### *What difference there is between compound light*
### *and compound shadow.*

**C**ompound shadow is that which participates more in the shadowy than in the luminous; compound light is that which participates more in the luminous than in the shadowy. ### Of the compound derivative shadow.

**T**he compound derivative shadow loses its darkness in proportion to how far it becomes remote from the simple derivative shadow. Therefore, *i* is the privation of light, and the beginning of the simple derivative shadow, and thus we have defined the compound derivative shadow. (*Fig. 2. Plate IX.*)

### *Nature or condition of the shadow.*

No shadow exists without reflection, which reflection either increases or weakens it; that reflection increases it which arises from a thing darker than the shadow itself, and that other reflection weakens it which is born from a thing brighter than the shadow itself.

## *Whether the primitive shadow is more powerful than the derivative shadow.*

**T**he primitive shadow <note>The shadow on the object itself.</note>, being simple, will be of equal darkness to the simple derivative shadow <note>The cast shadow.</note>. This is proven: let the simple primitive shadow be *d e*, and the simple derivative be *f g*. I say, according to the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise], which states that darkness is the deprivation of light, it follows that a simple shadow is that which receives no illuminated reflection, and for this reason remains dark. Just as *d e* does not see the light *a*, neither does the simple derivative shadow *f g* see it; and therefore, these shadows are of equal darkness to one another, because both are deprived of light and of luminous reflection.
(*Fig. 11. Plate IX.*)

## *Of the motions of shadows.*

**T**he motions of shadows are of five natures. Of these, we shall say the first is that which moves the derivative shadow together with its shaded body, while the light causing that shadow remains immobile. The second, we shall say, is that in which the shadow and the light move, but the shaded body is immobile. The third will be that in which the shaded body and the luminous body move, but the luminous body moves more slowly than the shaded one. In the fourth motion of said shadow, the shaded body moves faster than the luminous one. And in the fifth, the motions of the shaded and luminous bodies are equal to each other; and these shall be treated distinctly in their proper place.

<note>Translator's note on technical vocabulary:
- <term>primitive shadow</term> (ombra primitiva): The shadow attached to the object itself, often called the "shading."
- <term>derivative shadow</term> (ombra derivativa): The shadow cast by the object onto another surface.
- <term>illuminated reflection</term> (reflessione alluminata): Light bouncing off one surface into a shadowed area.
- <term>shaded body</term> (corpo ombroso): The physical object that blocks the light.
- <term>causing light</term> (lume causatore): The primary light source creating the shadow.</note>

# *The striking of the derivative shadow, and its conditions.*

**T**he striking <note>The "percussione" refers to where a cast shadow hits or falls upon a surface.</note> of the derivative shadow <note>The cast shadow.</note> will never be similar to the primitive shadow <note>The shadow on the object itself.</note> unless it meets certain conditions: first, that the shaded body has no angles, nor is it perforated or jagged; second, that the shape of the luminous body is similar in shape to the shaded body; third, that the size of the luminous body is equal to the size of the shaded body; fourth, that the surface of the shaded ray <note>The "razzo ombroso" refers to the volume of darkness extending from the object.</note> is of equal length on every side; fifth, that the striking of the derivative shadow is created between equal angles; sixth, that such a striking is made upon a wall that is flat and uniform.

## *Of the derivative shadow, and where it is greater.*

**T**hat derivative shadow will be of greater quantity which arises from a greater quantity of light, and likewise the opposite. This is proven: *a b*, a small light, creates the derivative shadow, *c g e* and *d f h*, which are small; take the following figure: *n m*, the light of the sky, which being universal <note>A "universal light" refers to broad, diffused light like an open sky, rather than a single point source like a candle.</note> creates a large derivative shadow in *r t x*, and likewise the space *o s u*, because the part of the sky *p n* creates that shadow *r t x*, and likewise the space *l m*, a part of the sky, creates the opposite shadow *o s u*. (Fig. 12. *Plate IX.*)

## *Of the death of the derivative shadow.*

**T**he derivative shadow will be entirely destroyed in bodies illuminated by universal light. <note>Leonardo suggests that in perfectly diffused light, a cast shadow loses its definition and disappears.</note>

### *Of the supreme power of the derivative shadow.*

**I**n the case of particular lights <note>A "particular light" refers to a concentrated or point source of light, such as a candle or a small window, as opposed to the "universal light" of the open sky.</note>, the derivative shadow <note>The cast shadow.</note> will be of much greater power <note>Meaning it will be darker and more sharply defined.</note> the smaller the light source is in its perceptible quantity, and the more powerful its brightness.

### *Of the simple shadow of primary darkness.*

**T**he simple shadow is that which can be seen by no reflected light, but will only be increased by an opposing shadow. Let the spherical body <term>spherical</term> <note>original: "sperico"</note> $g$ be placed in the concavity $b c e f$, and let the particular light be $a$, which strikes at $b$ and reflects at $d$, and leaps with the second reflection into the spherical body $g$, which gathers part of the simple shadow <term>simple shadow</term> <note>A shadow that receives no secondary illumination from reflections.</note> in the angle, and which sees neither the incident light <term>incident light</term> <note>The primary ray of light hitting a surface.</note> nor the reflected light <term>reflected light</term> of any degree of reflection. Therefore, the shadow of the spherical body receives the reflection from the simple shadow $e$, and for this reason it is called a simple shadow. (*Fig. 13. Plate IX.*)

### *Of the three various figures of derivative shadows.*

**T**here are three varieties of derivative shadows <term>derivative shadows</term>, of which the first is wide at its origin <term>origin</term> <note>original: "nascimento," referring to the point where the shadow begins at the object.</note>, and the further it moves from such a beginning, the more it narrows. The second maintains an infinite length with the same width as its origin. The third is that which, at every degree of distance after the width of its origin, acquires degrees of width. (*Fig. 14. Plate IX.*)

## That derivative shadows are of three natures.

**D**erivative shadows <term>derivative shadows</term> <note>Shadows cast into the air or onto a surface, as opposed to the "primitive shadow" on the object itself.</note> are of three natures, of which one is dilating <note>Widening as it moves away from the object.</note>, the other columnar <note>Maintaining a constant width, like a cylinder.</note>, and the third converging at the point of the intersection of its sides; which, after such an intersection, are of infinite width, or rather straightness. And if you were to say that such a shadow is terminated at the angle of the conjunction of its sides, and passes no further, this is denied; because in the first [principles] of shadows it is proved that a thing is entirely terminated when no part of it exceeds its boundaries. Here, in such a shadow, the contrary is seen; for as soon as such a derivative shadow is born, there is clearly born the figure of two shadowy pyramids, which are joined at their angles. Therefore, if—according to the adversary—the first shadowy pyramid terminates the derivative shadow with its angle, from where then is the second shadowy pyramid born? The adversary says it is caused by the angle, and not by the shadowy body, and this is denied with the help of the second [proposition] of this [treatise] which says: shadow is an accidental quality created by shadowy bodies interposed between the location of said shadow and the luminous body. And because of this, it is clear that the shadow is not generated by the angle of the derivative shadow, but only by the shadowy body. (*Fig. 15. Plate X.*)

# *That derivative shadows are of three species.*

**D**erivative shadows <term>derivative shadows</term> <note>Shadows cast through space or onto a surface, distinct from the "primitive" shadow attached to the object.</note> are of three species: that is, either its intersection upon the wall where it strikes will be larger than its base <note>The "base" refers to the diameter of the object casting the shadow.</note>, or it will be smaller than said base, or it will be equal. And if it is larger, it is a sign that the light which illuminates the shadowy body is smaller than that body; and if it is smaller, the light is larger than the body; and if it is equal, the light is equal to that body.

## *Quality of shadows.*

**A**mong equal diminutions of light <note>original: "alleviazioni di luce"</note>, the proportion between the darkness of the generated shadows will be the same as the proportion between the darkness of the colors where such shadows are joined.

### *Of the motion of the shadow.*

**T**he motion of the shadow is always faster than the motion of the body that generates it, provided the light source is immobile. This is proved: let the light source be *a e*, the shadowy body *b e*, and the shadow *d*. I say that in the same time that the shadowy body moves from *b* to *c*, the shadow *d* moves to *e* <note>The original text says "moves in c," likely a transcription error for the shadow's destination point on the wall.</note>; and that proportion which exists between speed and speed made in the same time, is the same as the proportion between the length of one motion and the length of the other. Therefore, the proportion that the length of the motion made by the shadow-casting body *b* to *c* has with the length of the motion made by the shadow *d* to *e*, such is the proportion between the aforementioned speeds of their motions. But if the light source is equal in speed to the motion of the shadowy body, then the shadow and the shadowy body will be equal to each other in equal motions. And if the light source is faster than the shadowy body, then the motion...

### *Of the pyramidal shadow.*

### *Of the simple derivative shadow.*

**T**he simple derivative shadow is of three kinds: one finite in length, and two infinite. ### *Of the composite derivative shadow.*

**T**he composite derivative shadow <term>composite derivative shadow</term> <note>A complex shadow formed by multiple light sources or a broad luminous area, resulting in varying degrees of darkness (penumbra).</note> is of two kinds: namely, columnar and dilating.

### *Whether the shadow can be seen in the air.*

**T**he shadow will be seen through misty or dusty air; this is demonstrated to us when the sun penetrates through openings <term>openings</term> <note>original: "spiracoli"; small holes, vents, or apertures.</note> into dark places. Then one sees the shadow interposed between the two or more solar rays <term>solar rays</term> <note>original: "razzi solari"</note> that pass through said openings.

### On shadows.

**T**he shadow will never possess the true likeness of the outline of the body from which it originates—even if that body were spherical—unless the light source is of the same shape as the shaded body.

If the light source is of a long shape, and this length extends vertically, the shadows of the bodies illuminated by it will extend in width.

If the length of the light source is horizontal, the shadow of a spherical body will become long in its height; and thus, in whatever direction the length of the light is found, the shadow will always have its length intersected in the opposite direction, in the manner of a cross with the length of the light.

If the light source is thicker and shorter than the shaded body, the projection <term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussione"; refers to the point or surface where a projected shadow strikes or "hits."</note> of the derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra derivativa"; the shadow projected by an object onto another surface, as opposed to the "primitive shadow" on the object itself.</note> will be longer and thinner than the primitive shadow <term>primitive shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra primitiva"; the shadow residing on the part of the object not reached by light.</note>.

If the light source is thinner and longer than the shaded body, the projection of the derivative shadow will be thicker and shorter than the primitive one.

If the length and width of the light source are equal to the length and width of the shaded body, then the projection of the derivative shadow will be of the same shape in its boundaries as the primitive shadow.

## *Of the boundaries of the derivative shadow.*

**T**he boundaries <term>termini</term> <note>original: "termini"; refers to the edges or limits where shadow meets light.</note> of the derivative shadow are less perceptible in universal lights <note>Ambient or diffused light, like an overcast sky.</note> than in particular lights <note>Focused or point-source lights, like a candle or the sun.</note>.

## *Of the extension of the derivative shadow.*

**T**he boundaries of derivative shadows expand all the more around the shadowy body as the light generating them is of greater size.

## *Where the derivative shadow is darkest.*

**T**hat part of the derivative shadow will be darkest which is closest to its cause. It follows that the opposite is true: that part of the derivative shadow will be of lesser darkness which is most remote from its cause.

<note>Vocabulary used in this section:
- derivative shadow: the shadow traveling through the air.
- object: the physical body blocking the light.
- universal lights: diffused illumination.
- particular lights: direct, concentrated light sources.
- darkness: the intensity of the shadow.</note>

### *On the variations of shadows according to the changing sizes of the lights that generate them.*

**A** shadow increases behind a single body in the same proportion as the decrease of the light that generates it, provided the position remains unchanged.

### *On the variation of the shadow without a decrease in the light that causes it.*

**T**he shadow of a single body increases and decreases in proportion to the increase or decrease of the space placed between the light and the shadowy object, provided that the object is smaller than the luminous body <note>Leonardo is observing how moving an object closer to a light source (like a candle) makes its shadow larger on a wall.</note>.

### *On the shadow that is converted into light.*

**A** site shaded by means of the sun will remain illuminated by the air <note>The ambient light of the sky.</note> after the departure of said sun, because a lesser light is always a shadow in comparison to a greater light <note>original: "sempre il minor lume è ombra del lume maggiore." This is a fundamental principle for Leonardo: darkness is relative.</note>.

### *On the light that is converted into shadow.*

**A** site illuminated by the air will become shadowy if it is surrounded by the striking of solar rays; this occurs because the greater light makes the light of lesser brightness appear dark <note>This describes the optical effect of high contrast, where a moderately lit area looks black when placed next to direct, brilliant sunlight.</note>.

### *That shadows must always participate in the color of the shadowy body.*

**N**othing appears in its natural whiteness <note>original: "bianchezza"</note>, because the locations in which things are seen render them to the eye as much more or less white as that location is more or less dark. And the Moon teaches us this, which by day appears to us in the sky with little clarity, and at night with such splendor that she provides us a likeness of the Sun <term>simulacro del Sole</term>, and of the day, by her driving away of the darkness. And this arises from two things: the first is comparison, which by its nature shows things to be more perfect in the quality of their colors the more they are dissimilar [to their surroundings]; the second is that the pupil <term>pupilla</term> is larger at night than during the day, as is proven; and a larger pupil sees a luminous body with greater quantity and more excellent splendor than a smaller pupil does, as is proven by anyone who looks at the stars through a small hole made in paper.

### *Of white things remote from the eye.*

**A** white thing removed from the eye, the further it is removed, the more it loses its whiteness; and it does so even more when the Sun illuminates it, because it participates in the color of the Sun mixed with the color of the air that is interposed between the eye and the white object. This air, if the Sun is in the east, appears turbid and reddish due to the vapors that rise within it; but if the eye turns toward the east, it will see only the shadows of the white object participating in the blue color <note>Leonardo is observing "atmospheric perspective," where distance and light conditions change the perceived color of objects.</note>.

### *Of the shadows of remote things, and their color.*

**T**he shadows of remote things will participate more in the blue color the darker and more remote they are in themselves; and this happens because of the interposition of the brightness of the air, which comes between the darkness of the shadowy bodies placed between the Sun and the eye that sees them; but if the eye turns with the Sun behind it <note>original: "interposto al Sole"; meaning the observer is between the sun and the object.</note>, it will not see such a blue.

### *Which body receives a greater quantity of shadow.*

**T**hat body will be covered by a greater quantity of shadow which is illuminated by a smaller luminous body. **A** greater quantity of light is received by that body which is illuminated by a larger light source. ### *Which body receives a darker shadow.*

**T**hat body will receive a shadow of greater darkness which is more dense; even if such bodies are of the same color, I say that the shadow of a green cloth will be darker than that of a leafy tree, even if the green of the cloth and of the tree's leaves are of the same quality. And this is caused because the cloth is not transparent, as the leaf is, and does not have illuminated air interspersed between its parts, as the greenery of plants does, which serves to confuse <note>In this context, "confuse" means to blur or soften the intensity of the shadow by mixing it with light.</note> the shaded part.

### *On the quality of the darkness of shadows.*

**T**he darkness of derivative shadows <note>Derivative shadows are the shadows cast by an object into the air or onto another surface, as opposed to the "attached" shadow on the object itself.</note> is infinitely variable, possessing greater or lesser intensity depending on the greater or lesser distances at which the impacts of these derivative shadows are caused. This is proven: let the Sun be *a*, which generates the shadow *n p h i*, into which enters the light of the air that surrounds the solar rays—that is, *e b r s* from above, and *f c r s* from below. This air light brightens the shadow, which remains darkest only in the space *n p o*, where it sees neither the sun nor the air, except for its extremities *b c*. (*Fig. 31. Plate XI.*)

### *On the shadow of the greenery of meadows.*

**T**he greenery of meadows has minimal, indeed almost imperceptible shadow, especially where the grasses are minute and have thin leaves. For this reason, shadows cannot be generated, because the great hemisphere <note>The "hemisphere" refers to the entire dome of the sky providing ambient light from all directions.</note> surrounds the tiny stalks in a circle; unless there is a clump of wide leaves, the shadows of the grass are of little evidence.

### *Precept of painting.*

**I**n universal lights <note>Ambient or diffused light, such as an overcast sky, rather than a single point source like a candle.</note>, shadows occupy little space on the surfaces of bodies. This occurs because the vast amount of light from our hemisphere surrounds the shaded bodies even down to their lowest parts, provided the light is not blocked by its own horizon, and especially if the body is suspended above the ground. Let *f* be the shaded body, and the earth *a b c d* be our hemisphere, with *a d e* being the horizon of that hemisphere; thus, the darkness of the earth *u x* obscures as much of the shaded body as it... <note>The sentence breaks off here, likely continuing on the following page.</note>

### *On shadows that do not match the illuminated part.*

**V**ery rare are those shadows of opaque bodies that are true shadows of their illuminated parts. This is proven by the seventh [rule] of the fourth [book], which says that the surface of every shaded body participates in the color of its object <note>In this context, "object" refers to the surrounding things facing the body, which reflect their own color onto it.</note>. Therefore, the illuminated color of faces, having a black color as their object, will participate in black shadows; and it will do the same with yellow, green, and blue, and every other color placed opposite to it. And this happens because every body sends its likeness <term>similitudine: the visual image or "species" of an object traveling through space</term> through all its surrounding air, as is proven in perspective, and as is seen by the experience of the Sun, from which all objects placed before it participate in its light and reflect that light to other objects. This is seen with the moon and the other stars, which reflect to us the light given to them by the Sun. Darkness does the same thing, since it clothes with its own obscurity whatever is enclosed within it.

### *On the light of shaded bodies, which are almost never of the true color of the illuminated body.*

**W**e can say that it is almost never the case that the surface of illuminated bodies is of the true color of those bodies.

The seventh [rule] of the fourth [book] states the cause of what we have proposed, and further demonstrates to us that when a face placed in a dark location is illuminated on one side by a ray of air <note>Refers to natural daylight or atmospheric light entering a space.</note>, and on the other by a ray from a lit candle, it will undoubtedly appear to be of two colors. Before the air saw such a face, the candlelight appeared as its proper color, and the same occurred with the light of the air.

If you hold a white strip and place it in a dark location, and allow it to receive light through three openings—namely from the Sun, from fire, and from the air—that strip will be of three colors.

### *How shadows behave at a long distance.*

**S**hadows are lost at a long distance because the great quantity of luminous air, which exists between the eye and the thing seen, surrounds the shadow of that thing with its own color.

### *On the width of shadows and primary lights.*

**T**he expansion and retraction of shadows—or rather the greater or lesser width of shadows and lights upon opaque bodies—will be found in the greater or lesser curvature of the parts of the bodies where they are generated.

### *On the greater or lesser darkness of shadows.*

**T**he greater or lesser darkness of shadows is generated in the most curved parts of the limbs, and the least dark will be found in the broadest parts.

## *Where shadows deceive the judgment, which gives sentence on their greater or lesser darkness.*

**A**mong shadows of equal darkness, that one will appear less dark which is surrounded by lights of lesser power, such as the shadows generated among reflected lights; therefore, you, the painter, must take care not to deceive yourself by varying such a shadow <note>Leonardo warns that the surrounding environment changes our perception of a shadow's value, even if the shadow itself remains physically the same.</note>.

## *Where lights deceive the judgment of the painter.*

**A**mong lights of equal brightness, that one will seem more powerful which is smaller and surrounded by a darker field.

## *Of shadows in bodies.*

**W**hen you represent dark shadows in shaded bodies, always represent the cause of such darkness, and you shall do the same for reflections; because dark shadows arise from dark objects, and reflections from objects of little brightness—that is, from diminished lights. And such proportion exists between the illuminated part of bodies and the part brightened by reflection, as exists between the cause of the light of those bodies and the cause of such reflection <note>Leonardo is applying a mathematical principle to optics: the relationship between a direct light and its shadow is proportional to the relationship between a secondary light source and its corresponding reflection.</note>.

## *Of the qualities of shadows and lights.*

**T**he difference between lights and their shadows will be much greater in bodies placed in powerful lights than in those placed in dark locations.

### *Of the imperceptible boundaries of shadows.*

### *Of the qualities of lights and shadows in shaded bodies.*

<header>Of lights.</header>

### *Of lights and shadows.*

### *Of the lights and shadows that tint the surface of the landscapes.*

And these landscapes will participate in blue all the more as they are more remote from the eye; and that blue will become clearer as it rises toward the horizon, and this arises from the humid vapors. <note>This describes "aerial perspective," where distance makes objects appear bluer and paler due to the atmosphere.</note>

Things are less distinct in the shadows than in the lights, and the universal light <note><term>universal light</term>: diffused light from the sky rather than a direct, point-source like the sun.</note> surrounds the shaded bodies and leaves them with little relief when the eye is positioned between the shaded part and the light. The shadow to such an eye is invisible, but the bodies to the side at that time will show their lights in greater or lesser quantity, according as such bodies are nearer or further from the straight line that extends from one horizon to the other, passing through the two eyes viewing such a countryside.

### *Of derivative light.*

**D**erivative light <note><term>derivative light</term>: the light that emanates from an illuminated object or passes through a medium, as opposed to the primary source.</note> results from two things: namely, original light and a shaded body.

### *Of lights.*

**T**he lights that illuminate opaque bodies are of four kinds: namely, universal, such as that of the air which is within our horizon; and particular, such as that of the Sun, or of a window, or door, or other space. The third is reflected light. The fourth is that which passes through transparent things, such as cloth, or

### Of shadow and light.

**D**arkness is the deprivation of light, and light is the deprivation of darkness; shadow is the mixture of darkness with light, and it will be of greater or lesser obscurity according to whether the light that mixes with it is of lesser or greater power.

### *Of lights and shadows.*

**E**very part of the body, and every smallest particle that happens to have some degree of relief <term>relief: the quality of appearing three-dimensional or projecting from a surface</term>, I remind you to be careful to give it its primary shadows and lights.

### *Of shadow and light.*

**E**very part of the surface that surrounds bodies is transformed, in part, into the color of that object which is placed before it.

### *Example.*

**I**f you place a spherical body in the midst of various objects—that is, if on one side there is the light of the sun, and on the opposite side there is a wall illuminated by the sun, let it be green or another color, and the floor where it rests be red, and the two transverse sides be dark—you will see the natural color of said body participate in the colors of the objects surrounding it. The most powerful will be the luminous one <note>the direct sunlight</note>, the second will be that of the illuminated wall, the third that of the shadow; there remains then a quantity that participates in the color of the extremes <note>original: "stremi," referring to the edges or the furthest boundaries of the color zones</note>.

**S**ee, you who portray the works of nature, the quantity, the quality, and the shapes of the lights and shadows of each muscle; and note, along the length of their shape, toward which muscle they are directed by the straightness of their central lines.

## *Of lights within shadows.*

**W**hen you portray any body, remember when you make a comparison of the power of the lights of its illuminated parts, that the eye is often deceived, as a part appears brighter to it which is actually less bright. And the cause arises by means of the comparisons of the parts that border them; because if there are two parts of unequal brightness, and the less bright one borders dark parts, and the brighter one borders bright parts—such as the sky or similar brightnesses—then that which is less bright (or I should say luminous) will appear more luminous, and the brighter one will appear darker. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of simultaneous contrast, where the perception of a value changes based on its background.</note>

## *Of light and dark.*

**L**ight and dark, together with foreshortenings <term>foreshortenings: the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has to create the illusion of three-dimensional space</term>, are the excellence of the science of painting. (42)

## *Of light and dark.*

**L**ight and dark—that is, light and shadows—have a middle ground, which can be named neither light nor dark, but participates equally in both light and dark. And it is sometimes equally distant from the light and the dark, and sometimes closer to one than to the other.

## *Of the four things that must be principally considered in shadows and lights.*

**F**our are the principal parts which must be considered in painting: namely quality, quantity, position, and shape. By quality, it is understood which shadow, or which part of the shadow, is more or less dark. Quantity, that is, how great the size of such a shadow is in respect to the others nearby. Position, that is, in what manner they must be placed, and upon which part of the limb where it rests. Shape, that is, what the shape of that shadow is, such as saying if it is triangular, or partakes of a round or square form, etc.

The aspect <note>original: "aspetto"; here referring to the orientation or directional alignment of a shape</note> is also to be counted among the parts of the shadows; that is, if the shadow has length, to see toward which aspect the sum of such length is directed. If the shadow of an eyebrow is directed toward the ear, or if the lower shadow of the eye socket is directed toward the nostril of the nose, and thus by similar comparisons of various aspects, to situate those shadows. Therefore, the aspect is to be placed before the position.

## *Of the nature of the light illuminating shaded bodies.*

**T**he universal light <note>original: "lume universale"; likely referring to ambient or diffused light, such as the sky, rather than a direct point source like a candle</note> surrounds the part of the shaded body seen by it, and illuminates it, and varies the illumination of that body with greater or lesser clarity, according as the illuminated parts of such a body are seen by a greater or lesser quantity of that universal light.

<header>Of universal lights upon polished bodies.</header>

The universal lights surrounding polished bodies will provide a universal brightness to the surfaces of such bodies.

### *Of shaded bodies which are polished and lustrous.*

**O**f shaded bodies that have a polished and lustrous surface, those that have a particular light <note>original: "lume particolare"; a specific, directional light source like a lamp or the sun</note> vary their shadows and highlights <note>original: "lustri"; the specular reflections or "glints" on a shiny surface</note> in as many different positions as there are changes in the position of the eye that sees them.

In this case, the particular light can be immobile and the eye mobile, and likewise the reverse, which is the same thing regarding the changes of the highlights and shadows on the surfaces of these bodies.

### *How bodies surrounded by universal light generate particular lights in many of their parts.*

**P**articular lights are generated on the surfaces of shaded bodies even though their entirety is surrounded from above by the universal light of the sky without the sun—as it is when some dark cloud takes it from us and occupies it. And this arises from the inequality <note>original: "inegualità"; referring to the irregular or three-dimensional relief of a surface</note> that the surfaces of these bodies have, by means of the limbs joined to them. These limbs, by interposing themselves between the light and the shaded body, deprive that body of a great quantity of universal light; hence the light that penetrates between the limbs and the body will be a particular light—that is, a part of the whole light which embraces the exterior parts of each limb of the body.

<note>Leonardo is explaining that even under flat, overcast lighting, the "particular" or directional light effects are created by the body's own anatomy casting shadows on itself, effectively filtering the ambient sky light into specific beams.</note>

## *Of the shadows and lights with which natural things are imitated.*

**T**here are some who wish to see dark shadows in all their works, and thus they criticize those who do not do as they do. These people will be satisfied in part by using dark shadows and light shadows: the dark ones in dark places, and the light ones in open country under universal lights <note>The ambient, non-directional light of an overcast sky or open shade</note>.

### *Of shadows, and in which bodies they cannot have great power of darkness, and likewise the lights.*

**W**here shadows of great darkness are not generated, one cannot yet generate lights of great brightness. And this happens in trees with sparse and narrow leaves, such as willows, broom plants, junipers, and the like; and also in transparent fabrics, such as thin silks <note>original: "zendadi"; a fine, light silk fabric used in the Renaissance</note>, veils, and the like; and likewise in curly and loose hair. This happens because the entirety of each of the aforementioned species does not create highlights <note>original: "lustri"; specular reflections or glints</note> on its individual particles, and if they do exist, they are imperceptible, and their appearances barely move from the place where they are generated. 

The shaded parts of such particles behave similarly, and their whole sum does not generate a dark shadow because the air penetrates and illuminates them—the parts near the center as much as those on the outside. If there is any variety, it is almost imperceptible, and thus the illuminated parts of this whole cannot be too different from the shaded parts. Because the luminous air penetrates through all the particles as has been said, the illuminated parts are so close to the shaded particles that their appearances sent to the eye create a confused mixture, composed of tiny lights and darks, in such a way that one cannot discern in such a mixture

<summary>Leonardo explains that objects with fine or transparent structures, like willows or thin silks, cannot produce high-contrast light and shadow because ambient air and light penetrate their surfaces. He argues against a "one-size-fits-all" approach to dark shadows, noting that contrast depends on the material's density.</summary>

### *Of the particular light of the Sun, or of another*
### *luminous body.*

**T**hat part of the illuminated body will be of more intense brightness which is struck by the luminous ray <term>razzo luminoso: a straight line or beam of light</term> at more similar angles <note>meaning angles closer to perpendicular (90 degrees)</note>, and the least illuminated will be that which is found at the most unequal angles of those luminous rays.

The angle *n* on the side facing the sun, being struck by that sun at equal angles <note>original: "angoli eguali"; referring to the incident rays being perpendicular to the surface</note>, will be illuminated with a greater power of rays than any other part of that illuminated body. The point *c* will be less illuminated than any other part, because that point is struck by the solar body at more unequal angles than any other part of the plane <note>original: "planizia"</note> where such solar rays extend; and of the two angles, let the larger be *d c e* and the smaller *e c f*, and the equal angles, which I should have described first, are *a n o* and *b n r*, which are exactly equal, and for this reason *n* will be more illuminated than any other part. (*Fig. 34. Plate XI.*)

### *Of the universal light of the air, where*
### *the Sun does not strike.*

**T**hat thing will appear more illuminated which is seen by a greater quantity of the luminous source. For what has been said, *e* will be more illuminated than *a*, because *e* sees a greater sum of the sky, seeing *r s*, which *a* does not see, seeing only the sky *b c d*. (*Fig. 35. Plate XI.*)

### *Of universal illumination mixed with the particular light of the sun or other lights.*

**W**ithout doubt, that part of the <term>shaded body: an object that blocks light and thus creates shadows</term> which is seen by a smaller quantity of the universal and particular light source will be the least illuminated. This is proven: let *a* be the body of the sun placed in the sky *n a m*. I say that point *o* of the <term>shaded body</term> will be more illuminated by the <term>universal light: the broad, ambient light coming from the entire sky</term> than point *r*, because *o* sees, and is seen by, the entire portion of the <term>universal light</term> *n a m*, while point *r* is seen only by the portion of the sky *m e*. Furthermore, *o* is seen by the entire mass of the sun that is turned toward it, while *r* does not see any part of that sun. (*Fig. 36. Plate XI.*)

### *Of the middle shadow, which is placed between the illuminated and the shaded parts of bodies.*

**B**etween the illuminated part and the shaded part of bodies, the <term>middle shadow: the transitional half-tone or penumbra</term> is interposed, which varies its boundaries greatly; for where it ends against the shadow, it turns into shadow, and where it ends against the illuminated part, it takes on the brightness of that illumination. And if the <term>primary light: the direct, main source of illumination</term> is a particular one <note>such as a single lamp or the sun, rather than diffuse daylight</note>, then there will be <term>highlights: "lustri," the bright reflections or glints on a surface</term>, which are as clearly defined boundaries of the <term>middle shadow</term> as the shaded part itself.

### *Whether a large light of low power is equal to a small light of great power.*

**T**he shadow generated by a small and powerful light is darker than the shadow born from a larger light of lesser power.

### *Where and in which color shadows most lose the natural color of the shaded objects.*

**W**hite, which sees neither incident light nor any sort of reflected light, is that which first loses its own natural color entirely in its shadow—if indeed one can call white a color. But black increases its color in the shadows and loses it in its illuminated parts; and it loses it all the more as the illuminated part is seen by a light of greater power. And green and blue increase their color in the middle-shadows; and red and yellow acquire color in their illuminated parts. White does the same, and mixed colors participate in the nature of the colors that accompany such a mixture; that is, black mixed with white makes <term>berettino: a dull, ash-gray or leaden color common in Renaissance textiles and painting</term>. This color is not as beautiful in the deepest shadows as simple black is, and it is not as beautiful in the highlights as simple white is, but its supreme beauty is found between light and shadow.

### *Which color of a body will produce a shadow most different from the light, that is, which will be darkest.*

**T**hat body will have its shaded parts furthest removed from brightness in relation to its illuminated parts which is of a color closest to white.

## Which part of a body will be most illuminated by a light source of the same quality.

**T**hat part of a body which is illuminated by a luminous quality will be of a more intense brightness than that which is struck by a thicker <note>Leonardo uses "thicker" or "grosser" to mean a wider or more obtuse angle</note> luminous angle. This is proved: let the hemisphere be *r m c*, which illuminates the house *k d o f*; I say that the part of the house struck by the wider angle, born from the same luminous quality, will be more illuminated. Therefore, at *f*, where the angle *n f c* strikes, there will be a more intense brightness of light than where the angle *e d c* strikes; and the proportion of the lights will be the same as that of the angles, and the proportion of the angles will be the same as that of their bases *n c* and *e c*. Of these, the larger exceeds the smaller by the entire part *n e*. Thus, at *a*, under the eaves of the roof of such a house, there will be as much less light than at *d* as the base *b c* of the angle *b a c* is smaller than the base *e c*. And so it follows always proportionately, the light being of one and the same quality. And the same which is said above is confirmed in any body illuminated by our hemisphere <note>The "hemisphere" refers to the open sky or the dome of the heavens providing ambient light</note>. And here it is manifested in the part of the <term>spherical object: a round body used as a geometric model for light study</term> under the hemisphere *k* and *f*, which at point *b* is illuminated by the entire part *a c e*, and at part *d* by the hemisphere *e f*, and at *o* by *c f*, and *m n* by *m f*, and at *h* by *s f*; and thus you have learned where the primary light and the primary shadow are located in any body. (*Fig. 41 and 42, Plate XI.*)

That part of a shaded body will be more luminous which is illuminated by a greater sum of light. That part of the <term>reflected light</term> which partially clothes the surface of bodies will be as much less bright than the part illuminated by the air as it is less bright than the air itself.

And you, painter, who practice narrative scenes, ensure that your figures have as many varieties of lights and shadows as there are various objects that have created them; and do not create a <term>general manner: a repetitive or "formulaic" style of shading that ignores specific environmental lighting</term>.

The part of the surface of every body participates in as many various colors as there are those that stand before it as an object.

The countryside illuminated by the sun will have shadows of any object that are of great darkness; and to one who views it from the opposite side to that which the sun sees <note>meaning, looking toward the sun, seeing the shadowed side of objects</note>, it will appear extremely dark, and remote things will appear near.

But when you see things along the same line as the sun sees them <note>with the sun behind the viewer</note>, they will appear to you without shadows, and near things will appear remote and of unrecognizable shape.

An object that is illuminated by the air without the sun <note>under an overcast sky or in open shade</note> will have its darkest part where it sees the least amount of air; and it will be darker in proportion to the greater amount of dark surroundings it faces.

Things seen in the open countryside have little difference between their shadows and their lights, and their shadows will be almost imperceptible and without any sharp edges; rather, like smoke, they will fade away toward the luminous parts. Only there will the shadow be darkest where it is deprived of the <term>object of the air: the surrounding atmosphere that provides ambient light</term>.

An object seen in poorly lit places, or at the beginning of the night, will also have little difference between its lights and shadows; and if it is full night, the difference between lights and shadows is so imperceptible to the human eye that the object loses its shape entirely, and is only visible to the keen sight of nocturnal animals.

Things appear ambiguous and doubtful due to distance; paint them with such confusion, otherwise they will not appear to be at that same distance. Do not finish their boundaries with a certain definition, because boundaries are lines or angles; and since these are the smallest parts of things, they are invisible not only from afar, but even from up close.

If the line, and likewise the <term>mathematical point: a point that has position but no physical dimension</term>, are invisible things, and the boundaries of things are also lines...

### *Which colors produce the greatest variety between lights and shadows.*

**A**mong the colors, there will be a greater difference between their shadows and their lights in those which are most similar to whiteness; this is because white has a brighter illumination and a darker shadow than any other color, even though neither white nor black are counted among the number of true colors <note>Leonardo often argued that white and black were the "extremes" or "receptacles" of color rather than colors themselves.</note>.

### *All colors in distant shadows are unknown and indiscernible.*

**A**ll colors seen from a distance will be unknown when they are in shadow, because an object that is not touched by the principal light is not powerful enough to send its <term>similitude: the visual image or likeness of an object traveling through space</term> to the eye through the more luminous air, for the lesser light is overcome by the greater.

->Example.<-

**W**e see, while being inside a house, that all the colors upon the surfaces of the walls are seen clearly and distinctly when the windows of said dwelling are open; but if we go outside of that house and look from a little distance through those same windows to see the paintings made upon those walls, instead of those paintings we will see a continuous darkness.

### *Of the color of shadows, and how much they darken.*

**J**ust as all colors are dyed in the obscurity of the darkness of night, so the shadows of any color end in those same shadows. Therefore, you, painter, do not observe that in your final obscurities the colors that border one another must be recognizable; because if nature does not allow it, and you make a profession of being an imitator of nature as far as art permits, do not presume to correct her errors. For there is no error in her, but know that it is in you; since once a principle is given, it is necessary that a middle and an end follow that are consistent with that principle. <note>Leonardo is arguing that if a painter starts with a realistic premise, they must follow the laws of physics to the end, even if it means losing detail in the dark.</note>

### *Of the colors of the illuminating lights of shadowy bodies.*

**T**he shadowy body placed between nearby walls in a dark place—which on one side is illuminated by a tiny candlelight, and on its opposite side is illuminated by a tiny <term>vent: a small opening or crack</term> of air—if it is white, then such a body will appear yellow on one side and blue on the other, provided the eye is in a place illuminated by the air.

### *On the qualities of the air regarding shadows and lights.*

**T**hat body will show the greatest difference between its shadows and its lights when it is seen under the strongest light, such as the light of the Sun, or at night by the light of a fire. This is to be used sparingly in painting <term>pittura: the art of painting</term>, because the works remain harsh and without grace.

That body which finds itself in a moderate light <term>mediocre lume: middle or average light</term> will have little difference between its lights and its shadows.

And this occurs toward evening, or when it is cloudy. These works are soft, and every quality of face gains grace from it; thus, in everything, the extremes are flawed: too much light makes it harsh, too much darkness does not allow one to see; the middle ground is good.

### *On small lights.*

**L**ights created by small windows also make a great difference between the lights and the shadows, especially if the room illuminated by them is large; and this is not good to use.

### *Which surface has the greatest difference between light and dark.*

**T**he black surface (and also those that participate most in that blackness <term>negredine: an archaic term for deep blackness</term>) has less difference between its shadowed and illuminated parts than any other. This is because the illuminated part shows itself to be black, and the shadowed part cannot be anything other than black; but with little variety, it acquires somewhat more obscurity than the true illuminated part.

<summary>Leonardo advises painters to avoid harsh, high-contrast lighting in favor of the "graceful" soft light found at dusk or on cloudy days. He also explains how black surfaces minimize the visible distinction between light and shadow due to their inherent lack of reflected light.</summary>
<keywords>lighting, shadows, chiaroscuro, painting technique, grace, black surfaces, atmospheric light</keywords>

### *Where there is greater variety between shadows and lights, whether in near objects or remote ones.*

**T**hat shaded body will have less difference between its lights and shadows the further it is from the eye; and conversely, being near to the eye, the difference is greater. This is because of the density of the luminous air <note>original: "aria luminosa"</note>, which interposes itself with greater thickness between the eye and the shaded body when it is remote than when it is near. <note>Leonardo is describing "atmospheric perspective," where the air itself acts as a veil that softens contrasts over distance.</note>

### *Which body, of equal color and distance from the eye, varies its lights from its shadows the least.*

**T**hat body will show less difference from its shadows to its lights when it is in air of greater darkness. And conversely, the difference is greater when it is in air of greater splendor. We see this in things placed in the dark, which cannot be discerned, and in things placed before the splendor of the sun, where the shadows appear dark <note>original: "tenebrose"</note> compared to the parts struck by the solar rays <term>razzi solari: sunbeams or rays</term>.

### *Why the true figures of any body, clothed and defined in its surfaces, are recognized.*

**S**hadows and lights are the most certain cause for making the figures <note>In this context, "figures" refers to the three-dimensional form or shape of an object.</note> of any body known. This is because a color of equal brightness or darkness cannot demonstrate its relief <term>rilievo: the quality of appearing three-dimensional or projecting from a surface</term>; instead, it performs the function of a flat surface <term>superficie piana: a 2D plane</term>, which, being at an equal distance in all its parts, is equally distant from the splendor that illuminates it.

<summary>Leonardo explains how atmospheric density reduces contrast in distant objects and emphasizes that light and shadow are the essential tools for creating the illusion of three-dimensional relief on a flat canvas.</summary>

## On the discernment of shadows in locations, and of the things placed within them.

**I**f the Sun is in the east and you look toward the west, you will see all illuminated things to be entirely deprived of shadow, because you are seeing exactly what the Sun sees; and if you look toward the south or the north, you will see all bodies surrounded by shadow and light, because you are seeing both what the Sun sees and what it does not see. And if you look toward the path of the Sun <note>Looking directly toward the light source.</note>, all bodies will show you their shaded side, because that part which you see cannot be seen by the Sun.

### *On which surfaces the true and equal light is found.*

**T**hat surface will be equally illuminated which is equally remote from the body that illuminates it; as if from the light *a*, which illuminates the surface, equal lines were drawn to said surface. Then, by the definition of a circle, that surface will be equally illuminated in every part. And if such a surface were flat, as shown in the second demonstration *e f g h*, then if the ends of the surface were equally distant according to such lines, the middle *h* would be the part closest to that light; and it would be more illuminated than those ends in proportion to how much closer it is to the said light *e*. But if the ends of such a flat surface are removed from that light by unequal distances, as shown in the third figure *i k l m*, then the closest part and the most remote part will have such proportion in their lights as exists in their distances from the body that illuminates them.
(*Fig*. 53. *Plate XII.*)

<note>Leonardo is applying geometric principles to optics. He argues that light hits a curved surface (like a sphere) evenly if every point is equidistant from the source, but on a flat surface, the point directly opposite the light is brightest because it is the shortest distance away.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains how the observer's position relative to the sun determines the visibility of shadows and uses geometry to calculate how light intensity diminishes across a flat surface based on distance from the source.</summary>

But at point *s* one sees the shaded area *a b*, and also sees the shaded area *c d*; these two dark spaces are double the luminous body *b c*. However, the more you move from *s* toward *r*, the more you will lose of the darkness *a b*. Therefore, from *s* to *r*, the floor *s r* always brightens; furthermore, the more you move from *r* toward *o*, the less you will see of the luminous body. And for this reason, the floor *r o* darkens more as it approaches *o*. And by this discourse, we have proved that *r* is the clearest part of the floor *p s*.

### *Which light is it that, even if the eye is further removed from the shaded sphere than the light itself, can never see shadow while standing behind the light.*

**W**hen the <term>luminous body</term> <note>original: "luminoso"</note> is equal to, or larger than, the shaded sphere, then the eye that is behind such light can never see any part of the shadow on the shaded body due to the divergence of the said light.
