### On the shadow of the spherical opaque body resting upon the earth.

**B**ut the shadow of the spherical opaque body which rests in contact with the earth will be of greater darkness than the preceding one <note>Referring to the suspended sphere on the previous page.</note> which only sees the earth as its object. This is proved: let the opaque sphere be *n m s* resting upon the earth *a c* at point *s*, and let the arc *a b c* be our hemisphere; I say that the shadow which this sphere makes upon the earth where it rests will be darker than the aforementioned one, by the eighth [proposition] which says every cause is made a participant of its cause <note>A philosophical principle suggesting that the effect (the shadow) shares the qualities of its source (the dark earth).</note>, whence it follows that the earth, being the cause of such a shadow, will give the darkest shadow, which will be in itself darker, since the shaded part is darker than the illuminated part. And there it is concluded. (*Fig. 70. Plate XV.*)

### On the shadows of bodies that are somewhat transparent.

**N**o body participating in transparency <note>original: "trasparenza"; referring to translucent objects like leaves or fabric.</note> creates a dark shadow, unless it is shaded by the darkness of the shadows of many other similar bodies, such as the leaves of trees which cast shadows one upon the other.

### *On the boundaries of bodies which are the first to be lost to our perception.*

**T**he boundaries of opaque bodies are those of which, at a very short distance, perception is lost. That which is predicted to lose its perception is the surface of bodies—otherwise called the boundary of dense bodies—which, having no thickness, does not provide a clear perception of itself; and it provides even less the further it is removed from its investigator.

### *On the boundaries of opaque bodies.*

**T**he true boundaries of opaque bodies will never be seen with clear knowledge. And this arises because the <term>visual faculty</term> <note>original: "virtù visiva"; the power or mechanism of sight.</note> does not originate in a single point, as is proved in the fifth [proposition] of the fifth [book] of perspective, where it says the visual faculty is infused throughout the entire pupil of the eye. Therefore, the pupil *a b c* seeing the boundary of the body *n* at the extremity *m*, occupies the entire space *d e f* on the wall *g h*; because the upper part *a* of the pupil sees the boundary of the body *m* at point *d*, and the middle of the pupil *b* sees another lower boundary at point *e* which is higher than *d*, and the lower part of the pupil *c* sees another even lower boundary of the body, which is carried even higher on the said wall. And thus is proved the cause of the confusion of the boundaries possessed by shaded bodies. (*Fig. 71. Plate XV.*)

### *How the boundaries of shaded bodies seen by the same pupil are not in the same location on that body.*

**T**he boundaries of opaque bodies seen by the same pupil will never be in the same location on that body. This is proved: let the pupil *a b* see the upper part of the opaque body *n*. ### *On the proportion that the illuminated parts of bodies have with their reflections.*

**S**uch proportion will the part illuminated by the incident light <term>incident light: light falling directly from a source onto a surface</term> have to that which is illuminated by reflected light, as the incident light itself has to that reflected light. It is proven: let *a b* be the incident light that illuminates the sphere *c d m c n d* and passes with its rays to the object *e f*, and from there it is reflected into *c m d*; I say that if the light *a b* has two degrees of power and *e f* has one—which is sub-double <note>original: "subduplo"; a mathematical term meaning one-half.</note> to two—then the reflected light *c m d* will be sub-double to the light *c n d*. ### *On the darkest part of the shadow in spherical or cylindrical bodies.*

**T**he part of the shadow of spherical or cylindrical <note>original: "colonnali"; literally "column-like."</note> bodies will be positioned between its incident light and the reflected light.

### *How shadows made by specific lights should be avoided because their ends are similar to their beginnings.*

**S**hadows made by the Sun or other specific <note>original: "particolari"; referring to small, concentrated light sources like a lamp or the sun, which create harsh edges.</note> lights lack grace for the body they accompany, because they leave parts of the body in confusion with a sharp boundary between shadow and light; and these shadows are of equal intensity at their end as they are at their beginning.

### *On giving the proper lights to illuminated things according to their locations.*

**G**reat care must be taken regarding the lights assigned to the things they illuminate, since in a single narrative painting <note>original: "storia"; referring to a historical or figurative composition.</note> there may occur parts that are in the open country under the universal light of the sky, others that are in porticos—which are lights mixed of both particular and universal—and others under particular lights, that is, in dwellings that receive light from a single window. Of these three types of lights, for the first it is necessary for the lights to occupy large areas, according to the fourth rule of the first book which says: such proportion exists from the size to the size of the parts of the illuminated bodies, as exists from the size to the size of the objects of those illuminators <note>Leonardo is describing a geometric relationship where the breadth of the light source (like the whole sky) dictates the breadth of the light on the object.</note>. And furthermore, among these, some require reflections from one body to another where the light enters through narrow spaces between the bodies illuminated by the universal light; because for lights that penetrate between bodies close to one another, the same thing happens as with lights that penetrate through the windows and doors of houses, which we call particular lights; and thus we shall provide the proper reminders of this in its place. (44)

## On applying lights.

**F**irst, apply a universal shadow throughout the entire containing part that does not see the light; then apply the middle shadows and the principal ones in comparison to one another. **E**nsure that shadows cast upon the surface of bodies by various objects always tend to undulate with various twists, according to the variety of the members that create the shadows and of the thing that receives said shadow.

### *A method for giving figures a shadow that is a companion to the light and the body.*

**W**hen you create a figure and you wish to see if the shadow is a companion to the light—that is, that it is not more red or yellow than the nature of the color you wish to shade requires—you shall do this: cast a shadow with your finger over the illuminated part, and if the accidental shadow <note>original: "ombra accidentale." A shadow cast by an external object, in this case, the artist's own finger.</note> made by you is similar to the natural shadow made by the finger upon your work, it will be correct; and with your finger closer or further away, you can create darker or lighter shadows, which you should always compare with your own. (45) <note>This practical "finger test" allows the painter to check if their painted shadow matches the physical reality of light hitting that specific pigment.</note>

### *On the positions of lights and shadows of things seen in the countryside.*

**W**hen the eye sees all the parts of bodies that are seen by the sun, it will see all those bodies without shadow. This is proven by the ninth [proposition] which says: the surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its object <note>In Leonardo's terminology, the "object" is the source of light or color acting upon a surface.</note>. Therefore, the sun being the object of all those parts of the surface of bodies that see it, those parts of the surface participate in the brightness of the sun that illuminates them. The eye will look at these bodies, and it is impossible for it to see any part of such bodies other than that which is seen by the sun. Therefore, it will see neither the primary shadow <note>original: "ombra primitiva." This refers to the 'attached' shadow on the side of an object facing away from the light source.</note> nor the derivative shadow <note>original: "ombra derivativa." This refers to the 'cast' shadow projected by an object onto another surface.</note> of any of the aforementioned bodies.

### *If the sun is in the east, and the eye to the north or south.*

**W**hen the sun is in the east and the eye is to the north or south, then the eye will see the primary shadows of the eastern bodies, and the lights of the western bodies, and the eye itself will be exactly in the middle between the lights and the shadows of the bodies.

### *Of the sun and the eye placed in the east.*

**W**hen the sun and the eye are in the east, then all the parts of the surfaces that see the sun will appear illuminated to the eye, according to the ninth [proposition] of this [treatise].

### *Of the sun in the east, and the eye in the west.*

**W**hen the eye in the west sees the sun in the east, then...

### *In which part of shaded bodies their colors will show the most excellent beauty.*

**T**he excellent beauty of any color that does not possess its own luster <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "color," the inherent pigment of an object, and "luster," the shiny reflection of the light source itself.</note> will always be found in the excellent clarity of the most illuminated part of those shaded bodies.

### *Why the edges of shaded bodies sometimes appear lighter or darker than they actually are.*

**T**he edges <term>termini: the boundaries or outlines where an object meets its background</term> of shaded bodies appear lighter or darker than they truly are in proportion to how much the background <term>campo: the field or space surrounding the subject</term> bordering them is darker or lighter than the color of the body that defines that edge. <note>This describes the optical phenomenon of "simultaneous contrast," where our eyes perceive a value as lighter if it is next to something dark, and vice versa.</note>

### *What difference there is between the illuminated part on the surface of shaded bodies and the lustrous part.*

**T**he part of the shaded body that is illuminated will appear less bright the closer it gets to its luster. And this is caused by the great variety <note>original: "gran varietà," referring here to the high contrast or difference in intensity</note> that exists between them at their boundaries; this contrast is the reason why the less-shiny part appears dark at those boundaries, and the shiny part of the luster appears extremely bright. But such surfaces, which receive these impressions, are by nature like blurred mirrors, which confusedly capture the image <term>simulacro: a likeness or reflected image</term> of the sun and the sky which forms their background, and similarly the light of a window, and the darkness of the wall in which that window is made.

**O**f the lusters on bodies of equal smoothness <term>tersità: the quality of being polished, clean, or reflective</term>, that one will have the greatest difference from its background which is generated on the blackest surface. And because all mirrors return to the eye what they receive from objects, therefore every mirror that has the sun as its object returns that same sun in the same color; and the sun will appear more powerful against a dark background than against a light background.

### *How luster is more powerful on a black background than on any other background.*

**A**mong lusters of equal power, that one will show itself with the most excellent clarity which is on the darkest background. This is the same principle as above, but it varies in that the former speaks of the difference the luster has from its own background, while this speaks of the difference between a luster on a black background and a luster generated on other backgrounds.

### *What the difference is between luster and light.*

**T**he difference between luster <term>lustro: a specular highlight or reflection of the light source</term> and light <term>lume: the general illumination or diffused light on a surface</term> is that the luster is always more powerful than the light, and the light is of greater quantity than the luster. Furthermore, the luster moves along with the eye, or with its cause <note>the light source</note>, or with one or the other; but the light is fixed to a determined place, as long as the cause that generates it does not move.

### *Of light and luster.*

**T**he lights that are generated on the polished <note>original: "terse"</note> surfaces of opaque bodies will remain immobile on immobile bodies even if the eyes of the viewers move; but the lusters will be upon the same bodies in as many places on their surface as there are positions to which the eye moves.

### *Which bodies are those that have light without luster.*

**O**paque bodies that have a dense and rough surface never generate luster in any part of their illuminated side.

### *Of luster.*

**L**uster partakes much more of the color of the light that illuminates the body which shines, than of the color of that body itself. And this occurs on dense surfaces.

The luster of many dark <note>original: "ombrosi," referring here to opaque or deep-toned materials</note> bodies is entirely of the color of the illuminated body, such as that of burnished gold, silver, other metals, and similar bodies.

The luster of leaves, glass, and jewels partakes little of the color of the body where it originates, and much of the color of the light that illuminates it.

The lusters created in the depths of dense transparent materials are of the highest degree of beauty for that color, as is seen inside the ruby, the balas ruby <term>balassio: a rose-red variety of spinel often mistaken for a true ruby in the Renaissance</term>, glass, and similar things.

This happens because between the eye and that luster, the entire natural color of the transparent body is interposed.

The reflected lights of dense and lustrous bodies are of much greater beauty than the natural color of those bodies, as is seen in the folds that open in spun gold, and in other similar bodies where one surface reflects into the other opposite to it, and the other reflects back into the first, and thus they do so successively to infinity.

### Of the peaks of mountains viewed from above looking down.

**T**he peaks of mountains viewed one after another from high to low do not brighten in the same proportion as the distances they have between them, but much less so, according to the seventh [rule] of the fourth [book] which says: the distances of landscapes viewed from high to low toward the horizon go on darkening, and those which are viewed from low to high at the same distance as the first always go on brightening. This arises from the third [rule] of the ninth [book], which says the thickness of the air viewed from below looking up is much clearer and more radiant than that viewed from above looking down. And this derives from the fact that the air viewed from high to low is somewhat penetrated by the dark images <note>original: "specie oscure" — in Leonardo's optics, 'species' are the formal qualities or images of an object that travel through the air to the eye.</note> of the earth which lies beneath it. And therefore it appears to the eye darker than that which is viewed from below looking up, which is penetrated by the rays of the sun, which come to the eye with great brightness. ## Of the deception of the painter in the size of trees,
## and of other bodies in the countryside.

**J**udge well, O painter, or illuminator <note>original: "miniatore" — a specialist in small-scale manuscript painting.</note>, how far your painting must be seen from the eye, and imagine that at such a distance a small opening is seen, or if you prefer, a hole or window, through which the things placed before it can reach your eye; and truly you will judge the things seen to be so minute, that not only the limbs, but the whole will seem almost impossible for you to represent. As if the eye were *o* and the hole of a quarter of a <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> equal to your painted panel were *a b*, distant from the eye half a braccio, then you will see through that space all the things that can be seen within the length of a horizon of a hundred miles in such confused diminution, that not only could you not represent any part of them that has a shape, but you will hardly be able to place a point of the brush so small that it is not larger than any great building situated ten miles away.
(*Fig. 98. Plate XVII.*)

### *Why mountains at a great distance appear darker at the summit than at the base.*

**T**he air, which acquires degrees of thickness <note>original: "grossezza" — referring to atmospheric density or opacity.</note> at every degree of its lowliness and its distance, is the reason why the peaks of mountains, which rise higher, show more of their natural darkness; this is because they are less hindered by the thickness of the air at the summit than at their base, or in proximity rather than in remoteness. This is proven: *o p d s c r a k* are degrees of the air that always become thinner the higher they rise; *a f f h h k* are the other transverse degrees where the air acquires thinness the closer it approaches <note>Leonardo is likely referring to the vertical thinning of the atmosphere as one moves away from the earth's surface.</note>. It follows that the summit of mountain *e* is darker at the top than at the base, because, as has been said, the air is thicker below than above. Furthermore, mountain *e* is darker than mountain *g*, because there is a lesser thickness of air between *d* and *g*; and the summit *g*, being higher than its base, behaves similarly to mountain *e*, becoming darker the higher it rises. And at an equal distance, as *y g* indicates, it would appear darker than the summit *c* because it reaches into air that hinders less by being thinner. From this it does not follow that the proportion of the darkness of mountains is the same as that of their proximity—which would follow if the peaks of the mountains were of equal height—but *g*, by rising higher, does not observe this, because it penetrates into thinner air. ### *How one should not depict mountains as blue in winter as in summer.*

**L**andscapes created in the depiction of winter should not show their mountains as blue as one sees in the mountains of summer. This is proven by the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise], which says: among mountains seen at a great distance, the one that is naturally darker in itself will appear to be of a deeper blue color. Therefore, since plants are stripped of their leaves, they appear to be a grayish-brown color <note>original: "berettino" — a dull, ash-gray or brownish-gray color typical of dormant vegetation.</note>, whereas when they have leaves, they are green; and just as green is darker than grayish-brown, the green will appear more blue than the grayish-brown. Furthermore, by the fifth [proposition] of this [treatise], the shadows of plants clothed in leaves are as much darker than the shadows of those plants stripped of leaves, as the leaf-clothed plants are less sparse <note>original: "rare" — meaning the density of the foliage creates deeper, more solid shadows.</note> than those without leaves. And thus we have proven our intent.

The definition of the blue color of the air gives the judgment as to why landscapes are bluer in summer than in winter.

### *How mountains shaded by clouds partake of a blue color.*

**M**ountains shaded by clouds partake of a blue color when the weather is clear around said cloud. And this is caused because the air illuminated by the sun possesses great brightness; thus, the image of the darkness of the mountain shaded by the cloud, passing to the eye through the aforementioned brightness of the air, becomes blue in color, as was proven in the fifth [proposition] of the second [book]. <note>Leonardo refers to his theory that "blue" is not an inherent color of the sky, but the result of darkness (the void of space or a shaded mountain) being seen through a layer of illuminated "white" atmosphere.</note>

...resolved by the solar rays <note>original: "razzi solari"; referring to the melting of snow and ice by the sun's heat</note> of the summer; (which resolution is the generation of waters gathered from many small streams concurring from various aspects into the larger rivers), they grow in magnitude as they acquire motion, until they assemble at the great Ocean sea, always taking from one of the banks and giving to the other, until they seek the width of their valleys; and not content with that, they consume the roots of the lateral mountains, which, collapsing upon these rivers, close the valleys, and as if they wished to avenge themselves, they prohibit the course of such a river and convert it into a lake, where the water with very slow motion appears humbled, until such time as the generated blockage of the ruined mountain is again consumed by the course of the aforementioned water.

Therefore we shall say, that that water which finds itself in a narrower and shorter path consumes less of the place where it passes, and conversely consumes more where it is very wide and deep. It follows from this that the highest ridges of the mountains <note>original: "gioghi dei monti"</note>, being most of the time clothed in snow, and the rains striking them for only a short time, and the rivers not being there—until such time as the few droplets of rain remaining after the absorption of the arid summit begin to generate the most minute branches of very slow motion, which have no power to become turbid with any particle of earth moved by them, by means of the old roots of the minute grasses. For which reason such mountain ridges have more eternity in their surfaces than in their roots, where the furious courses of the gathered waters, continually unsatisfied with the carried earth, remove the hills covered with plants together with the largest stones, rolling them for a long space until they have reduced them to minute gravel <note>original: "minuta giara"</note>, and at last into fine silt <note>original: "sottil litta"</note>. (47)

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s observations on the geological transformation of the Earth, specifically how rivers widen valleys and how the scarcity of nutrients on mountain peaks affects the appearance of vegetation—a crucial guide for the realistic painter.</meta>

<header>Painting and how the mountains grow.</header>

**B**y what has been concluded previously, it is necessary to concede that the bases of mountains and hills are continually narrowing. This being so, it cannot be denied that the valleys are widening; and because the width of the river cannot then occupy the full width of its increased valley, it instead continually changes its position, leaving its course from that place where it has discharged the most material. This material, eroding and removing the gravelly banks until it has carried everything away, allows the previously deposited material to regain its ancient bed, from which it does not depart until another similar accident removes it from the aforementioned site. And so, from rain to rain, occurring from time to time, each valley goes on discharging itself of material and weight.

## *On the shadow and light of shaded bodies.*

**A**ll parts of bodies that the eye perceives between light and shadow must be strongly defined by that light and shadow; however, the parts turned toward the light will be blended in such a way that there will be little difference within the illuminated area itself. The shaded parts, unless a reflection occurs there, will—just like the illuminated ones—possess little variety between the more or less dark areas.

---

## *Of bodies illuminated by the air without the sun.*

**F**or figures and other bodies seen by the light of the air without the sun <note>This refers to "diffuse light," such as on an overcast day or in open shade, which Leonardo considered ideal for capturing subtle beauty.</note>, you shall create their shadows according to the fifth [rule] of the fourth [book], which teaches us that the part of any opaque body will be most illuminated when it is seen by the largest portion of the body that illuminates it. Therefore, consider this: draw imaginary lines from the illuminating body <note>In this case, the sky or the atmosphere.</note> to the illuminated body; observe which part sees more of the light and is thus more illuminated. In these conditions, reflections have little appearance; this is a method common to all objects under the illuminated air when a cloud covers the sun's light, or indeed when the sun has just set, when the sky gives us a "dead light" <note>original: "lume morto" — a soft, flat, or muted light without harsh highlights.</note>. In such light, every body shows the boundaries between shadows and their lights upon the shaded bodies in an imperceptible manner.

### *Which shadow is darker.*

**T**hat part of the shadow will be darkest which is closest to its origin.

### *Of light.*

**T**hat light will be of greater quantity which is generated upon a body of lesser curvature, provided such light is produced by the same cause.

Those bodies that are illuminated by the air along with the sun create shadows with an excessive sharpness of their boundaries.

### *Precept.*

**B**odies illuminated by different qualities of colored lights do not have the illuminated parts of their surfaces matching the colors of their shaded parts.

It is very rare that the colors of the surfaces of opaque bodies possess the proper colors in their shadows that correspond to the colors of their illuminated parts.

This proposition arises because the objects that cast shadows upon such bodies are not of the natural color of those bodies, nor of the same natural color as the source of illumination <note>original: "alluminatore" — the light source or the body providing the light</note>.

### *On the boundaries of bodies against their backgrounds.*

**T**he boundaries of bodies seen against their backgrounds always appear varied with more darkness or brightness than the rest of the object. This occurs because of the second [rule] of this [treatise] which proves: that the boundaries of white objects appear brighter the more they border on darker boundaries. And the boundaries of shaded objects appear darker the more they border on a whiter object. The primary example is shown in a white surface seen partly in the sun; the illuminated part appears whiter in comparison to the shadow, and the shadow appears darker in comparison to the light. This is clearly seen on the surfaces of walls and other flat bodies.

### *On the imitation of colors at any distance.*

**W**hen you wish to counterfeit a color, take care that while you are standing in a shaded spot, you do not try to imitate a luminous spot, because you would deceive yourself with such an imitation. What you must do in such a case, if you wish to work with the certainty required for <term>mathematical demonstrations</term> <note>Leonardo frequently used this phrase to emphasize that painting should be treated as a rigorous science based on optical laws</note>, is to ensure that all the colors you have to imitate are compared—the imitating color with the imitated—under the same light, and that your color is adjacent to the visual line of the natural color.

Let us say you wish to imitate a mountain in the part that is seen in the sun. Place your colors in the sun, and in that same light make your <term>mixture</term> <note>original: "mistione" — the physical blending of pigments</note> of colors to be imitated, and compare them under the same solar light, holding your color directly against the color being imitated. For example: I have the sun at midday, and I am depicting the mountain to the west, which is half in shadow and half in light. But here I want to imitate the luminous part, and I will take a small piece of paper coated in that color which seems to me similar to the thing imitated, and I will place it against the object itself, in such a way that between the true and the false no space is seen; and thus I will let the <term>rays of the sun</term> <note>original: "razzi del sole"</note> fall upon it, and I will add varieties of colors until the color of...

### On reflected light.

**T**o the same degree that the illuminated object is less luminous than its illuminant <note>The source of light, such as the sun or a lamp</note>, its reflected part will be less luminous than the illuminated part.
That object will be more illuminated which is closer to the illuminant.
To the same degree that *b c* enters into *b a*, it will be more illuminated in *a d* than in *d c*.
That wall which is more illuminated will appear to have its shadows of greater darkness. (*Fig. 107. Plate XVIII.*)

### On Perspective.

**W**hen two equal objects are seen with two eyes, and each object is smaller than the interval between the pupils of those eyes, then the second object will appear larger than the first. The pyramid *a c* encompasses the first object, and the pyramid *b d* encompasses the second object. Now, the object *m* will appear larger than *n* to the same extent that the width of the pyramid *b d* is greater than *a c*. (*Fig. 108. Plate XVIII.*)

# BOOK SIX.

## ON TREES AND GREENERY.

---

### Discourse on the quality of flowers in the branching of herbs. <note>Note 49: Leonardo uses "herbs" (erbe) to refer generally to non-woody plants and vegetation.</note>

**O**f the flowers that grow upon the branches of plants, some bloom first at the very highest points of those branches, and others open their first flower at the lowest base of their stem.

### *On the branching of plants.*

**F**irst, every branch of any plant that is not weighed down by its own weight curves upward, lifting its tip toward the sky. Second, the small shoots <term>ramiculi: the smaller, secondary branches or twigs</term> of tree branches that grow from underneath are larger than those that grow from above. Third, all the small shoots born toward the center of the tree perish in a short time because of the excessive shade. Fourth, those branchings of plants will be more vigorous and favored which are closer to the uppermost parts of those plants, because of the air and the sun. Fifth, the angles of the divisions of the branchings of trees are equal among themselves. Sixth, but those angles become more obtuse <note>Wider or more blunt</note> as the branches on their sides grow older. Seventh, the side of that angle becomes more oblique <note>Slanted</note> when it is made of a thinner branch. Eighth, every bifurcation of branches joined together restores the thickness of the branch with which it connects. <note>Leonardo’s Rule: the sum of the cross-sections of the branches is equal to the cross-section of the trunk or parent branch.</note>

<summary>Leonardo transitions to botany, detailing the growth patterns of flowers and the mathematical principles governing how tree branches divide and thicken.</summary>

### *On the proportion that the branchings of plants have among themselves.*

**S**uch proportion as the thicknesses of the branching of each plant born in the same year have with their first stem, so do the preceding and succeeding branches of all other past and future years; that is, that every year the branches that each plant has acquired when they have finished growing—their thicknesses being calculated and joined together—are equal to the branch born the previous year which produced them, and so they continue forward, and so they shall be found in their future times. For example, the branches *a d* and *b d*, the last of the plant, being joined together will be equal to the branch *d c* which produced them <note>This is "Leonardo's Rule" for tree branching, suggesting that the cross-sectional area of branches is conserved at every stage of the tree's height</note>. (*Fig. 6. and 7. Plate XIX.*)

### *On the branching of Trees.*

**T**he branching of trees, when burdened with fruit and leaves, changes position from that which they held during the winter. But from branch to branch, the thickness of the branches that bifurcate <note>split into two</note> does not vary, except almost imperceptibly; and if one were to replace the small shoots <term>ramiculi<gloss>the smallest or secondary branchlets</gloss></term> that are born between those main branchings, it would restore the thickness to be exactly equal throughout.

### *On the branching of plants.*

**P**lants that spread out extensively have the angles of the partitions that separate their branchings more obtuse the lower their origin <note>original: "nascimento"</note> is—that is, the closer they are to the thickest and oldest part of the tree. ### *On the origin of leaves upon their branches.*

**T**he thickness of any branch never diminishes in the space between one leaf and the next, except by the thickness of the eye <note>the bud or "occhio"</note> that is above that leaf. This thickness is missing from the branch that follows until the next leaf. Nature has arranged the leaves of the latest branches of many plants so that the sixth leaf is always above the first, and so it follows successively, if the rule is not impeded. And this was done for two benefits to these plants. The first is because, as the branch and the fruit grow in the following year from the twin vein <note>original: "gemella vena," referring to the vascular connection</note> of the bud which is in contact with the attachment <note>original: "appiccatura"</note> of the leaf, the water that wets such a branch can descend to nourish that twin by the droplet stopping in the concavity of the origin of that leaf. And the second benefit is that when such branches grow the following year, one does not cover the other, because the five branches are born facing five different aspects. The sixth is born above the first, quite far removed. (*Fig. 11. Plate XIX.*)

## On the branching of plants with their leaves.

**T**he branchings of plants, some like the elm are wide and thin like an open hand seen in foreshortening <note>term: "iscorto" — a perspective technique where an object appears shorter than it is to create the illusion of depth</note>, and these show themselves in their quantities; from below they show from the upper side; and those that are higher show from below, and those in the middle show partly from below and partly from above. And the upper part is at the extreme end of that branching. This middle part is more foreshortened than any other of those that are turned with their tips toward you; and of these middle parts of the height of the plant, the longest will be toward the ends of those trees. Such branchings act like the leaves of the wild fern <note>original: "felice salvatica"</note> that grows along the banks of rivers. Other branchings are round, like those of trees that put out small shoots <note>original: "ramiculi"</note> and leaves where the sixth is above the first; and others are sparse and transparent like the willow and similar trees. The ends of the branchings of plants, if they are not overcome by the weight of fruit, turn toward the sky as much as possible. The upper surfaces <note>original: "parti dirette"</note> of their leaves stay turned toward the sky to receive the nourishment of the dew that falls at night. The sun gives spirit and life to plants, and the earth nourishes them with moisture. Regarding this case, I tried leaving only a tiny root on a gourd <note>original: "zucca"</note>, and I kept that nourished with water; and such a gourd brought to perfection all the fruits it could generate, which were about 60 gourds of the wide variety. And I applied my mind with diligence to such a life, and I recognized that the dew of the night was that which, with its moisture, penetrated abundantly through the attachments <note>original: "appiccature"</note> of its large leaves to the nourishment of that plant with its offspring.

### *On the birth of branches in plants.*

### *Why many times the wood is not straight in its grain.*

**W**hen the branches that follow in the second year upon those of the past year do not have similar thicknesses centered over the preceding branches, but are to the side, then the vigor of that lower branch twists itself to nourish the one that is higher, even though it is a little to the side. But if such branchings have equality in their growth, the veins <note>term: "vene" — referring here to the grain or fibers of the wood</note> of their trunk <note>term: "fusto" — the main stem or stalk of the plant</note> will be straight and equidistant at every degree of height of their plant. Therefore you, painter, who do not have such rules, to avoid the blame of those who understand these things, should be eager to portray—

### *Of Trees.*

**A**lways toward the bottoms of valleys and the branches of said valleys, the trees are larger and thicker than toward the summits of the hills. The peaks of the mountains will be more grassy than their slopes, because there is no rush of water there to wash them away, as occurs on the slopes.

### *Of Trees.*

**I**f the branch of the tree appears to you in <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "iscorto" — a technique in art to represent an object receding into the distance to create the illusion of depth</note>, its leaves will show themselves to you from the front or nearly so. And if the branch shows itself in its true shape, its leaves will show themselves improperly, that is, in <term>foreshortening</term>. When the tree, due to great distance, no longer sends the true or deceptive shape of its leaves to the eye, then there remains the shape of the placement of the branches with a certain quantity and quality. When the shape of the placement of the branches fails due to distance, there remains to the eye only the sum of its <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro scuro" — the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting</note>. ### *Which branches of the trees are those that grow most in a year.*

**T**he largest ramifications of the primary branches are always those that sprout from the side of the branch that faces the earth, and the smaller ones sprout above that same primary branch. And such greatness of the lower branch arises because the moisture of the branch—when it is not struck by the heat of the sun—always falls back into the underside of its branch; therefore, the moisture provides more nourishment where there is a greater abundance of it. And for this reason, the branch always has thicker bark on the bottom than on the top. This is the most powerful cause for why the small shoots of that branch are much larger below than above; and because of this, trees put out many branches downwards, which are the reason that the branch succeeding it from below does not put out large shoots against the branch that sits above it. And for this reason, the plants do not become confused, nor do they take the air from one another despite the proximity of so many ramifications, because they give way to one another; and if that branch, as has been said, grows significantly downwards, the one growing toward it grows very little upwards.

### *Why trees beyond a certain distance become brighter the further away they are.*

Because the trees possess a dark color in themselves, the whiteness of this interposed air makes their shadowed parts appear more blue than their illuminated parts.

### *On the light upon the branching of trees.*

**B**ased on what was said above, regarding the masses of illuminated tree branches: even though each individual leaf is separated from the others by a shadowed space, it happens that at a distance the shadowed part, being minute, is lost. This occurs because, as stated, it is overtaken and overwhelmed by the luminous part, which does not diminish across distance as much as the shadowed part does. From this it follows that the mass of leaves on a single branch appears, at a certain distance, to be almost of a single color. And even if a keen eye can somewhat discern the shadows of those aforementioned gaps interspersed between the leaves, they do not appear with their proper darkness. This arises from two causes: the first is the thickness of the air <note>A reference to atmospheric perspective, where the density of the atmosphere softens colors and contrasts.</note> that is interposed between the eye and the shadowed object; the second is because the minute details <note>original: "specie." In Leonardo's optics, "species" are the visual images or "similitudes" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> at such a long distance blend together at their edges and confuse our perception of them. Since the illuminated part remains more noticeable than the shadowed part, the shadows appear to have little darkness.

### *On shadows and lights and their magnitude in leaves.*

**T**he branchings of plants are seen either from below, or from the middle. ### *On the illumination of plants.*

**F**rom the position of the eye which sees that part of the plants illuminated which faces the light source, one plant will never be seen illuminated in the same way as another. I say that such an eye *c* will not see the lights in the same proportion to their shadows in one tree as in the other. Because that tree which is closer to the Sun will appear so much more shadowed than the one which is more remote, as the one tree is closer to the convergence of the solar rays coming to the eye than the other. You see that of tree *d*, nothing is seen by eye *c* but the shadow, and from the same eye *c*, tree *b* is seen half illuminated and half in shadow. (*Fig. 18. Plate XX.*)

### Reminder of plants for the painter.

**R**emember, O painter, that the darkness of shadows in the same species of plants varies as much as the rarity or density of their branches varies.

### *On the universal light illuminating plants.*

**T**hat part of the plant will show itself clothed in shadows of lesser darkness which is more remote from the earth. This is proven: let *a b* be the plant, let *a b c* be the illuminated hemisphere <note>The "illuminated hemisphere" refers to the entire dome of the sky providing diffused light.</note>; the lower part of the tree sees the earth *p c*, that is the part *o*; and it sees a little of the hemisphere in *c d*, but the highest part in the concavity *a* is seen by a greater portion of the hemisphere, that is *b c*; and because of this, since it does not see the darkness of the earth, it remains more illuminated. But if the tree is thick with leaves, like the laurel, fir, and boxwood, then it is varied; because even though *a* does not see the earth *c*, it sees the darkness of the leaves divided by many shadows, which darkness reflects <note>original: "riverbera"</note> upwards onto the undersides of the leaves placed above them; and such trees have shadows that are darker the closer they are to the center of the tree. (*Fig. 19. Plate XX.*)

### Of trees and their light.

**T**he true method for a practitioner in depicting the countryside—I mean landscapes <note>original: "paesi"</note> with their plants—is to choose that the sun be hidden in the sky, so that the countryside receives universal light, and not the particular light of the sun, which makes the shadows sharp <note>original: "tagliate," literally "cut" or high-contrast.</note> and very different from the lights.

<summary>Leonardo advises painters on how diffused sky light affects tree shading, noting that upper branches are brighter because they face the sky rather than the dark earth. He recommends painting landscapes under overcast skies to avoid the harsh, distracting shadows caused by direct sunlight.</summary>

### *On the illuminated part of greenery and mountains.*

**T**he illuminated part will show its natural color more clearly at a long distance when it is struck by a more powerful light.

---

### *On the highlights of dark leaves.*

**T**he highlights <note>original: "lumi," referring to the brightest points of light on a surface.</note> of those leaves will partake more of the color of the air <note>In this context, "air" refers to the blue sky.</note> that is reflected in them, specifically those which are of a darker color. This is caused because the brightness of the illuminated part, when combined with the darkness inherent in the leaf, composes a blue color. This brightness arises from the blue of the air, which is mirrored in the polished surface of such leaves, and it increases the blue that said brightness usually generates when combined with dark objects.

---

### *On the highlights of greenish leaves tending toward yellow.*

**B**ut the leaves of greenery tending toward yellow, when reflecting the air, do not produce a luster <note>original: "lustro," the specular reflection or "glint" on a smooth surface.</note> participating in blue; for everything that appears in a mirror partakes of the color of that mirror. Therefore, the blue of the air mirrored in the yellow of the leaf appears green, because blue and yellow mixed together compose a most beautiful green. Consequently, the lusters of light-colored leaves tending toward a yellow color will be greenish-yellow.

---

### *Of trees that are illuminated by the sun and by the air.*

**R**egarding trees illuminated by the sun and by the air, if they have leaves of a dark color, they will be illuminated on one side

### *On the highlights of the leaves of plants.*

The leaves of plants commonly have a polished surface, for which reason they partially mirror the color of the air. Because this air partakes of white—being mixed with thin and transparent clouds—the surface of those leaves, when they are dark by nature like those of elm trees (provided they are not dusty), renders their highlights <note>original: "lustri"</note> in a color partaking of blue. This occurs because of the seventh [rule] of the fourth [book] which shows that light mixed with darkness composes blue; and such leaves have highlights on their branches that are more blue as the air mirrored in them is more purified and blue. 

But if such leaves are young, as on the tips of branches in the month of May, then they will be green with a participation of yellow; and if their highlights are generated by the blue air mirrored in them, then those highlights will be green, according to the third [rule] of the same fourth [book] which says: the color yellow mixed with blue always generates a green color.

The highlights of all leaves with a dense surface will partake of the color of the air, and the darker the leaves are, the more they will take on the nature of a mirror, and consequently, such highlights will partake more of blue.

### *On the green of leaves.*

**The** most beautiful greens that the leaves of trees can possess occur when their thickness is interposed between the eye and the air <note>In this context, "air" refers to the bright sky or background light.</note>.

### *On the darkness of the tree.*

**That** part of the tree which is silhouetted against the open air is much darker than the part which is seen against a forest, or mountains, or hills.

### *On trees.*

**When** plants are viewed toward the sun, they appear to be a more beautiful green toward their edges than they were before, due to the transparency of their leaves. Toward the center, they will appear very dark; those leaves that are not transparent will be the ones showing you their "right" side <note>The upper surface of the leaf.</note>, and they will catch very prominent highlights <note>original: "lustri," referring to specular reflections or glints of light.</note>.

But if you look at the plants from the side opposite the Sun, you will see them with few shadows and many highlights on the leaves, provided they are dense.

### *On trees positioned below the eye.*

**Trees** positioned below the eye—even if they are of equal height, equal color, and equal density of branching—will nonetheless acquire a greater degree of darkness at every step of distance. This arises because, for the tree closest to you, since you are above it, you see that part of it which is exposed to the sky, the illuminator of all things,

# On the Sun that illuminates the forest.

**W**hen the sun illuminates the forest, the trees of the woods will show themselves with distinct shadows and lights, and for this reason they will appear to have moved closer to you, because they take on a more recognizable form <note>original: "cognita figura," meaning a shape that is easily identified by the eye due to high contrast.</note>; and whatever part of them is not seen by the sun appears equally dark, except for their thin parts, which are interposed between the eye and the sun, and which become bright through their transparency; and this results in a smaller quantity of highlights <note>original: "lumi"</note> in trees illuminated by the sun than by the open sky, because the sky is larger than the sun, and a larger cause produces larger effects in this case.

As the shadows of the plants become smaller, the trees will appear to be no longer sparse, especially where they have a uniform color, and where by their nature they have sparse branches and thin leaves, such as the peach <note>original: "persico"</note>, the plum <note>original: "susino"</note>, and the like; because as their shadow retreats toward the center of the plant, the plant itself appears to have diminished, and the branches that remain entirely outside of the shadow appear to be of the same color and background <note>original: "campo," the visual field or space behind the object.</note>.

## *On the luminous parts of the greenery of plants.*

**T**he luminous parts of the greenery <note>original: "verdure," referring to the green foliage.</note> of plants in the vicinity of the eye appear brighter to that eye than those of remote plants, and their shadowed parts appear darker than those of the same remote plants. Remote plants show their luminous parts darker than those of nearby plants, and their shadowed parts appear brighter than the shadowed parts of those nearby plants; and this arises because the convergence of the visual images <note>original: "specie," a technical term in Renaissance optics referring to the 'likenesses' or rays of light traveling from an object to the eye.</note> of these shadowed and luminous parts blend and mix—

### *On plants that are between the eye and the light.*

**O**f the plants that are between the eye and the light, the front part will be bright, and this brightness will be mixed with the branching of transparent leaves seen from the back, along with lustrous leaves seen from the front; and their background below and behind will be of dark greenery, being the shadow on the front part of the said plant; and this occurs in plants that are higher than the eye.

**A** mixture will be formed from the accidental parts of the leaves of plants at a long distance, which will partake most of that accident which possesses the largest shape.

### On the shadows of plants.

**T**he shadows of plants placed in landscapes do not show themselves arranged in the same way in the plants on the right as in those on the left, especially when the sun is to the right or to the left. This is proved by the fourth [rule] which says: opaque bodies <note>An "opaque body" is any solid object that does not allow light to pass through it.</note> placed between the light and the eye appear entirely in shadow; and by the fifth: the eye placed between the opaque body and the light sees the opaque body entirely illuminated; and by the sixth: when the eye and the opaque body are placed between the darkness and the light, the body will be seen half in shadow and half in light.

### *On never feigning leaves transparent to the Sun.*

**N**ever feign <note>In this context, "feign" means to represent or paint artistically.</note> leaves as transparent when facing the sun, because they are confused; and this happens because upon the transparency of one leaf there will be imprinted the shadow of another leaf that stands above it. This shadow has sharp edges and a definite darkness, and sometimes it covers a half or a third of that leaf which is in shadow; thus, such ramification is confused, and its imitation is to be avoided. The upper small shoots of the lateral branches of plants draw closer to their master branch than do those below. That leaf is less transparent which receives the light at the most unequal angles. The lower branches of plants that produce large leaves and heavy fruits—such as walnuts, figs, and the like—always direct themselves toward the earth.

-># On Oriental Trees.<-

**W**hen the sun is in the east, trees viewed toward that eastern direction will have light surrounding them, encircling their shadows, except toward the ground—unless the tree had been pruned <note>original: "rimondo"; refers to thinning out branches which allows light to pass through to the base</note> the previous year. And the southern and northern trees will be half-shadowed and half-lit, being more or less shadowed or lit according to whether they are more or less toward the east or the west.

The eye, whether positioned high or low, varies the shadows and the lights in the trees, because the high eye sees the trees with few shadows, and the low eye with many shadows.

The greens of plants are as varied as their species.

When the sun is in the east, its trees <note>trees positioned between the viewer and the sun</note> are dark toward the center, and their edges are luminous.

### *Of the shadows of oriental plants.*

**T**he shadows of oriental plants occupy a large part of the plant, and they are darker the more the trees are thick with leaves.

### *Of southern plants.*

**W**hen the sun is in the east, the southern and northern plants have almost as much light as shadow; however, they have a greater amount of light the more they are toward the west, and a greater amount of shadow the more they are toward the east.

## *On Meadows,*

**W**hen the sun is in the east, the greenery of the meadows and other small plants are of a most beautiful green because they are transparent to the sun <note>This refers to "translucency," where light passes through the thin blades of grass</note>; this does not happen in western meadows. The southern and northern grasses are of a mediocre beauty in their greenery.

## *On the Grasses of the Meadows.*

**A**mong the grasses that catch the shadows of the plants growing amidst them: those that are on this side of the shadow <note>between the viewer and the shadow</note> have their stalks <term>festuchi</term> <note>original: "festuchi"; refers to the stems or stalks of grass or hay</note> illuminated against a shadowy field. Conversely, the grasses that are themselves shaded have dark stalks against a light field—that is, against the ground that lies beyond the shadow.

## *On the Shadow of Greenery.*

**T**he shadows of greenery always participate in blue, and likewise every shadow of every other thing; and they take on more of this blue the further they are from the eye, and less as they are nearer. <note>Leonardo is describing "atmospheric perspective," where the air between the viewer and the object adds a blue tint to distant shadows</note>

## *On Landscapes in Painting.*

**T**he trees and the mountains in painted landscapes must show their shadows on the side from which the light comes, and they must show the illuminated part on the side from which the shadows come <note>This likely refers to the contrast of a dark object against a light sky, or a light object against a dark background, to create depth</note>; and let them show the light and the shadows as the eye sees them, where it sees the light and the shadows. This is proven by the figure in the margin. <margin>See Fig. 26, Plate XX.</margin>

### On the leaves of the walnut tree.

**T**he leaves of the walnut, distributed throughout the shoot <term>ramiculo: a small young branch or shoot</term> of that year, are further apart from one another and greater in number the younger the branch is from which that shoot grows. They are closer together at their base and fewer in number when the shoot grows from an older branch. Its fruits grow at the very tip of its shoot, and its larger branches are located below the branch from which they spring. This happens because the weight of its fluid <term>umore: the sap or internal moisture of the plant</term> is more inclined to descend than to rise; for this reason, the branches that grow above them, reaching toward the sky, are small and thin. When the shoot faces toward the sky, its leaves spread out from its end with equal divisions at their tips. But if the shoot faces the horizon, the leaves remain flattened; this occurs because leaves universally keep their underside <term>rivescio: the back or ventral side of the leaf</term> turned toward the earth.

And within the western semicircle, the greens have a dull color in the humid and turbid air, colored like dark ash, because they are not transparent like the eastern side, which is all the more brilliant the more humid it is.

### *On the transparency of plants within themselves.*

**T**he transparency <term>trasforazione: literally "boring through," referring here to the way light or sight passes through the gaps in foliage</term> of the air within the bodies of plants, and the transparency of plants against the air at a long distance, are not demonstrated to the eye; for where the whole is perceived with effort, the parts are recognized with difficulty. Instead, a confused mixture is created, which partakes more of that which is the greater sum, combined with the gaps of the tree consisting of particles of illuminated air. These [gaps] are much smaller than the plant, and therefore they are lost to our notice sooner than the plant itself; but it does not follow from this that they are not there. Thus, by necessity, a mixture is made of the air and the darkness of the shaded tree, which together reach the eye that sees it.

### *Of trees that occupy the gaps of one another.*

**T**hat part of the tree will be less transparent where a greater sum of another tree is opposed behind it, between the tree and the air. For example, in tree *a* the transparency is not blocked, nor in *b*, because there are no trees behind them; but in *c*, only half is transparent—that is, *c* is occupied by tree *d*, and [further back] occupied by tree *e*. A little further on, all the physical transparency of the trees is lost. (Fig. 30. Plate XXI.)

### *Precept.*

Regarding the branching of plants, some are sharp and some are rounded.
The thickest tips of the tree branches produce larger leaves, or a greater quantity of them, than any other extremity of the branch.
The tips of the branches are always those that are first to fill with leaves.
The thickest tips of the branches are always the masters <note>The primary or dominant growth points</note> of the larger branches of the trees; and conversely, the thinnest tips of these branches are more remote from the masters of such branches.

### *Precept on plants.*

Regarding branches or their parent plants, some are entirely guided by nature, and some are hindered by natural deficiencies; these dry up by themselves, either wholly or in part. Some lack their natural quantity due to pruning done by men, and some due to the breaking caused by lightning bolts <note>original: "saette"</note>, or by winds, or other storms.
Trees that grow near the seashores, which are exposed to the winds, are all bent by the wind; they grow bent in this way, and so they remain.

# BOOK SEVEN.

## ON CLOUDS.

---

### *On the nature of clouds.*

Clouds are mists drawn upward by the heat of the sun, and their elevation reaches the point where their acquired weight becomes equal in power to the force that moves them. This acquired weight arises from their condensation, and this condensation originates from the heat infused within them, which flees from the outer edges that have been penetrated by the cold of the middle region of the air. The moisture follows the heat that led it up there, moving toward wherever that heat escapes; and because the heat flees toward the center of each globule of the clouds, these globules condense with defined surfaces like dense mountains, and they take on shadows by means of the solar rays <note>original: "razzi solari"</note> that strike them there.

Clouds are seen at times to receive the solar rays and illuminate themselves in the manner of dense mountains, and at other times the same clouds remain very dark, without any part of that darkness varying. This arises from the shadows cast upon them by other clouds that block the solar rays, interposing themselves between the sun and those darkened clouds.

### *On the redness of clouds.*

That redness with which the clouds are tinted arises with more or less intensity when the sun is at the horizons in the evening or morning; and because that body which

<term>middle region of the air</term> <note>original: "mezza regione dell’ aria"; in Renaissance meteorology, the atmosphere was divided into three regions, with the middle one being the coldest where vapors condense into clouds.</note>, <term>globule</term> <note>original: "globbosità"; refers to the rounded, billowing shapes of cumulus clouds.</term>

<summary>This page explores the physical formation of clouds through the interaction of solar heat and atmospheric cold, explaining their mountain-like appearance and the causes of their shadows and coloration.</summary>
<keywords>meteorology, cloud formation, atmospheric optics, solar rays, condensation, light and shadow</keywords>

<page-num>441</page-num>

tion are generated, because the dispersed and evaporated moisture, in
concurring to the creation of clouds, leaves the place from
which it fled empty; and because a vacuum does not exist in nature,
it is necessary that the parts of the air surrounding the flight
of the moisture fill the initiated vacuum with themselves, and this
very motion is called wind. But when, by means of the heat of the
sun, such clouds are resolved into air, then a contrary
wind is generated, created by the destruction and evaporation of the com-
posite cloud; and both occurrences, as stated, are
causes of wind, and such winds are generated in every part
of the air that is altered by heat or cold, and their mo-
tion is straight, and not curved, as the adversary claims <note>The "adversary" likely refers to Aristotelian or scholastic philosophers who argued for circular or curved elemental motions.</note>;
because if it were curved, it would not be necessary to raise or lower the
sails of ships to seek wind from above or below; ra-
ther, that sail which was struck by a wind would be con-
tinually accompanied by that same wind as long as it lasted.
Experience shows us the contrary, in seeing the surface <note>original: "pelle dell'acqua" (skin of the water)</note> of the water struck in different parts of the same sea,
with brief and short expandable motions—manifest signs that from
different places, with different obliquities of motion, the
winds descend from high to low; and such motions scatter in different
directions from their origins; and because the sea has a
spherical surface, many times the waves run without wind, since
the elevated wind abandons them, whereby they move with the ini-
tiated impetus <term>impeto: the force or momentum possessed by a moving body</term>.

### On clouds, and their gravity and levity.

**T**HE cloud is lighter than the air that stays below it, and is
heavier than the air that stays above it.

### *Why fog turns into clouds.*

**F**og, when struck by various currents of wind, condenses and becomes a cloud with various globular shapes <note>original: "globbulenze"</note>.

### *On the entirely cloudy air.*

**T**he entirely cloudy air renders the countryside beneath it brighter or darker according to the lesser or greater thickness of the clouds that interpose themselves between the sun and said countryside. When the thickened air is interposed between the sun and the earth and is of uniform thickness, you will see little difference between the illuminated part and the shaded part of any object.

### *On the shadow of clouds.*

**L**et the shadows of the clouds be cast upon the earth with intervals struck by the solar rays, possessing greater or lesser splendor according to the greater or lesser transparency of those clouds. The clouds are of a much greater redness the closer they are to the horizon, and they are of much less redness the more remote they are from that horizon.

### *On clouds.*

**W**hen the clouds interpose themselves between the sun and the countryside, the greenery of the woods will show shadows of little darkness, and the differences between them and the highlights will be of little variety in darkness or clarity; because being illuminated by the great sum of light from their hemisphere <note>The "hemisphere" refers to the entire visible dome of the sky acting as a light source</note>, the sha—

### On Clouds.

The cloud that finds itself between the sun and the eye is such that one [part] or another, or those most remote, are brighter; and the parts of the cloud interposed between the sun and the eye—of the actual cloud—become brighter than any other similar part found in the transparency of the more remote clouds. Therefore, at every degree of distance, the middle of the clouds is the brightest, and their outer edges are of greater darkness. Or, if we wish to say of greater darkness, the extremes of their darkness are softened <note>original: "sfumate," a term often used by Leonardo da Vinci to describe the smoky blurring of edges</note> into their transparent clarity, and possess smoky or confused boundaries. A similar law applies to the extremes of their clarity toward where they terminate in the air. Clouds of small thickness are the most transparent, and more luminous in the middle than at the edges. And if it is of a red or reddish color, the red color is diffused. And the further the clouds are from the Moon, the higher their light is, which they held together with the darkness of the cloud, especially toward the light; and that which is beneath the sun has no shadow, as with the grass and the tree, although in it there appeared the darkness of the night, which shows itself in the air.

### On Clouds.

When the clouds interpose themselves between the sun and the earth, and the clouds cast their shadow upon the earth, the clouds are of much greater <unclear>darkness</unclear> the closer they are to the horizon.

# BOOK EIGHT.

## ON THE HORIZON.

---

->*What the true location of the horizon is.*<-

**H**orizons <term>horizon: the line where the earth's surface and the sky appear to meet</term> exist at various distances from the eye, because that is called the <term>horizon</term> where the clarity of the air ends at the boundary of the earth. It is seen in as many locations along the same perpendicular line above the <term>center of the world</term> <note>The "center of the world" refers to the center of the Earth in the Aristotelian/Ptolemaic sense</note> as there are heights of the eye that see it. For the eye placed at the surface of a calm sea sees that <term>horizon</term> at a distance of half a mile or thereabouts; and if a man rises with his eye to the height of his average stature, the <term>horizon</term> is seen seven miles remote from him. And so, at every degree of height, he discovers a more remote <term>horizon</term> from himself. Whence it happens that those who are on the summits of high mountains near the sea see the circle of the <term>horizon</term> very remote from them. But those who are inland do not have an <term>horizon</term> at an equal distance, because the surface of the earth is not equally distant from the <term>center of the world</term>; therefore it is not of perfect <term>sphericity</term>, like the surface of the water. And this is the cause of such variety of distances between the eye and the <term>horizon</term>.

The <term>horizon</term> of the <term>sphere</term> of water will never be higher than the soles of the feet of the one who sees it while standing in contact with those soles—at the contact that the boundary of the sea has with the boundary of the earth uncovered by the waters.

The <term>horizon</term> of the sky is sometimes very close, and especially to one who finds himself beside the summits of moun—

<summary>This page explains that the distance of the horizon depends on the observer's height and the Earth's lack of perfect sphericity on land compared to the sea. It establishes that the horizon's position shifts relative to the eye's elevation above the center of the world.</summary>

### On the horizon.

**T**he horizon will never be equal to the height of the eye that sees it. That figure which is closer to the horizon will have that horizon closer to its feet, provided you remain stationary while looking at it. That thing is higher which is more distant from the center of the world <note>In the Aristotelian/Ptolemaic worldview, the "center of the world" refers to the center of the Earth.</note>.
    Therefore, a straight <term>horizontal line</term><note>original: "equigiacente"; literally "equally-lying," referring to a line parallel to the horizon</note> is not of equal height throughout, and consequently is not truly horizontal; hence, if you speak of a line of equal height, it must be understood as being nothing other than curved. If *a b* are two men, the horizon *n* will reach the level of their height. (->*Figure 6, Plate XXII.*<-)

### On the horizon.

I say then—

### On the horizon mirrored in running water

**T**he water that flows between the eye and the horizon will not re-
flect such a horizon to that eye, because the eye does not
see that side of the wave which is seen by the horizon,
nor does the horizon see that side of the wave which is seen by the eye.
Therefore, by the sixth [proposition] of this [treatise], our
proposition is concluded, which sixth says: it is impossible for the
eye to see the <term>simulacrum</term><note>original: "simulacro"; an optical reflection or image of an object.</note> where it does not see the real thing and
the eye at one and the same time.

Let the wave be *c b*, and the horizon *d*; I say that the eye *a*,
not seeing the sides of the wave *b g*, will not see the si-
mulacrum of *d* which is mirrored on that side. (->*Fig. 9. Plate XXII.*<-)

<note>Translator's Guide to Terms:
- **Primitive Shadow (ombra primitiva):** The shadow on the object itself (attached shadow).
- **Derivative Shadow (ombra derivativa):** The shadow cast by the object through the air or onto another surface (cast shadow).
- **Simple/Composite (semplice/composta):** Refers to shadows created by a single light source versus multiple or diffused light sources.</note>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations by Giovan Gherardo de Rossi regarding the life and intellectual character of Leonardo da Vinci, following the index of the newly expanded "Treatise on Painting."</meta>

(1) *Page* 2. That Leonardo da Vinci was one of those original geniuses who, by themselves and without other aids, are capable of conceiving new things, examining objects in nature unobserved by others, and investigating the origins and causes of effects known to all, has already been repeated so many times by the learned that it would be vain to wish to demonstrate it here. It would have been much desired that Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Renaissance artists.</note>, who gave us the greatest information regarding Leonardo, had also told us which learned men he had as masters in the sciences he practiced; since, beyond his alliance with the mathematician Luca Pacioli <note>A friar and mathematician who collaborated with Leonardo on "De divina proportione."</note>, we know nothing else of his studies. It is a very curious thing that in the writings of this Author <note>Leonardo</note> one never finds any citation whatsoever, and that he makes use of no author, nor leans upon the authority of anyone. From this, it would be increasingly proven that his works were the children of his genius alone. The manner he maintained in writing does not approach at all that of the writers of his century, who made a great display of Greekisms and Latinisms, and by this altered and defiled the beautiful simplicity of the authors of previous centuries. He is not always a writer of polished elegance; but in some passages, which I shall go on indicating, one recognizes in him that elegance which arises from the liveliness of wit and from learning. This part of his writings, which had not yet seen the light of day, proves that he was not ignorant of that manner of writing and questioning ingeniously—perhaps even too much so—on topics that had become fashionable particularly in Florence through the work of the Greek refugees, who made the Aristotelian Philosophy and its method of disputation familiar and esteemed. In this book, despite some excessive subtlety that he sometimes employs, it cannot be denied that Leonardo appears as a valiant reasoner even in matters that do not concern so closely mathematics, physics, and the theoretical precepts of his beloved painting.

(2) *Page* 25. By King Matthias, he surely means Matthias Corvinus <note>King of Hungary (reigned 1458–1490), a great patron of the arts and sciences.</note>, King of Hungary, who in his response, though very subtle, shows that he was well instructed in philosophy. The unfortunate poet had poorly positioned himself if he expected the King to prefer the harmony of his verses to the image of the beloved person. Leonardo gathers as many arguments as he can in favor of his art, and with much ingenuity finds the primary source of the nobility of Painting in the imitation of the works of the Divine Creator. One must believe that in those times there was some writing circulating,

He also identifies King Matthias Corvinus in Leonardo's anecdotes and defends the nobility of painting as a divine imitation.</summary>

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Giorgio Vasari, Luca Pacioli, Matthias Corvinus, Aristotelian philosophy, Florence, art theory, Renaissance humanism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Leonardo da Vinci's intellectual priorities, specifically his defense of painting as a science and its relationship to music and poetry.</meta>

that he argued against Painting and toward its debasement; for the Author <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note> complains that it was excluded from the liberal arts <note>The traditional academic curriculum consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note>, an exclusion that certainly cannot be granted to it, and which we cannot suppose was given by the Greeks, who were then the fashionable scientists; since Greece always held it in such high esteem.

(3) *Page* 27. The preeminence that Leonardo gives to sight over hearing leads him to argue that Music is the younger sister of Painting, a point he noted in the chapter title but then forgot to repeat in the body of the text. The argument regarding the speed with which the delight of Music flees is most just, and the apostrophe <note>A rhetorical address to a personified object or absent person.</note> with which he turns to praise the duration that the art of Painting gives to fleeting human beauties is full of wit and eloquence.

(4) *Page* 31. One must grant to our Writer—as a man who was excellent in Music, and who through it, perhaps even more than through Painting, found the favor of the great—the superiority that he grants to Music even over Poetry. We know, however, that he was also a poet, and that he sang extemporaneously; hence his name can be numbered among the celebrated improvisers. But we also know that the grace of his voice and the harmony of his instrument <note>Leonardo was famous for playing a silver lyre he fashioned himself in the shape of a horse's skull.</note> cooperated greatly in his successful poetic encounters. That single sonnet of his preserved for us by Lomazzo <note>Giovan Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592), an artist and writer who preserved fragments of Leonardo's thought.</note> can be called more a piece of rhymed Philosophy than a piece of Poetry. His genius truly does not seem to have been made for great progress in Poetry. The slowness of scrupulous geometric demonstrations and the flights of fantasy can ill be combined together. Perhaps in a moment when his soul opened to joy, he was capable of some graceful improvised song; but among his writings, we find no sketch of any rhymes.

(5) *Page* 33. One will not find total exactness of terms in this writing of Leonardo. Above, he complained that Painting was not counted among the liberal arts; now he laments that it has not been honored as a science. Most wise, however, is that reflection he makes on the difficulty of Painting, which leaves no room for distraction in other studies. Unfortunately, this distraction deprived us of many beautiful works of which Leonardo could have been the author; for while giving preference to Painting over every science, he nevertheless occupied himself for so much time with the sciences that he left little for the use of the brush.
