<meta>This page continues the editor's critical commentary on Leonardo da Vinci's treatise, transitioning from his views on music and poetry to his controversial critique of sculpture and the editor's own methodology in presenting Leonardo's dense technical prose.</meta>

It must be observed that as learned as he was in providing the precepts of art, he wrote too much for the learned, and did not incline himself enough toward the artists, who, even by his own admission, do not make a profession of letters <note>Meaning they were not formally educated in the humanities or classical languages.</note>. In the publication of this codex, my first thought was to make Leonardo’s work more intelligible to artists by means of notes, and to extract, so to speak, from his geometric demonstrations and scientific reflections the bare and simple precept or warning they contain; since not all artists are capable of following such great learning, and they might therefore profit from the precept without examining its proofs. Mr. Manzi, however, made me reflect that there was no place to do this in simple notes to a text that was being given in its entirety, and that my project could instead provide the subject for a small book which, containing an extract of Vinci’s maxims, might succeed through a shorter reading and with greater ease in instilling the precepts into students of drawing. The correctness of Mr. Manzi’s reflection made me turn from my purpose, and perhaps one day I will attempt to carry out, if my strengths permit, the useful work he suggested to me.

(6) *Page 34.* Vinci begins to explain his ill-humor against Sculpture, of which he speaks with such disfavor that it seems ill-suited to a man who also practiced it. He tortures his intellect to highlight everything that can be said against it, going so far as to wish to diminish its value because of the sweat and toil it demands of its practitioner; concluding then in the following chapter that the sculptor carries out his works with greater physical labor, while the painter does so with greater mental labor. He regards the sculptor only from the side of mechanical execution, even making a crime of the dust that soils him, and reduces him almost to being an ordinary copyist who, by force of measurements, can do everything and can copy the beauty and greatness of nature. Leonardo wrote this way, but he likely had some unknown purpose in doing so. Perhaps it is not impossible that he declaimed so much against Sculpture out of the resentment he felt toward Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), Leonardo's younger contemporary and fierce rival.</note>, who had made himself so famous for his marbles; while Vinci, with the labors and studies of so many years, had barely managed to complete that horse <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive bronze monument intended for Francesco Sforza, which never progressed beyond a clay model.</note>, which remained as a model and was later miserably destroyed. By diminishing the value of the art, he consequently diminished that of his rival artist.

The word *posati* <note>original: "posati" - meaning "settled" or "placed."</note> is used by Vinci to express postures,

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo Buonarroti, Sculpture vs. Painting, artistic rivalry, Mr. Manzi, art education, Sforza Horse, Paragone</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the editor's critical commentary on Leonardo da Vinci's "Treatise on Painting," specifically addressing Leonardo's arguments against sculpture and the editor's observations on the Della Robbia family's glazed terracotta techniques.</meta>

and the tranquil poses in which the figure rests in a certain way, and he therefore places them in opposition to movements. This word <note>Referring to a specific technical term for "repose" or "stillness" used by Leonardo.</note> was not known to Baldinucci <note>Filippo Baldinucci (1624–1697), an influential Florentine art historian and author of a major biographical dictionary of artists.</note>, and it is not reported in his Dictionary.

(7) *Page* 37. The invention by Luca della Robbia <note>A 15th-century Florentine sculptor famous for developing durable tin-glazed terracotta.</note> of executing figures in terracotta, which then, with the glaze of majolica <term>majolica: a type of Italian tin-glazed pottery</term>, appear to be actual marble, was very praiseworthy. However, his having added color to these types of sculptures did not make them absolutely more beautiful, and perhaps in the opinion of many, it diminished their merit. The colors applied with the fire-glaze proper to majolica take on something crude and unharmonious; and when Luca made paintings on a flat surface of terracotta, it cannot be denied that they possessed a value that was not absolute, but relative to the difficulty and novelty of the art. This love of novelty perhaps induced Vinci to so highly praise such an invention of coloring on clay; and perhaps also the finding of one more weapon against Sculpture made him speak very favorably of a thing that is quite far from his own style of painting, which is most correct and highly finished. In Rome, the sculpture of the Della Robbia family is almost unknown, and only in the old small palace of Innocent VIII <note>The Belvedere at the Vatican.</note> did there exist two festoons of fruit in relief and color, which adorned the coat of arms of the said Pontiff above a door. That Pope likely had them brought from Florence; since the elder Luca was never in Rome, and only in the time of Leo <note>Pope Leo X (Giovanni de' Medici).</note> did another Luca, nephew of the first, come to Rome, and this nephew worked on the floors in the rooms of Raphael. The festoons of which I speak were taken away when, under the Pontificate of Clement XIV, the small palace of Innocent VIII was converted into a Museum. Whether they still exist in some Vatican warehouse is unknown to me.

In Viterbo, above the three doors of the famous church of the Quercia <note>The Sanctuary of Santa Maria della Quercia.</note>, one sees relief figures of glazed terracotta that absolutely belong to Luca or his brothers; and having been exposed for three centuries to the inclemency of the seasons in an open countryside, they remain intact, as if they had left the hand of the artist yesterday. I do not know why this beautiful way of working has been abandoned. It would be more stable and durable than stucco, and would resist rain and frost much better than it.

--- Page 549 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor's commentary on Leonardo da Vinci’s views on sculpture, specifically contrasting Leonardo’s theories with the practices of Ghiberti and the classical ancients, before moving on to Leonardo's "Treatise on Shadows" and his educational philosophy.</meta>

must be employed in it. It cannot be denied that the moderns <note>The "moderns" here refers to Renaissance artists of the 15th and 16th centuries.</note> have attempted to overcome many difficulties in this manner of sculpting that the ancients did not address; I will not decide, however, if they did so with complete success. The ancients constantly avoided everything that forced the chisel to alter the truth, and they took, I shall say, an ideal middle path between the real imitation of relief and the perspective of it. For this reason, one rarely encounters heads facing forward in ancient bas-reliefs <term>bas-relief: a sculpture with a slight projection from the background</term>, and if they are encountered, they are then in full relief. In the backgrounds, to show the distance of the figures behind, they used to place them at a smaller size on different planes; but they did not take care to modify the relief to suggest distance, nor to account for the intermediate planes. Leonardo, who had before his eyes the stupendous bas-reliefs of Ghiberti <note>Lorenzo Ghiberti (1378–1455), famous for the "Gates of Paradise" on the Florence Baptistery.</note>, is quite right to highlight the difficulties of perspective encountered in this genre of sculpture. And indeed, there is no difficulty of art that Ghiberti did not courageously confront in the work of the doors of San Giovanni, and often with excellent results.

(9) *Page* 49. Regarding the shadows of bodies, in addition to what had already been published by Leonardo, we have in this manuscript a new and precious Treatise, in which—despite the fact that many propositions, due to their geometric demonstrations, will not be within the reach of some artists who are skilled in art but not very scientific—there are nevertheless, in the main, such clear and practical precepts that they make it precious and useful. The fact that Vinci wrote about this repeatedly proves how much importance he placed on such a study.

(10) *Page* 50. In pointing out to young people the path by which to advance in art, Leonardo does not speak at all of the study of ancient works. It is not, therefore, that he wants the youth not to seek the choice of the beautiful and to servilely imitate nature. He wants them to study proportions, which he calls *measures*, and then to learn from a good Master how to accustom oneself to "good limbs" <note>Leonardo's term for well-proportioned anatomical parts.</note>. What else does this mean but to seek beauty? We know from history that the brave Tuscan artists of the golden age of art studied the ancient marbles collected by the Magnificent Lorenzo de' Medici. It seems that Vinci did not approach such monuments. This man always recognizes nature as his teacher, and this principle bound him to the imitation of nature alone.

(11) *Page* 52. This precept of solitude in study may not...

<meta>This page continues the editor's commentary on Leonardo da Vinci’s "Treatise on Painting," specifically critiquing Leonardo's strict views on artistic solitude and the necessity of specializing in specific genres of art.</meta>

must be adaptable to everyone, and the dilemma with which Leonardo wishes to conclude—that company is either harmful or useless—is not always true. The fine Arts have such a large mechanical component of execution that the spirit can very well be delightfully entertained by pleasant conversation while the hand performs its work. The greatest among modern artists <note>Likely a reference to Antonio Canova or another contemporary of the editor, though some might interpret this as Michelangelo.</note> desires the labor of his chisel to be accompanied by the reading of the best authors, and finds in this a relief that, without distracting him from the work, gently comforts him.

(12) Page 52. Da Vinci speaks in this passage as if all artists possessed that sublimity of intellect capable of embracing all things, with which he himself was endowed. Unfortunately, art is so great and difficult that some, who do not have enough genius to succeed in every part of it, are very much to be esteemed if they dedicate themselves to one area and seek to become excellent in that. If Claude Lorrain <note>Claude Lorrain (c. 1600–1682), a famous French Baroque landscape painter.</note> had wanted to achieve excellence in figures, to which his talent was poorly suited, we would easily be deprived of the most graceful imitator of nature in rural beauties. How many similar examples does the history of art not give us?

(13) Page 56. It seems that it can almost be deduced from what Leonardo says in this passage that he wrote these things in France between 1515 and 1519; since, speaking of Botticelli <note>original: "Botticella"</note>, it seems that he was no longer living, as he uses the words *said* and *did* for him. Now, Botticelli died in 1515; therefore, these things must have been written after that time. And indeed, we know that Leonardo produced almost nothing in France with the brush; thus it is likely that he employed himself in writing about his favorite art.

(14) Page 58. In this place, Da Vinci uses the word *matter* <note>original: "materia"</note> to mean materiality or rather ignorance, and shrewdly points out to the painter that his errors last as long as the work itself, and that the honor acquired by the beauties of a work is worth much more than the money that can be acquired through carelessness and negligence.

(15) Page 67. He returns to urging professors not to let themselves be seduced by the hope of gain, and particularly urges them not to work in a "manner" <term>maniera: a stylized or artificial way of painting that relies on a set "formula" rather than observing nature</term>; but always to consult the truth in nature. This precept can never be recommended enough to young people, and particularly to those who are endowed with greater talent; because trust—

--- Page 551 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor's commentary on Leonardo da Vinci’s "Treatise on Painting," moving from a discussion of artistic specialization to the dangers of "mannerism" and the importance of studying nature over imitation.</meta>

settling into that, and listening too much to the praise that their inventions encounter, they abandon themselves to working from imagination and memory, and end up regressing instead of advancing in art. In my time, I have seen students who promised immense progress run aground because they gave themselves up as prey to <term>manner<note>The term "maniera" or mannerism refers to a style where an artist imitates the stylistic quirks of other artists or their own habits rather than observing nature directly.</note></term>.

(16) Page 69. This teaching of Leonardo should be equally present to the students and the masters of art; so that the former do not lose sight of the original beauties of nature, and the latter do not demand that their pupils follow only in their footsteps. Golden was the saying of Michelangelo, *that he who walks behind others never passes ahead*.

(17) Page 72. Contained in this chapter is one of the most useful precepts for students, which is not to begin studying separate parts before having well-composed and drawn the entire figure. This precept (a Master told me) is much more necessary now, when with the convenience of imitating ancient fragments, young people easily limit themselves to drawing and imitating from those the separate parts appropriate to their needs, without reflecting well on the whole of their figure. Hence it often happens that one recognizes a servile imitation of detached parts without them corresponding to the whole. Also, the symmetrical arrangement of figures is mentioned here by Leonardo, and the few teachings he gives on this subject are drawn from exact observations of nature, and not from arbitrary whims of <term>counterpositions<note>original: "contraposizioni." In art, this refers to the balanced arrangement of opposing figures or elements (contrapposto).</note></term>.

(18) Page 73. It is easier to point out with Da Vinci the defect of which he speaks than to hope for a total correction in artists. Overcoming the inclination toward which our soul tends is almost impossible, especially in things that are performed with a certain enthusiasm, which is precisely necessary in the fine arts. Therefore, the artist must stay on guard as much as he can against himself. It is also true that the painter not only paints his own soul in his works, but even his own figure. <note>Leonardo famously noted that painters often unconsciously give their figures their own physical characteristics.</note>

(19) Page 83. In writing these things, Leonardo had in mind the style that was then familiar in art, of introducing different episodes of a story into a single painting. The author turns against the clumsiness of some who placed figures one above the other, and teaches that by using a single point, they must be placed in the distance with the proper de—

In later times, this warning has become unnecessary, since the method of uniting multiple events within the same painting has been distanced from Painting; a style almost always contrary to the accuracy of imitation and to the beautiful illusion that it ought to produce. <note>The commentator refers to the "continuous narrative" style common in Medieval and early Renaissance art, where the same character appears multiple times in one frame to show a sequence of events.</note>

(20) Page 85. Not only in this place, but in others as well, the reader will observe that Leonardo goes about stinging those who abuse their anatomical knowledge, and surely in this he has in his sights his rival Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), Leonardo's younger contemporary and fierce rival.</note>, who made such a display of anatomy.

(21) Page 92. This description of the storm, and even more so the following one of the battle, show how much Leonardo was worth in eloquence, and with what energy and truth he knew how to express his ideas by adapting the most robust epithets, and not omitting any of the most important circumstances for the subject. To be useful to artists, he enters into the most minute details, but he does so with such skill that his description of the battle is truly a painting that represents it. In my belief, if this man had one day methodically ordered his work and brought these sketches of his to completion, we would have had a work that, even from the perspective of style, would have been adorned with the greatest merits.

(22) Page 110. A most beautiful warning is that of our Author, who advises examining the movements of the body in the act when they have their natural energy through the impetus of the passions, and ensuring that this is not diminished or cooled in the slightest. It is also unfortunately true that men taken as models, being obliged to express a passion that they do not actually feel at that moment, express it with coldness.

(23) Page 124. Vinci’s observations on colors are the consequence of his very long experiments, in which, however, he occupied himself too much; and with his natural uncertainty, he never arrived at secure methods, and always in search of new things, he spoiled his works through such attempts. The negligence in the preparation of colors by Italian painters has deprived us of a great part of the most beautiful products of art; therefore, this part is not to be neglected, although one should not over-sophisticate it as much as Leonardo. A useful book on the colors used in painting has been published in Rome by Mr. Lorenzo Marcucci, where with good reasoning—

(24) *Page* 150. It seems to me that the *Author's* idea is that while the Painter should avoid every monstrosity in his figures, he should nevertheless aim to vary them in the same way that nature itself is varied, and not adopt such a precise quality of structure and form as immutable that it makes one and the other totally similar. This observation was necessary in the times of *Leonardo*, in which painters imitated nature with a certain timidity that led them to a sort of uniformity in their works. Would to Heaven that after many years, this had not been succeeded by a courage that was little restrained. <note>The commentator suggests that while Leonardo's peers were too stiff, later artists became too bold or exaggerated in their style.</note>

(25) *Page* 157. At first glance, this warning seems almost useless, containing something that everyone understands on their own; and yet, how many artists fail against it! While they employ all their study to achieve expression in the faces <note>original: "vulti"</note> of their figures, they do not remember that all parts of the body must correspond to it, especially when the body is set in motion by violent passion.

(26) *Page* 163. The *Author* inculcates the study of anatomy, and in particular the knowing by heart the variety of the parts and the action of the muscles. The reason he points out for this necessity is the scarcity of good and well-proportioned nudes that can serve as examples. Those who have denied that *Leonardo* had ideal beauty in mind—that is, the selection of parts—should observe that even in this precept he includes nothing else but the duty to supplement those which nature does not present as such with already fixed ideas of beautiful muscles. <note>This defends Leonardo against the charge of being a mere "naturalist," arguing he sought to improve upon nature's flaws through mental ideals.</note>

(27) *Page* 170. Without making a precise distinction between the different characters that can be given to various figures, the *Author* gives excellent precepts for obtaining their gracefulness by means of hiding the muscles and making them appear with sweetness. His purpose was never to make mention of ancient marbles, which give us sublime examples of every diversity of figures. *Leonardo* inspires artists to give movement to the heads, because in truth, the excessive coldness of movements was the defect of the painters who had preceded him.

(28) *Page* 178. Some will suspect that in this chapter he intended to sting *Buonarroti* <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti</note> for the display of anatomy that he made.

(29) *Page* 192. All the reflections that *Vinci* makes upon the art that expresses living things without life are very judicious; and the insinua—

The recommendation to the painter regarding the continuous observation of the movements of figures in the various expressions of the passions can never be repeated enough. All the more so, because in this, he is asked for something from which he can profit at every moment, even in the midst of recreation and fun. Truly, the expression in the actions of the mute is accompanied by a certain caricature <note>The term "caricatura" here refers to an exaggeration or heightening of features to convey meaning without speech.</note> that distinguishes them; hence, from movements alone, we recognize that the speaker does not have the use of speech. Our Author naturally knew this very well; but experience dictated to him that an expression, even if exaggerated when transferred to the canvas, naturally moderates and cools down, and does not maintain itself as it was seen in nature; therefore, from the caricature, it returns to its proper state.

(30) *Page 212.* This precept is given by Leonardo because, after perspective had been put so much in fashion by Paolo Uccello <note>A 15th-century pioneer of linear perspective.</note>, and the degradation of colors in the distance <term>atmospheric perspective: the way colors become paler and bluer as they recede</term> being ignored in order to make them recede, in many paintings the buildings appeared attached to the figures, and the inconveniences noted here by the Author arose.

(31) *Page 213.* All the reflections that Leonardo makes in this place on the loss of outlines in the backgrounds and in the figures are most useful. It seems, however, to result from them that if he had a tendency toward a defect in his sight, he might have tended toward being nearsighted.

(32) *Page 218.* The division he assigns here to his works on Painting clearly demonstrates that the things he wrote about it are nothing but thoughts and ideas that he went about collecting and throwing onto paper, in order to then organize them in his own time. One recognizes in these thoughts that sometimes while he was writing on one subject, another came to his mind, and so as not to lose the idea, he noted it down, not worrying about the unsuitable location; because he intended to reduce his work to methodical separations later on.

(33) *Page 248.* This precept on the choice of light was not followed in Italy by Caravaggio, by Guercino, and by others of their imitators, who sought by force of shadow and small lights to obtain relief. Rembrandt obtained a wonderful effect of chiaroscuro <term>chiaroscuro: the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting</term> by using little light; but a few examples do not destroy the correct precept of the Author.

(34) *Page 255.* The Author returns to the same idea that we already pointed out in note 32 regarding the distribution of the work, and gives new proof of what was asserted therein.

(35) said *Page*. Here is a thought on <term>Sculpture</term>—or rather, on the mechanical part of it—which falls from his pen in the midst of two ideas, one theoretical and the other practical, regarding <term>Painting</term>.

(36) *Page* 256. It is very difficult to understand what method of painting he intends to teach here; but it seems it must refer to that <term>glazed</term> <note>original: "invetriato"</note> painting, which was mentioned when he cited della Robbia <note>Luca della Robbia was famous for his glazed terra-cotta sculptures.</note>.

(37) This is the only place in which Leonardo proposes the imitation of the Greeks and Romans <note>original: "Greci e Latini"</note>, and in comparison to so many other more essential parts of art, he proposes it in a matter that is not of the highest gravity; he then limits the imitation of the <term>drapery</term> <note>original: "panneggiamenti"</note> of the ancients only to making the limbs appear beneath the cloth agitated by the wind. It is also to be noted that he proposes the Greeks and the Romans equally as models.

(38) *Page* 269. Da Vinci knew how much modern dress degrades the nobility of a figure, and he wants the arts of design to preserve the memory of it only in sepulchral monuments, almost as a testimony to the follies of men in their fashions. Yet, who would believe it, this warning of our Author is now forgotten; it is forgotten in order to imitate the costumes and dress not of our own times—which one might believe he would wish to see painted *in the style of the age in which it is painted* <note>original Latin: "aere dato qui pingitur"</note>—but to push oneself back several centuries and imitate the distortion of times in which, unfortunately, the strange and forced fashions of men's and women's clothing acted as an obstacle to the advancement of art.

(39) *Page* 275. Anton Raphael Mengs <note>A famous 18th-century German Neoclassical painter.</note>, whose works on Painting would have produced even greater utility if they had been published exactly as he had written them without pretending to put them into order and rules; Raphael Mengs had put on paper many observations on <term>shadow</term> and <term>light</term>, and particularly on the distribution of greater or lesser shadows in the different <term>planes</term> represented in a narrative scene <note>original: "storia"</note>. What became of this writing, I do not know; I can only say that I heard it read in the year 1785 by his son Alberico, who is no longer among the living.

(40) *Page* 281. Leonardo's definitions are so exact and evident that a small extract could easily be drawn from this Treatise that would impress upon students the beautiful precepts scattered here, which are sometimes demonstrated with excessive subtlety.

(41) *Page* 308. The Author doubles his observations and precepts on the greater and lesser darkness of shadows and the vividness of lights.

derived from the contrast of nearby lights and shadows, so that the artist does not allow himself to be deceived by general rules, and observes the particular exception that must be applied to them.

(42) *Page 315.* I believe that by calling <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.</note> and <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scorti"; the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has.</note> the "excellence of the science" here, he intends it in relation to the difficulties that these parts carry with them, and the merit acquired by one who manages to master them; otherwise, it might seem to some that the excellence of art should be fixed upon more noble objects.

(43) *Page 350.* Here is another book that he meditated on making, and which certainly would have required the most subtle research, dealing with a subject (which he calls a "discourse") that is very difficult.

(44) *Page 354.* Here too, regarding a very important subject, he refers back to what he intended to write later.

(45) *Page 361.* This practical precept given by Leonardo will seem too ordinary to some; and yet, if one reflects well upon it, it will be seen that it can be very useful to the artist while he works.

(46) *Page 371.* It seems that in this place he speaks to himself as if distracted by a thought: that the pen, while inspiring the theories of art, cannot reach where the painter reaches with his brushes. This sudden speaking to himself is another proof that he wrote down whatever came into his imagination, intending to later revise and arrange his writings.

(47) *Page 381.* It should be noted that when Leonardo speaks of things that do not belong entirely to art, and contemplates nature by investigating her secrets, he changes his language, and his style becomes more eloquent, copious, and singularly rich in well-adapted epithets.

(48) *Page 383.* Here is another place where he makes a display of eloquence, and seems in a certain way to want to ignite the painter by means of a lively phrasing, so that he might execute that selection which he suggests.

(49) *Page 391.* In this book, while the Author often speaks as a <term>naturalist</term> <note>A student of natural history or the physical world.</note> and makes observations on plants that do not belong to Painting, he does not fail to insert precepts and observations on lights, distances, the various tints of plants, and many other things that can be extremely useful to painters of landscapes. That <term>cartoon</term> <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco or painting.</note> of Adam and Eve of which Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari, the 16th-century biographer of Italian artists.</note> spoke with such praise, particularly for the trees painted in it, demonstrates how much love he had for this genre of painting.

--- Page 557 ---
<meta>Continuing the numbered commentary on Leonardo da Vinci’s "Treatise on Painting," specifically focusing on Leonardo's botanical observations, the balance between rules and natural intuition, and his alleged invention of optical devices.</meta>

<page-num>509</page-num>

(50) *Page 397.* The author himself confesses that he expands into research that is not useful to the painter, but he cannot restrain himself from recording things that he had studied attentively since his youth. Since that <term>cartoon</term> <note>original: "cartone"; a full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco or painting.</note> of which I spoke above was one of his youthful works, and since **Vasari** <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists.</note> says it was painted with such naturalism, one recognizes that the most minute observations of herbs and trees were observed within it. I remember that the **Abbot Correa**, a learned Portuguese naturalist, used to complain about certain landscape painters who, being entirely ignorant of natural history, would join together cliffs and layers of soil that could not be so arranged in nature, and would cover them with herbs and plants that were not suited to them.

(51) *Page 409.* I am persuaded that these exact divisions for understanding the effect that the branching of trees produces to the eye at different distances will be extremely useful to a landscape painter in forming—so to speak—his countryside while observing nature. After the study of nature, the truth of imitation must remain impressed upon his mind: for if at every step he wished to go on ruminating over the rules, he would be like that writer who consults the grammar and the <term>dictionary</term> <note>original: "calepino"; named after Ambrogio Calepino, this term was commonly used to refer to a large Latin dictionary or reference book.</note> at every single word.

(52) *Page 438.* It almost seems that in this place he wishes to teach the method of painting and imitating the leaves of trees when a branch, or the entire tree, must be painted in the foreground of the picture, so that every part is rendered imitable as if nearby and seen directly before the eye. Otherwise, the green of the leaves would be poorly copied by imitating the green of a leaf held close to the eye, when we know—and he himself has asserted above—that the green of trees changes according to the different ways in which they receive the light, and according to the distances from which they are seen. It surprises me that our Author has not given methods for studying from life, and for the choice of those beautiful "accidents" <note>In art theory, "accidents" refer to fleeting effects of light, shadow, or atmosphere.</note> of which nature is so rich.

If one is to lend faith to the tradition that exists among artists, it seems that the <term>camera obscura</term> <note>original: "camere ottiche"; literally "optical chambers," devices that project an image of surroundings onto a screen, used as a drawing aid.</note> and the other machines for copying nature exactly ought to be attributed to **Leonardo**.

# APPROVAL.

It was reserved for the most illustrious Mr. Guglielmo Manzi <note>A noted librarian and scholar (1784–1821) who discovered the more complete Vatican manuscript of Leonardo's treatise.</note> to enrich Roman Typography by obtaining from the distinguished Mr. de Romanis a clean and accurate edition of Vinci's *Treatise on Painting*. It was likewise reserved for this sagacious and indefatigable investigator of the unpublished works of the most brilliant writers of our language <note>original: "favella"; literally "speech" or "tongue," referring here to the Italian literary tradition.</note> the beautiful fate of publishing the aforementioned work of the immortal Leonardo in its entirety, exactly as he wrote it. Such a labor was well-suited to two celebrated members of our Academy of Archaeology; and a work so foundational for the fine arts should not have been published, and learnedly illustrated, except by two archaeologists. Lovers of Painting will have the satisfaction of being able to provide themselves at will with an edition of Vinci that not only approaches the merit of the Parisian edition <note>Referring to the 1651 edition published in Paris by Du Fresne, which was the standard but incomplete version for over 150 years.</note>, but far surpasses it in the purity and integrity of the text, in its correction, and in its wise and erudite illustrations. With the greatest pleasure, I have read—by order of the Most Reverend Father Master of the Sacred Palace—this work with its new and copious additions, which well deserved to see the light of day before now for the great profit of the lovers and practitioners of the Fine Arts. If our forefathers were grateful for the zeal of Rafaelle Du-Fresne for having delivered them from the danger of seeing such a celebrated work lost, what thanks do we not owe to Mr. Manzi, who has given us this completed *Treatise*, which so honors the Italian Language and is so fit to promote and perfect good taste in the arts of design.

->Minerva <note>Likely referring to the location of the office or the press near the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome.</note> June 25, 1817.<-

->Friar **Giuseppe Vincenzo Airenti** of the Order of Preachers, Casanate Theologian<-
->and Honorary Librarian of the University of Genoa, etc.<-

From the Roman College, this 15th day of July, 1817.

->**Filippo Aurelio Visconti**<-
->*Examiner of the Sacred Palace, and President of the Roman Academy of Archaeology.*<-

***

# APPROVAL.

I have read, by order of the Most Reverend Father Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, the *Treatise on Painting* by Leonardo da Vinci, reduced to its true integrity by the care and diligence of the most illustrious Mr. Guglielmo Manzi, and I have found nothing in it contrary to the Catholic Faith or good morals; on the contrary, I have found it most useful for the progress of the Fine Arts, and worthy of being given to the public.

From the Convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, this 20th day of July, 1817.

->**Friar Tommaso Domenico Piazza**<-
->*of the Order of Preachers, Master of Sacred Theology, and Provincial of the Roman Province.*<-

***

->**LET IT BE PRINTED,**<-
If it so pleases the Most Reverend Father Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace.
->**C. Cuccovilla, Vicegerent.**<-

***

->**LET IT BE PRINTED,**<-
->**Friar Filippo Anfossi, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace.**<-
